m: to fill someone or something deeply with a feeling, quality, or idea
x: Her grandmother's stories imbued the old house with a warmth that no renovation could ever replace.
A good manager can imbue even a tired, cynical team with a fresh sense of purpose.
The professor's lectures were imbued with a genuine love of mathematics that rubbed off on his students.
The new constitution was meant to imbue citizens with a sense of shared national identity.
Growing up in Dhaka during the monsoon imbued him with a lifelong fondness for the smell of rain.
tc: Rather than leaving the poem flat and lifeless, the translator managed to ______ it with the same passion as the original.
'Rather than leaving the poem flat and lifeless' signals the opposite idea: filling it with feeling.
se: Great teachers try to ______ their students with a love of learning that lasts long after graduation.
infuse
Both 'imbue' and 'infuse' mean to fill someone with a quality, and both work with 'with'.

m: perfectly clean and tidy, or completely free from flaws and mistakes
x: Despite having three young children, they somehow keep their living room immaculate.
The auditors found her accounts immaculate, without a single figure out of place.
His thesis was submitted in immaculate condition, with every reference formatted exactly as the department required.
The surgeon's immaculate record over twenty years made the hospital's sudden lawsuit all the more surprising.
She turned up for the interview in an immaculate white shirt, determined to make a good first impression.
tc: Although the rest of the house was cluttered and dusty, the kitchen was ______, with every surface gleaming.
'Although' contrasts the kitchen with 'cluttered and dusty', and 'every surface gleaming' confirms it was perfectly clean.
se: The museum keeps its vintage cars in ______ condition, polishing them every single week.
pristine
Both 'immaculate' and 'pristine' describe something kept perfectly clean and unspoiled.

m: to shut someone in or confine them, as if behind walls
x: After the scandal, the writer immured himself in his country house and refused all visitors.
Some junior analysts feel immured in their cubicles, rarely seeing daylight during the busy season.
Historians describe how some medieval nuns chose to be immured in small cells attached to their churches.
For years, political prisoners were immured in the fortress without trial or any contact with their families.
Grief immured her in silence, and even her closest friends struggled to reach her.
tc: Determined to finish the novel before his deadline, the author decided to ______ himself in his study, seeing no one for weeks.
'Seeing no one for weeks' restates the idea of shutting oneself away.
se: The tyrant's plan was to ______ his rivals in a remote prison where no one could reach them.
confine
Both 'immure' and 'confine' mean to shut someone in, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: to pass on information, knowledge, or a quality to someone or something
x: My father imparted one simple lesson to all of us: never borrow money you cannot repay.
Senior engineers are expected to impart their technical know-how to new hires during the first six months.
A good tutor does more than impart facts; she teaches students how to think for themselves.
A pinch of saffron imparts a rich golden color and a delicate aroma to the rice.
Before she moved abroad, my best friend imparted one last piece of advice about trusting my instincts.
tc: The old craftsman was eager to ______ his skills before retiring, so he spent his final years training apprentices.
Spending years 'training apprentices' shows he wanted to pass on his skills.
se: Teachers should not merely ______ information; they should also encourage students to question it.
convey
Both 'impart' and 'convey' mean to pass information on to others.

m: to formally charge a public official with serious wrongdoing while in office
x: Over dinner, my uncle insisted that any leader who lies under oath deserves to be impeached.
Union members moved to impeach their own president after he secretly signed a deal with management.
In our civics class, we learned that a judge can be impeached only for serious misconduct, not for unpopular rulings.
The legislature voted to impeach the governor after evidence of bribery came to light.
She felt deeply betrayed when members of her own party joined the vote to impeach her.
tc: Lawmakers argued that the judge's acceptance of bribes was serious enough to ______ him and remove him from the bench.
The bribery and the goal to 'remove him from the bench' point to formally charging an official with misconduct.
se: The House voted to ______ the president, sending the case to the Senate for trial.
indict
In this context both words mean to formally charge an official so that a trial can follow.

m: to drive, push, or force someone to do something
x: Hunger finally impelled me to leave my desk and walk down to the canteen.
A sense of duty impelled her to report the accounting errors, even though it might cost her the promotion.
Curiosity about how stars form impelled him to switch from engineering to astrophysics.
Rising food prices impelled thousands of people to take to the streets in protest.
What impels someone to forgive a friend who has betrayed them so completely?
tc: It was not ambition but a deep sense of injustice that seemed to ______ her to spend her life defending the poor.
The sentence names the force behind her choice, so the blank must mean to drive or push her.
se: Fear of failure can ______ students to work harder than they otherwise would.
drive
Both 'impel' and 'drive' mean to push someone to act, giving the same meaning.

m: not feeling or showing any regret for having done wrong
x: Even after breaking his mother's favorite vase, the impenitent toddler simply grinned and ran off.
The manager remained impenitent about the layoffs, insisting they had saved the company.
Historians portray the general as impenitent to the end, never admitting that the massacres had happened.
The judge noted that the defendant appeared entirely impenitent and imposed the maximum sentence.
She could forgive the lie, but not his impenitent shrug when she confronted him about it.
tc: Far from apologizing for his offensive remarks, the comedian was utterly ______, repeating them at his next show.
'Far from apologizing' and repeating the remarks show he felt no regret at all.
se: The court gave the thief a harsh sentence because he was ______ and showed no sign of regret.
unrepentant
Both 'impenitent' and 'unrepentant' mean feeling no regret for wrongdoing.

m: rude and disrespectful, especially toward someone older or more senior
x: In many Bangladeshi families, it is considered impertinent to interrupt your elders while they are speaking.
The intern asked the CEO an impertinent question about his salary in front of the whole team.
When a student made an impertinent remark about her accent, the lecturer calmly ignored it.
Reporters were criticized for asking impertinent questions of the grieving family at the funeral.
Forgive me if this sounds impertinent, but are you sure he really loves you?
c: at the risk of sounding impertinent
tc: The headmaster punished the boy for his ______ reply, which mocked the teacher in front of the whole class.
A reply that 'mocked the teacher' is rude and disrespectful.
se: My grandmother thought it ______ of children to call adults by their first names.
disrespectful
Both 'impertinent' and 'disrespectful' describe behavior that lacks proper respect for elders.

m: a force or motivation that drives something forward or makes it happen
x: A looming exam was all the impetus I needed to finally organize my notes.
The new contract gave fresh impetus to the stalled software project.
Her early research provided the impetus for a whole new field of study.
Devastating floods became the impetus for major investment in the city's drainage system.
His father's illness was the impetus behind his decision to become a doctor.
tc: The reforms had stalled for years, but the scandal finally provided the ______ needed to push them through parliament.
'Had stalled' contrasted with 'push them through' shows the scandal supplied the driving force.
se: The government hoped the tax break would provide the ______ for small businesses to expand.
stimulus
Both 'impetus' and 'stimulus' mean something that encourages activity or growth.

m: lack of respect for God, religion, or things regarded as sacred
x: Some villagers regarded the plan to cut down the ancient temple tree as an act of impiety.
His colleagues joked that skipping the founder's annual memorial lecture was a form of corporate impiety.
Students of philosophy learn that Socrates was tried in Athens for impiety and for corrupting the young.
The playwright was accused of impiety after his comedy poked fun at a revered religious festival.
She felt a pang of guilt at her own impiety when she giggled during the solemn prayer.
tc: Whereas his father was known for deep devotion, the son was notorious for his ______, openly mocking religious rituals.
'Whereas' contrasts the blank with 'devotion', and 'mocking religious rituals' confirms a lack of reverence.
se: In earlier centuries, writers who questioned church doctrine were often punished for ______.
irreverence
Both 'impiety' and 'irreverence' mean a lack of respect for religion.

m: unwise and likely to cause trouble, especially in a social or political situation
x: It would be impolitic to mention your pay rise at a family dinner where your cousin has just lost his job.
Criticizing the client's design in the very first meeting was an impolitic move that cost us the contract.
The graduate student realized it was impolitic to question her supervisor's data at a public seminar.
The minister's impolitic remarks about farmers sparked protests across the country.
Telling her new boyfriend that she preferred his brother was, to say the least, impolitic.
tc: Although his criticism of the board was accurate, it was ______ to voice it just before the vote on his promotion.
'Although ... accurate' signals that the problem was not truth but poor judgment about timing.
se: The ambassador decided it would be ______ to raise the border dispute during the celebratory dinner.
injudicious
Both 'impolitic' and 'injudicious' mean showing poor judgment in a delicate situation.

m: impossible to capture, break into, or defeat
x: Our neighbor has installed so many locks that his front door now seems impregnable.
The company's market position looked impregnable until a small startup launched a cheaper product.
Medieval engineers designed the castle walls to be impregnable to any siege.
With a two-thirds majority, the ruling party appears politically impregnable for now.
After the divorce, she built an impregnable wall around her heart.
tc: Attackers had besieged the fortress for months, yet its walls remained ______, without a single breach.
'Yet' and 'without a single breach' show the walls could not be broken.
se: After winning every election for two decades, the party seemed ______.
unassailable
Both 'impregnable' and 'unassailable' mean impossible to defeat or challenge.

m: not planning or saving for the future; careless with money
x: My improvident cousin spends his whole salary in the first week and borrows for the rest of the month.
Improvident spending on lavish office parties left the firm with no reserves when the recession hit.
As a student, I was improvident with my scholarship money and ended up skipping meals by the end of term.
Economists warned that the government's improvident borrowing would burden future generations.
She loved him dearly but worried that his improvident habits would make married life a constant struggle.
tc: Unlike her ______ brother, who never saved a penny, she put aside part of every paycheck for emergencies.
'Unlike' and 'never saved a penny' show the brother failed to plan for the future.
se: Years of ______ spending left the city unable to repair its crumbling bridges.
wasteful
Both 'improvident' and 'wasteful' describe careless spending without thought for the future.

m: not showing care or good judgment; unwise
x: It would be imprudent to go hiking alone without telling anyone where you are going.
Signing the contract without reading the fine print was an imprudent decision she later regretted.
The professor warned that drawing firm conclusions from such a small sample would be imprudent.
Regulators blamed imprudent lending by banks for the housing crisis.
He soon realized it had been imprudent to confide in a colleague who loved to gossip.
tc: Investing your entire savings in a single untested startup is ______; a wiser approach is to spread the risk.
'A wiser approach' signals that the first choice shows poor judgment.
se: Doctors say it is ______ to stop taking antibiotics as soon as you feel better.
unwise
Both 'imprudent' and 'unwise' mean showing poor judgment.

m: not alive, or showing no sign of life or movement
x: Toddlers often talk to inanimate objects such as teddy bears and toy cars as if they were friends.
Our office printer is the only inanimate object I have ever genuinely hated.
In biology class, we learned to distinguish between living organisms and inanimate matter.
Scientists are still debating how life first emerged from inanimate chemicals on the early Earth.
She lay on the sofa, as inanimate as a rag doll, too heartbroken to move.
tc: Unlike a living cell, which grows and reproduces, a crystal is ______ and cannot respond to its environment.
'Unlike a living cell' signals that the blank means not alive.
se: Young children sometimes give names and personalities to ______ objects like spoons and shoes.
lifeless
Both 'inanimate' and 'lifeless' describe objects that are not alive.

m: glowing with light from great heat; also strikingly brilliant or full of intense emotion
x: We finally replaced all the old incandescent bulbs in the flat with energy-saving LEDs.
Her incandescent presentation won over even the most skeptical investors in the room.
In the physics lab, we heated the wire until it became incandescent and began to glow orange.
Critics praised the young actor's incandescent performance in the new stage production.
He was incandescent with rage when he discovered that his best friend had lied to him.
tc: Though the rest of the cast was forgettable, the lead actress was ______, lighting up every scene she appeared in.
'Though ... forgettable' sets up a contrast, and 'lighting up every scene' points to brilliance.
se: Lava pouring from the volcano was so ______ that it lit up the entire night sky.
glowing
Both 'incandescent' and 'glowing' describe something giving off light because it is extremely hot.

m: to put someone in prison or confine them
x: He joked that working from home during the lockdown felt like being incarcerated in his own flat.
Our law firm provides free legal help to workers who have been wrongly incarcerated.
Criminologists study why some countries incarcerate far more of their citizens than others.
The government was widely criticized for incarcerating journalists without trial during the election campaign.
Her brother was incarcerated for five years, and she visited him every single month.
tc: Reformers argue that it is costly and counterproductive to ______ minor offenders, who are better served by community service.
The contrast with 'community service' shows the blank means to put in prison.
se: The regime used vague security laws to ______ anyone who dared to criticize it.
imprison
Both 'incarcerate' and 'imprison' mean to lock someone up in prison.

m: something that encourages or motivates a person to do something
x: My mother's promise of homemade pitha was all the incentive we needed to finish our homework.
Sales staff receive a quarterly bonus as an incentive to exceed their targets.
Scholarships give talented students from poor families an incentive to stay in school.
Generous tax incentives have encouraged many households to install solar panels.
Knowing his daughter would be proud of him was all the incentive he needed to quit smoking.
tc: Because workers received the same pay no matter how much they produced, they had little ______ to work harder.
'The same pay no matter how much they produced' explains why there was no reason to work harder.
se: Lower interest rates give businesses a strong ______ to invest in new equipment.
motivation
Both 'incentive' and 'motivation' mean a reason that encourages action.

m: the beginning or start of an organization, activity, or project
x: Since its inception, our neighborhood book club has met on the first Sunday of every month.
She has led the project from its inception and knows every detail of the design.
The journal has published groundbreaking work in economics since its inception in 1950.
From the inception of the policy, critics warned that it would hurt small farmers.
Their friendship, from its very inception, was built on long late-night conversations about books.
tc: The charity has grown enormously; at its ______ it had only two volunteers, but today it employs hundreds.
The contrast with 'today' shows the blank refers to the charity's beginning.
se: From the ______, the founders insisted that the company should be environmentally responsible.
outset
'From the inception' and 'from the outset' both mean from the very beginning.

m: to encourage or stir up violent, angry, or unlawful behavior
x: The older boys incited the younger ones to throw stones at the neighbor's windows.
An anonymous email incited panic among staff by claiming the company was about to close.
Historians debate whether the pamphlet actually incited the uprising or merely reflected existing anger.
He was arrested for posting messages that incited violence against a religious minority.
Her jealous friend tried to incite a quarrel between her and her fiancé.
tc: Rather than calming the angry crowd, the speaker's fiery words seemed to ______ it to further violence.
'Rather than calming' signals the opposite: stirring the crowd up.
se: Authorities accused the group of trying to ______ unrest through social media.
foment
Both 'incite' and 'foment' mean to stir up trouble or unrest.

m: unclear, confused, or hard to understand; not logically connected
x: Half asleep, I mumbled an incoherent reply when my roommate asked where the keys were.
The project brief was so incoherent that nobody on the team knew what the client actually wanted.
Examiners penalize essays whose arguments are incoherent, even if the grammar is perfect.
Critics described the government's energy policy as incoherent and contradictory.
She was so overwhelmed with grief that her words came out incoherent through her sobs.
tc: Whereas his first speech was clear and well organized, his second was ______, jumping from topic to topic without any logic.
'Whereas' contrasts the blank with 'clear and well organized', and 'without any logic' confirms the meaning.
se: The witness was so shaken that her account of the accident was almost ______.
unintelligible
Both 'incoherent' and 'unintelligible' mean impossible to follow or understand.

m: the quality of being out of place, inconsistent, or not fitting together
x: There was a comic incongruity in seeing my strict grandfather dancing wildly at the wedding.
Nobody at the meeting mentioned the incongruity of our sustainability manager arriving in a huge SUV.
Literary critics have noted the incongruity between the poem's cheerful rhythm and its dark subject.
Reporters highlighted the incongruity of luxury apartments rising beside overcrowded slums.
She sensed an incongruity between his kind words and the coldness in his eyes.
tc: Visitors are often struck by the ______ of a sleek glass tower standing among centuries-old temples.
The clash between a modern tower and ancient temples signals something out of place.
se: Investigators were puzzled by the ______ between the suspect's modest salary and his lavish lifestyle.
discrepancy
Both 'incongruity' and 'discrepancy' mean a mismatch between two things that should agree.

m: to make someone appear guilty of a crime or wrongdoing
x: My little brother's chocolate-smeared face incriminated him the moment Mom asked who had eaten the cake.
The leaked emails incriminated several senior managers in the fraud.
The researchers' data incriminated a common pesticide in the decline of local bee populations.
Under the constitution, no one can be forced to incriminate themselves in court.
She refused to say anything that might incriminate her closest friend.
tc: The suspect insisted he was innocent, but the fingerprints found on the weapon seemed to ______ him.
'But' contrasts his claim of innocence with evidence that points to his guilt.
se: The accountant feared that the missing receipts might ______ her in the theft.
implicate
Both 'incriminate' and 'implicate' mean to make someone appear involved in a crime.

m: required as a duty or responsibility (usually 'incumbent on' or 'incumbent upon' someone)
x: It is incumbent on parents to make sure their children get enough sleep before exams.
As team leader, she felt it was incumbent upon her to take responsibility for the missed deadline.
It is incumbent upon researchers to disclose any funding that could create a conflict of interest.
Many experts argue that it is incumbent on wealthy nations to help poorer ones adapt to climate change.
He felt it incumbent on him to visit his aging parents every weekend.
tc: Since you are the only person who witnessed the accident, it is ______ on you to tell the police what happened.
Being 'the only person who witnessed' it creates a duty, so the blank means obligatory.
se: Under the new rules, attendance at the annual meeting is ______ on all board members.
binding
Both 'incumbent on' and 'binding on' mean that board members are obliged to attend.

m: done without care, judgment, or selection; random and wide-ranging
x: Indiscriminate snacking in front of the television is the main reason I gained weight this year.
The new manager's indiscriminate praise soon lost all meaning for the team.
Doctors warn that the indiscriminate use of antibiotics is creating drug-resistant bacteria.
Human rights groups condemned the indiscriminate bombing of residential areas.
Looking back, she regretted her indiscriminate trust in people she barely knew.
tc: Rather than choosing her friends carefully, she was ______ in her affections, befriending anyone who smiled at her.
'Rather than choosing ... carefully' signals that the blank means unselective.
se: Farmers have been criticized for the ______ spraying of pesticides on their crops.
haphazard
Both 'indiscriminate' and 'haphazard' describe spraying done carelessly, without judgment.

m: to teach someone to accept a set of beliefs without questioning them
x: Some parents worry that constant advertising indoctrinates children into wanting more and more toys.
New recruits at the firm are quickly indoctrinated with its belief that the customer is always right.
The historian examined how schools were used to indoctrinate young people in the 1930s.
Extremist groups increasingly use social media to indoctrinate vulnerable teenagers who feel isolated.
It took her years to question the beliefs her strict family had indoctrinated her with.
tc: The cult did not encourage open discussion; instead, it tried to ______ new members until they accepted every rule without question.
'Accepted every rule without question' defines the blank as teaching beliefs uncritically.
se: The regime used state television to ______ citizens into believing that the war was justified.
brainwash
Both 'indoctrinate' and 'brainwash' mean to force beliefs on people so they stop questioning.

m: allowing someone to have or do what they want; generous or lenient
x: Her indulgent grandparents let her stay up late and eat ice cream for breakfast.
Our boss is indulgent about long lunches as long as the work gets done on time.
Professor Rahman is known for his indulgent attitude toward late assignments.
Critics accused the regulators of being far too indulgent toward the big banks.
He gave his wife an indulgent smile as she told the same joke for the third time.
tc: Unlike her strict father, who punished every mistake, her mother was ______ and rarely said no.
'Unlike her strict father' and 'rarely said no' show the blank means lenient.
se: Some teachers believe that ______ parents raise children who struggle with discipline.
permissive
Both 'indulgent' and 'permissive' describe parents who allow children too much freedom.

m: hard-working and steadily busy
x: Our industrious neighbor grows vegetables, repairs bicycles and still finds time to help everyone on the street.
The company's success is largely due to its small but industrious team of engineers.
An industrious student, she spent every evening in the library working through practice problems.
Ants are often cited as an example of industrious creatures that work tirelessly for the colony.
He admired his industrious mother, who raised four children while running a small tailoring business.
tc: Though her brother was notoriously lazy, she was remarkably ______, often working well past midnight.
'Though ... lazy' signals a contrast, and 'working well past midnight' confirms she is hard-working.
se: The firm prefers to hire ______ graduates who are willing to put in long hours.
diligent
Both 'industrious' and 'diligent' mean hard-working.

m: drunk; affected by alcohol
x: At the wedding reception, an inebriated guest insisted on giving a second speech.
Company policy forbids employees from operating heavy machinery while inebriated or under the influence of drugs.
The study measured how quickly inebriated volunteers could react to a flashing light.
Police arrested an inebriated driver who had crashed into a lamppost late at night.
She didn't want to have a serious conversation with him while he was inebriated.
tc: After several glasses of wine, he became so ______ that he could barely walk in a straight line.
'Several glasses of wine' and being unable to walk straight point to drunkenness.
se: The bartender refused to serve the customer because he was clearly ______.
intoxicated
Both 'inebriated' and 'intoxicated' mean drunk.

m: impossible to avoid or escape; inevitable
x: Rising rents seem to be an ineluctable part of life in any fast-growing city.
Many workers see automation as an ineluctable force that will reshape every industry.
The novel traces the hero's ineluctable decline from wealthy merchant to beggar.
Some scientists warn that, without drastic action, further rises in sea level are ineluctable.
She slowly came to accept the ineluctable truth that their marriage was over.
tc: No matter how hard he tried to delay it, the confrontation with his father felt ______.
'No matter how hard he tried to delay it' shows the confrontation could not be avoided.
se: Given all the evidence, the ______ conclusion was that the drug did not work.
inescapable
Both 'ineluctable' and 'inescapable' mean impossible to avoid.

m: extremely small; almost too small to measure
x: The chance of winning the lottery is infinitesimal, yet millions of people buy tickets every week.
The software update made only an infinitesimal improvement to the system's speed.
Calculus deals with infinitesimal changes in a quantity, such as speed at a single instant.
Scientists detected infinitesimal amounts of the toxin in the city's water supply.
The difference between the two dresses was infinitesimal, but she agonized over the choice for an hour.
tc: Although the change in temperature was ______, the highly sensitive instrument still managed to detect it.
'Although' and 'highly sensitive instrument' imply the change was extremely small.
se: The risk of a serious side effect is ______, so most doctors recommend the vaccine.
minuscule
Both 'infinitesimal' and 'minuscule' mean extremely small.

m: physical or mental weakness, especially caused by old age or illness
x: Despite his infirmity, my grandfather still insists on walking to the market every morning.
The company offers flexible hours to employees caring for relatives with long-term infirmities.
Medical students study how the infirmities of old age affect memory and balance.
The government plans to expand support for citizens who cannot work because of infirmity.
She hid her growing infirmity from her children so they would not worry about her.
tc: Though once a champion runner, the old man now moved slowly, bowed by ______ and age.
'Though once a champion' contrasts his past strength with present weakness.
se: As her ______ increased, she could no longer climb the stairs without help.
frailty
Both 'infirmity' and 'frailty' mean physical weakness from age or illness.

m: the arrival of a large number of people or things at the same time
x: Every Eid, there is a huge influx of visitors to my grandparents' village.
Our support team was overwhelmed by the influx of complaints after the software update.
Universities are preparing for an influx of international students next autumn.
The sudden influx of refugees placed enormous strain on local schools and hospitals.
After the wedding photos went online, she received an influx of messages from old friends.
tc: The usually quiet town could barely cope with the summer ______ of tourists, which nearly doubled its population.
'Nearly doubled its population' shows a large number of people arriving.
se: The sudden ______ of foreign capital pushed up property prices in the capital.
inflow
Both 'influx' and 'inflow' mean a large amount coming in.

m: to fill someone or something with a quality, feeling, or energy
x: She infused the tiny apartment with warmth, filling it with plants and handmade cushions.
The new CEO infused the company with energy and optimism after years of decline.
Her essays are infused with a deep knowledge of classical literature.
In the 1960s, the reform movement infused national politics with fresh ideas and younger leaders.
Falling in love infused his days with a happiness he had never known before.
tc: The players had grown tired and cynical, so the coach tried to ______ them with fresh enthusiasm before the final.
'Tired and cynical' explains why the coach wanted to fill them with enthusiasm.
se: The young director managed to ______ the old play with a modern sense of humor.
imbue
Both 'infuse' and 'imbue' mean to fill something with a quality.

m: so good or unusual that it is impossible to copy
x: My mother cooks fish curry in her own inimitable style, and no restaurant has ever matched it.
Our office manager handled the crisis with her usual inimitable calm.
Former students still quote the professor's inimitable lectures, full of jokes and unexpected insights.
The late comedian's inimitable style influenced a whole generation of performers.
He wrote her a love letter in his own inimitable handwriting, complete with little drawings.
tc: Many writers have tried to copy her distinctive voice, but none has succeeded, for her style is truly ______.
'Tried to copy ... none has succeeded' defines the blank as impossible to imitate.
se: Fans adored the singer for her ______ voice, which no one could ever reproduce.
unique
Both 'inimitable' and 'unique' describe a voice unlike any other.

m: grossly unfair and morally wrong
x: Charging stranded travelers ten times the normal price for water seemed iniquitous to everyone at the station.
Workers protested against the iniquitous practice of withholding their wages for months.
The historian described colonial land laws as iniquitous, designed to strip farmers of their property.
Campaigners called the new tax iniquitous because it hit the poorest families hardest.
She could never forgive the iniquitous way her uncle had cheated her mother out of her inheritance.
tc: Far from being fair, the old law was ______, punishing the poor while letting the rich go free.
'Far from being fair' and the unequal punishment show the blank means grossly unjust.
se: Reformers worked for decades to end the ______ system of child labor.
unjust
Both 'iniquitous' and 'unjust' describe a system that is morally wrong and unfair.

m: an official order or warning, especially a court order requiring or forbidding an action
x: Despite my doctor's injunction to cut down on sugar, I still have two sweets after dinner.
The company obtained an injunction preventing a former employee from sharing its trade secrets.
Students routinely ignored the librarian's injunction against eating in the reading room.
A court issued an injunction halting construction of the dam until an environmental review is completed.
She has always followed her late father's injunction to treat everyone with kindness.
tc: The judge granted the residents' request and issued the ______, ordering the factory to stop dumping waste into the river.
'Issued' by a judge and 'ordering the factory to stop' define a court order.
se: The protesters defied the court's ______ and continued to block the road.
order
Both 'injunction' and 'order' mean an official command from the court.

m: an indirect remark or hint that suggests something bad or improper about someone
x: Family gatherings are always full of innuendo about which cousin will be the next to get married.
Office gossip, full of innuendo, damaged her reputation even though nothing improper had happened.
The seminar examined the sexual innuendo hidden in Shakespeare's comedies.
The campaign relied on innuendo rather than evidence to attack its opponent.
He was deeply hurt by her constant innuendo that he had married her for money.
tc: The article never directly accused the senator of bribery; instead, it relied on ______ and carefully worded hints.
'Never directly accused' and 'carefully worded hints' point to indirect, damaging suggestion.
se: The report contained no real evidence, only ______ and speculation.
insinuation
Both 'innuendo' and 'insinuation' mean indirect, unproven suggestions of wrongdoing.

m: unusually or unreasonably large; excessive
x: I spend an inordinate amount of time choosing what to watch on streaming services.
Meetings at the firm take up an inordinate share of the working day.
The thesis committee felt that the background chapter was inordinate in length.
Critics say the bill would give the president inordinate power over the courts.
She has always taken inordinate pride in her son's smallest achievements.
tc: The project should have taken a week, yet it dragged on for months because of ______ delays at every stage of approval.
'Should have taken a week, yet ... months' shows the delays were excessively long.
se: The coach was criticized for placing ______ pressure on his young players.
excessive
Both 'inordinate' and 'excessive' mean far more than is reasonable.

m: impossible to satisfy; always wanting more
x: My little nephew has an insatiable appetite for mangoes during the summer.
The sales director's insatiable demand for growth left the whole team exhausted.
As a child, she had an insatiable curiosity about how machines worked.
The world's insatiable demand for oil continues to drive drilling in fragile ecosystems.
His insatiable need for reassurance eventually exhausted his girlfriend's patience.
tc: No matter how many books he read, he always wanted more; his thirst for knowledge was ______.
'No matter how many ... always wanted more' defines something that can never be satisfied.
se: Teenage boys often seem to have ______ appetites, emptying the fridge within hours.
voracious
Both 'insatiable' and 'voracious' describe an appetite that is never satisfied.

m: impossible to understand or read; mysterious
x: My cat stared at me with an inscrutable expression, then calmly walked away.
The CEO's inscrutable face gave no hint of whether he liked our proposal.
For first-year students, the professor's handwriting was as inscrutable as his equations.
Financial markets often react in ways that seem inscrutable even to experienced economists.
Her feelings for him remained inscrutable, and he never knew whether she truly cared.
tc: The poker player's face was utterly ______, so his opponents had no idea whether he held a strong hand.
'Had no idea' shows that his face could not be read or understood.
se: The Mona Lisa is famous for her ______ smile, which seems to hide a secret.
enigmatic
Both 'inscrutable' and 'enigmatic' mean mysterious and hard to interpret.

m: to suggest something unpleasant in an indirect and sly way
x: Are you insinuating that I was the one who ate the last piece of cake?
My colleague insinuated that I had been promoted only because I was friends with the director.
The reviewer insinuated that the author had borrowed her ideas from a little-known study.
The tabloid insinuated that the athlete had used banned drugs, without offering any proof.
She insinuated that her sister's marriage was in trouble, which upset the whole family.
tc: He never said directly that his partner was dishonest, but he managed to ______ it through sly remarks and raised eyebrows.
'Never said directly' and 'sly remarks' point to suggesting something indirectly.
se: The lawyer tried to ______ that the witness had been paid for her testimony.
imply
Both 'insinuate' and 'imply' mean to suggest something without stating it outright.

m: impossible to overcome or deal with successfully
x: Getting tickets for the cricket final seemed an insuperable challenge until my cousin found two spare ones.
The merger collapsed because of insuperable differences between the two management teams.
For many rural students, the cost of university remains an insuperable barrier.
Negotiators insisted that the obstacles to peace were serious but not insuperable.
She believed love could overcome anything, but for them the distance proved insuperable.
tc: The team faced what looked like ______ odds, yet through sheer determination they won the championship.
'Yet ... they won' contrasts the victory with odds that seemed impossible to overcome.
se: For the small charity, the legal costs proved ______, and it was forced to close.
insurmountable
Both 'insuperable' and 'insurmountable' mean impossible to overcome.

m: essential and necessary to make something complete
x: Sunday lunch with the whole family is an integral part of my weekend.
Clear communication is integral to the success of any engineering project.
Lab work is integral to the chemistry degree, not an optional extra.
Better public transport is integral to any serious plan for reducing urban pollution.
Trust is integral to a healthy marriage; without it, everything else falls apart.
tc: The software is not an optional add-on but is ______ to the machine; without it, nothing works.
'Not an optional add-on' and 'without it, nothing works' show the blank means essential.
se: Fieldwork is ______ to the course and cannot be skipped.
essential
Both 'integral' and 'essential' mean a necessary part of the whole.

m: lacking self-control; excessive or extreme, especially in language or drinking
x: His intemperate eating habits finally caught up with him at his annual check-up.
The manager apologized for his intemperate email, which he had sent in a moment of frustration.
Even in heated debates, scholars should avoid intemperate language when criticizing rival theories.
The senator's intemperate remarks about immigrants drew condemnation from both parties.
She regretted her intemperate outburst at her brother during the family argument.
tc: Unlike his calm and measured colleagues, the committee chairman was known for his ______ outbursts during debates.
'Unlike his calm and measured colleagues' signals that the blank means lacking self-control.
se: The editor removed the most ______ passages from the article to avoid offending readers.
unrestrained
Both 'intemperate' and 'unrestrained' describe language that lacks self-control.

m: to bury a dead body in a grave or tomb
x: My grandfather asked to be interred in the village graveyard beside his parents.
Our firm handled the paperwork when the founder's ashes were interred in the family plot.
Archaeologists believe the king was interred with his weapons and jewelry.
The unknown soldiers were finally interred in a national cemetery after decades in unmarked graves.
She stood silently in the rain as they interred her mother.
tc: After the funeral service, the family gathered at the cemetery to ______ the body in the family plot.
'Funeral', 'cemetery' and 'family plot' all point to burying the body.
se: The poet asked his family to ______ him beneath the old oak tree he loved.
bury
Both 'inter' and 'bury' mean to place a dead body in the ground.

m: to officially forbid something, or to intercept and stop something from getting through
x: Our landlord has interdicted pets in the building, much to the disappointment of the children upstairs.
The company interdicted the use of personal email accounts for client communication.
Medieval popes sometimes interdicted entire cities, forbidding religious services there.
Coast guard vessels interdicted a boat carrying two tons of cocaine.
Her pride seemed to interdict any apology, even when she knew she was wrong.
tc: Although the old rules had permitted trade with the neighboring country, the new government moved to ______ all such commerce.
'Although ... had permitted' signals the opposite, so the blank means to forbid.
se: The navy was ordered to ______ any ship trying to carry weapons into the war zone.
intercept
Here both 'interdict' and 'intercept' mean to stop the ships before they get through.

m: happening at irregular intervals; stopping and starting rather than continuous
x: Intermittent power cuts during the summer make it hard to keep food fresh.
The Wi-Fi in our office is intermittent, so video calls keep dropping.
The researchers recorded intermittent bursts of radio signals from a distant galaxy.
Forecasters predict intermittent showers throughout the weekend, so you may want to keep an umbrella handy.
Their friendship survived years of only intermittent contact after university.
tc: The rain was not constant but ______, stopping and starting throughout the afternoon.
'Not constant' and 'stopping and starting' define the blank.
se: The patient reported ______ chest pains that came and went over several days.
sporadic
Both 'intermittent' and 'sporadic' describe something that happens irregularly.

m: to make someone very curious or interested
x: The strange smell coming from the kitchen intrigued the children, who crept in to investigate.
What intrigued the hiring manager most was her experience building a solar project in a remote village.
Physicists have long been intrigued by the question of why time seems to move in only one direction.
The discovery of a new species in the deep ocean has intrigued marine biologists around the world.
She was intrigued by the quiet stranger who always sat alone at parties.
tc: At first the subject bored him, but the professor's unusual examples began to ______ him, and he soon read everything he could find.
'At first ... bored' contrasts with reading everything he could find, so the blank means to arouse interest.
se: Mysteries that cannot be easily solved tend to ______ readers and keep them turning the pages.
fascinate
Both 'intrigue' and 'fascinate' mean to capture someone's curiosity.

m: to speak or write angrily and at length against something
x: My grandfather loves to inveigh against modern music whenever the radio is on.
At every staff meeting, he inveighs against the endless paperwork that slows the team down.
The essay inveighs against the use of standardized tests in university admissions.
Activists inveighed against the new law, calling it an attack on free speech.
She would inveigh against her ex-husband for hours, until her friends begged her to change the subject.
tc: Rather than quietly accepting the decision, the opposition leader went on television to ______ against it in the harshest terms.
'Rather than quietly accepting' and 'in the harshest terms' show the blank means to protest angrily.
se: Every Sunday, the preacher would ______ against greed and corruption.
rail
Both 'inveigh against' and 'rail against' mean to criticize something angrily.

m: likely to cause resentment or offence, especially by being unfair or making unjust comparisons
x: Parents should avoid making invidious comparisons between their children, since it only breeds resentment.
As team lead, I was put in the invidious position of choosing which colleague to let go.
The study warned that invidious distinctions between public and private universities discourage talented students from applying.
Critics argued that the new visa rules drew invidious distinctions between applicants based on their nationality.
She felt it would be invidious to praise one friend's wedding speech and ignore the others.
tc: Judges try to avoid ______ comparisons between contestants, because singling out one performer unfairly can create bitterness among the rest.
'Singling out one performer unfairly' and 'create bitterness' point to a word meaning unfair and likely to cause resentment.
se: The manager refused to make ______ distinctions between staff who had joined from the rival firm and those who had been there for years.
discriminatory
Both 'invidious' and 'discriminatory' describe distinctions that unfairly favour one group, so the sentence means the same either way.

m: never to be broken, infringed or dishonoured; protected from any violation
x: In our house, Sunday lunch with the whole family was an inviolable tradition.
The company treats client confidentiality as an inviolable rule, and breaking it means instant dismissal.
Many legal scholars regard freedom of speech as an inviolable right in any genuine democracy.
The treaty declared the border inviolable, yet both armies continued to skirmish along it for years.
For my grandfather, a promise made to a friend was inviolable, no matter what it cost him.
tc: Although most of the office rules were loosely enforced, the ban on sharing client passwords was ______ and no exception was ever made.
'Although... loosely enforced' sets up a contrast, and 'no exception was ever made' shows the rule could never be broken.
se: The constitution states that the privacy of personal letters is ______ and may not be breached by any authority.
sacrosanct
Both 'inviolable' and 'sacrosanct' mean too important to be violated, matching 'may not be breached'.

m: extremely angry
x: An irate customer stormed back into the shop, waving a phone that had stopped working within a day.
My boss was irate when he discovered that the report had been sent to the client without his approval.
The professor received several irate emails from students who felt the exam had been unfairly difficult.
Irate commuters crowded the platform after the third train in a row was cancelled without explanation.
She grew irate when her brother borrowed her car again without asking.
tc: Far from accepting the apology calmly, the passenger became more ______ with every excuse the airline offered.
'Far from accepting the apology calmly' and 'more... with every excuse' show growing anger.
se: Residents were ______ when they learned the council had approved the factory without consulting them.
furious
Both 'irate' and 'furious' mean extremely angry, which fits residents ignored by the council.

m: showing bright, shimmering colours that seem to change when seen from different angles
x: A thin film of oil on the puddle turned it iridescent after the rain.
The designer chose an iridescent fabric that shifted from blue to purple under the showroom lights.
Under the microscope, the students could see how tiny structures make butterfly wings appear iridescent.
Scientists are studying the iridescent feathers of peacocks to develop new kinds of colour-shifting paint.
She kept the iridescent shell her father had found on the beach at Cox's Bazar.
tc: The soap bubble was ______, its surface rippling with shifting bands of pink, green and gold as it drifted across the room.
The restatement 'shifting bands of pink, green and gold' describes a surface with changing, shimmering colours.
se: The inside of the oyster shell was ______, glowing with soft rainbow colours whenever it caught the light.
opalescent
Both 'iridescent' and 'opalescent' describe a surface that shows shifting rainbow colours in the light.

m: annoying or irritating, especially because tedious or repeated
x: Waiting in line for an hour just to pay the electricity bill is an irksome chore.
Filling in the same expense form every week became increasingly irksome for the sales team.
Students found the rule against using laptops in the library irksome, especially during exam season.
Residents say the constant construction noise is irksome but admit the new metro line will help.
His habit of checking his phone during dinner was irksome to his wife.
tc: Though the job paid well, the endless paperwork it required was so ______ that she began to dread Mondays.
'Though the job paid well' signals a drawback, and 'began to dread Mondays' shows the paperwork was annoying.
se: The neighbour's dog, which barked every night at midnight, was ______ to everyone on the street.
irritating
Both 'irksome' and 'irritating' mean annoying, which suits a dog that barks every night.

m: a contrast between what is expected and what actually happens, or between what is said and what is meant
x: The irony is that I bought the expensive alarm clock and still overslept on the first day.
With some irony, the manager who preached punctuality arrived late to his own meeting.
Our literature professor asked us to identify the dramatic irony in the final act of the play.
Many observers noted the irony of a climate summit attended by leaders who flew in on private jets.
She spoke with gentle irony, saying she just loved spending her birthday in hospital.
tc: There was a bitter ______ in the fact that the fire-safety inspector's own house burned down because of a faulty smoke alarm.
A fire-safety inspector suffering a fire from a faulty alarm is the opposite of what we would expect, which is irony.
se: Few people missed the ______ of a speech about honesty delivered by a politician who had just been caught lying.
incongruity
Both 'irony' and 'incongruity' point to the striking mismatch between the speech's message and the speaker's conduct.

m: lively, cheerful and self-confident in manner or appearance
x: He wore his cap at a jaunty angle and whistled all the way to the market.
Despite the bad quarterly numbers, the CEO opened the meeting in a jaunty, upbeat tone.
The orchestra closed the concert with a jaunty tune that had the audience tapping their feet.
The advertisement's jaunty music hid the fact that the product had been recalled twice.
After the phone call from her daughter, my mother walked with a jaunty step for the rest of the day.
tc: Rather than looking nervous before his interview, Rafi strolled into the lobby looking ______, smiling and greeting everyone he passed.
'Rather than looking nervous' sets up a contrast, and 'smiling and greeting everyone' shows he was lively and confident.
se: Delighted that the exams were over, she seemed ______ all afternoon, humming as she tidied her room.
cheerful
Both 'jaunty' and 'cheerful' describe the happy, lively mood implied by 'delighted' and 'humming'.

m: to throw away or abandon something no longer wanted, such as a plan, idea or cargo
x: When we moved into the small flat, we had to jettison half of our furniture.
The company jettisoned its expansion plans after the investors pulled out.
The researchers jettisoned their original hypothesis once the data clearly contradicted it.
To stay afloat in the storm, the crew jettisoned much of the cargo into the sea.
She finally jettisoned the idea that she had to please everyone in her family.
tc: Faced with a shrinking budget, the director decided to ______ the costly special effects rather than delay the film's release.
'Shrinking budget' and 'rather than delay' show the expensive effects were thrown out to save money.
se: If the new software keeps crashing, we may have to ______ it and return to the old system.
scrap
Both 'jettison' and 'scrap' mean to get rid of something that is not working.

m: a huge, powerful and overwhelming force or organisation that crushes whatever is in its path
x: Our tiny corner shop could not compete once the supermarket juggernaut opened next door.
Within five years, the start-up had grown into a juggernaut that dominated online payments.
Historians describe the Roman army as a military juggernaut that few rivals could withstand.
Bangladesh's garment industry has become an export juggernaut, employing millions of workers.
His fear of the exam grew into a juggernaut that crushed every other thought in his head.
tc: The small independent bookstores could do little to resist the online retail ______, which seemed to crush every competitor in its path.
'Crush every competitor in its path' restates the idea of an overwhelming, unstoppable force.
se: Within a decade the streaming service had become the industry's ______, leaving smaller rivals struggling to survive.
behemoth
Both 'juggernaut' and 'behemoth' mean an enormous, dominant organisation that overwhelms smaller rivals.

m: a particular point in time, especially a critical one in a series of events
x: At this juncture, I think we should stop for lunch before we argue any further.
At this juncture in the negotiations, both companies are reluctant to make further concessions.
My thesis supervisor reminded me that choosing a research topic is a crucial juncture in a PhD.
Analysts say the economy has reached a critical juncture, with inflation finally starting to ease.
Their marriage reached a difficult juncture when he was offered a job in another country.
tc: Coming just as the company was deciding whether to expand abroad, the CEO's resignation could hardly have arrived at a worse ______.
'Just as the company was deciding' shows the blank refers to a critical point in time.
se: At this ______, it is too early to say whether the new treatment will work.
point
'At this juncture' and 'at this point' both mean at this particular moment in events.

m: the theory and philosophy of law, or the body of law built up from court decisions
x: My cousin is studying jurisprudence at Dhaka University and hopes to become a judge.
The firm hired a young lawyer whose knowledge of tax jurisprudence impressed every partner.
Our jurisprudence seminar explored whether laws must be moral in order to be valid.
The Supreme Court ruling marked a turning point in the nation's jurisprudence on privacy rights.
He enjoyed debating jurisprudence with his father, a retired judge, over long Sunday dinners.
tc: Rather than memorising individual statutes, the course examines ______, asking what law is and why people feel bound to obey it.
'Asking what law is and why people feel bound to obey it' defines the philosophy of law.
se: Decades of ______ have established that police need a warrant to search a private home.
precedent
Both 'jurisprudence' and 'precedent' here mean the accumulated court decisions that settle a legal question.

m: dishonest or deceitful behaviour; trickery
x: The used-car dealer's knavery became obvious when the engine failed a week after we bought it.
An audit exposed years of knavery in the accounts department, including forged invoices.
The novel is full of courtly knavery, with ministers plotting against the king and each other.
Voters had grown tired of the knavery of officials who pocketed money meant for flood relief.
She could forgive his forgetfulness, but not the knavery of reading her private messages.
tc: The swindler's ______ was finally revealed when investors discovered that the gold mine he had sold them shares in did not exist.
Selling shares in a mine that does not exist is deceit, so the blank means dishonest trickery.
se: Customers were shocked by the ______ of a bank that had secretly charged them fees for services they never used.
dishonesty
Both 'knavery' and 'dishonesty' describe the deceitful conduct of secretly charging customers.

m: a complicated network of paths in which it is easy to get lost; any confusingly intricate system
x: Old Dhaka is a labyrinth of narrow lanes where even locals sometimes lose their way.
Getting a refund meant navigating a labyrinth of forms, phone menus and unhelpful managers.
New graduate students often struggle with the labyrinth of rules governing thesis submission.
Investigators spent months tracing the money through a labyrinth of offshore shell companies.
His mind became a labyrinth of doubts after she cancelled their plans without explanation.
tc: The hospital's winding, identical corridors formed the kind of ______ in which visitors could easily lose their way for an hour.
'Winding, identical corridors' and 'easily lose their way' describe a confusing maze.
se: Tourists without a map soon got lost in the ______ of alleys behind the old mosque.
maze
Both 'labyrinth' and 'maze' mean a confusing network of paths, which is why the tourists got lost.

m: to tear or deeply cut flesh; figuratively, to hurt someone's feelings severely
x: The broken glass lacerated his foot when he stepped off the pavement barefoot.
In the meeting, the director lacerated the team's proposal, pointing out every flaw in detail.
Medical students practised stitching wounds on pig skin that had been deliberately lacerated.
Doctors said the victim's arms had been badly lacerated by the shattered windscreen.
Her cruel remarks lacerated his pride more than any failure ever had.
tc: The thorny bushes were so sharp that they would ______ the skin of anyone who tried to push through them without gloves.
'So sharp' and 'without gloves' indicate the bushes would cut and tear the skin.
se: Rusty wire along the fence could easily ______ a child's hand, so the school had it removed.
gash
Both 'lacerate' and 'gash' mean to cut the skin deeply, which is the danger of rusty wire.

m: tearful or inclined to weep; also tending to make people cry
x: My aunt becomes lachrymose at every wedding, even when she barely knows the couple.
After a few drinks at the farewell party, our normally stern manager turned unexpectedly lachrymose.
Critics dismissed the film as a lachrymose melodrama designed purely to make audiences cry.
The retiring cricketer gave a lachrymose farewell speech that left the whole stadium in tears.
She grew lachrymose whenever she looked at old photographs of her late grandmother.
tc: Unlike his stoic brother, who never showed emotion at funerals, Karim was ______ and wept openly through the entire service.
'Unlike his stoic brother' signals a contrast, and 'wept openly' restates the meaning of tearful.
se: After the breakup, Nadia remained ______ for weeks, crying at the smallest reminder of him.
tearful
Both 'lachrymose' and 'tearful' mean inclined to cry, as 'crying at the smallest reminder' shows.

m: to lose strength or vitality, or to be kept in a bad or neglected state for a long time
x: The houseplants languished while we were away on holiday for a month.
My application languished on someone's desk for six weeks before anyone looked at it.
Without funding, the promising research project languished and was eventually abandoned.
Thousands of refugees continue to languish in overcrowded camps with little access to clean water.
He languished in a dull marriage for years before finally admitting he was unhappy.
tc: While its rivals thrived on new investment, the old textile mill was left to ______ for decades, its machines rusting and its workers drifting away.
'While its rivals thrived' sets up a contrast, and rusting machines show slow decline through neglect.
se: Without regular watering, the seedlings will ______ and die within a week.
wither
Both 'languish' and 'wither' mean to lose vitality, which is what happens to unwatered seedlings.

m: freedom from narrow limits; scope to act or think as one chooses
x: My parents gave me a lot of latitude in choosing my friends as a teenager.
Our new manager allows employees considerable latitude in deciding how and when to work.
The professor gave us wide latitude in choosing topics for our final research papers.
The law gives judges some latitude in sentencing first-time offenders.
In a healthy relationship, both partners allow each other the latitude to pursue their own interests.
tc: Unlike her previous employer, which dictated every detail of her day, the start-up gave her great ______ to set her own schedule.
The contrast with an employer that 'dictated every detail' shows the blank means freedom to choose.
se: The editor gave reporters considerable ______ in how they approached the story.
leeway
Both 'latitude' and 'leeway' mean freedom to act as one sees fit.

m: to lighten or enliven something serious or dull by adding a contrasting quality
x: She leavened the long family drive with silly games and plenty of snacks.
The speaker leavened his dry presentation on tax law with a few well-timed jokes.
Good textbooks leaven dense theory with real-world examples that students can relate to.
The grim news broadcast was leavened by a brief story about a rescued kitten.
Even in his darkest letters from prison, his humour leavened the sadness.
tc: The memoir deals with poverty and loss, but the author manages to ______ its sombre themes with flashes of warm humour.
'But' and 'flashes of warm humour' show the blank means to lighten something serious.
se: A few personal anecdotes would ______ an otherwise dry lecture on statistics.
enliven
Both 'leaven' and 'enliven' mean to make something dull livelier, matching 'otherwise dry'.

m: showing excessive or offensive sexual desire
x: She changed seats on the bus to escape the lecherous stares of the man beside her.
The company finally fired the lecherous supervisor after several employees filed complaints against him.
The novel's villain is a lecherous old landlord who preys on his young tenants.
The investigation revealed that the lecherous official had harassed staff for over a decade.
Her friends warned her about the lecherous neighbour who always lingered too long at her door.
tc: Far from being the respectful gentleman he pretended to be, the director was ______, constantly making crude advances toward young actresses.
'Far from being the respectful gentleman' signals a contrast, and 'crude advances' shows offensive sexual desire.
se: Female guests complained about the ______ comments the hotel manager made about their appearance.
lewd
Both 'lecherous' and 'lewd' describe offensively sexual remarks that would prompt complaints.

m: a person, usually a man, who lives without moral restraint, especially in sexual matters
x: Everyone at the party knew him as a charming libertine who never stayed with one partner for long.
Her colleagues gossiped that the new director had been a libertine before he married.
The seminar examined how eighteenth-century novels portrayed the aristocratic libertine as both fascinating and dangerous.
The newspaper described the late tycoon as a libertine who squandered his fortune on gambling and lavish parties.
She refused to marry a libertine, however wealthy, who treated loyalty as a joke.
tc: The austere old priest was horrified to learn that his only son had become the town's most notorious ______, known for drinking, gambling and chasing women.
'Drinking, gambling and chasing women' describes someone living without moral restraint, in contrast to the austere priest.
se: The play's central character is the archetypal ______, a charming nobleman who seduces every woman he meets and feels no remorse.
rake
Both 'libertine' and 'rake' mean a man who pursues pleasure, especially women, without moral restraint.

m: thin, supple and graceful in movement
x: The lithe cat leapt onto the kitchen counter without disturbing a single dish.
Our yoga instructor was so lithe that she could fold herself in half effortlessly.
The biology students filmed lithe cheetahs to study how their spines flex during a sprint.
Critics praised the lithe young dancer whose movements seemed to defy gravity.
He envied his sister's lithe figure, which years of swimming had kept strong and graceful.
tc: Years of gymnastics had made her body ______, so that she could twist and bend in ways her stiff-jointed teammates could only envy.
'Twist and bend' and the contrast with 'stiff-jointed teammates' point to a supple, graceful body.
se: The ______ acrobat slipped through the narrow hoop without touching its edges.
agile
Both 'lithe' and 'agile' describe a body that moves easily and gracefully, as the clean pass through the hoop shows.

m: to feel intense dislike or disgust for someone or something
x: I loathe waking up early on Fridays, my only day off.
Most of the staff loathe the new open-plan office because it is impossible to concentrate.
Many students loathe group projects, where one person often ends up doing all the work.
Voters in the district seem to loathe both candidates, which may explain the low turnout.
They had loathed each other at school, so nobody expected them to fall in love years later.
tc: She doesn't merely dislike spiders; she has come to ______ them so intensely that she refuses to enter a room where one has been seen.
'Doesn't merely dislike' and 'so intensely' show the blank is a much stronger word for hatred.
se: I have always enjoyed cooking, but I ______ washing up afterwards.
detest
Both 'loathe' and 'detest' mean to dislike intensely, contrasting with 'enjoyed cooking'.

m: a rude, clumsy or aggressive man or boy
x: Some lout pushed past me in the queue and didn't even apologise.
The office lout made crude jokes at meetings until HR finally had a word with him.
The professor warned that any student behaving like a drunken lout on the trip would be sent home.
Police arrested several louts who had thrown bottles at fans after the cricket match.
She was tired of dating louts who thought burping at dinner was funny.
tc: Everyone was surprised that the elegant, soft-spoken heiress had chosen to marry the ______ who chewed with his mouth open and shouted at waiters.
The contrast with the 'elegant, soft-spoken heiress' and his crude habits point to a rude, uncouth man.
se: Some drunken ______ kept shouting at the actors until security escorted him out of the theatre.
boor
Both 'lout' and 'boor' mean a rude, ill-mannered man, which fits someone heckling actors.

m: growing thickly and richly; abundant and lush
x: After the monsoon, the paddy fields around our village turn a luxuriant green.
The office lobby was filled with luxuriant plants that the receptionist watered every morning.
Botany students compared the luxuriant growth of the rainforest with the sparse vegetation of the desert.
Scientists say the warmer, wetter climate has produced luxuriant algae blooms in the lake.
He had always been proud of his luxuriant black beard, until his daughter called it scratchy.
tc: Whereas the hillside had been bare and scorched the previous summer, by August it was covered in ______ vegetation.
'Whereas... bare and scorched' signals a contrast, so the blank must mean thick and abundant.
se: The rain had left the garden ______, with vines and flowers spilling over every wall.
lush
Both 'luxuriant' and 'lush' describe thick, rich growth, as the spilling vines and flowers show.

m: a situation of violent confusion or turmoil; originally a powerful whirlpool
x: Crossing Gulistan at rush hour means plunging into a maelstrom of buses, rickshaws and shouting vendors.
The newsroom was a maelstrom of ringing phones and shouting editors on election night.
Her thesis analyses how the poet's work was shaped by the maelstrom of the First World War.
The small country was swept into the maelstrom of the regional conflict despite declaring neutrality.
After his father's death, he was caught in a maelstrom of grief, anger and guilt.
tc: Within minutes of the announcement, the calm of the trading floor gave way to the ______ of shouting brokers and flashing screens.
'The calm... gave way to' signals a contrast, so the blank must mean noisy, violent confusion.
se: Thrown into the ______ of a bitter divorce, she struggled to keep her business running.
turmoil
Both 'maelstrom' and 'turmoil' mean a state of great confusion and upheaval.

m: a person who is chronically dissatisfied and inclined to complain or rebel
x: Every family seems to have one malcontent who complains about the food at every gathering.
The new manager tried to win over the office malcontents by asking for their suggestions.
In the history seminar, we discussed how royal malcontents plotted against the young king.
The government blamed the protests on a handful of malcontents rather than on genuine grievances.
She worried that she was becoming a malcontent, unhappy with every job and every friend.
tc: No matter how many improvements the club made, Hasan remained its resident ______, grumbling about the fees, the coaches and even the colour of the jerseys.
'No matter how many improvements' and 'grumbling about' everything describe a chronically dissatisfied person.
se: The party leader dismissed his most vocal critic as a chronic ______ who would complain about any decision.
complainer
Both 'malcontent' and 'complainer' describe someone who is always dissatisfied, as 'complain about any decision' shows.

m: a curse; words that call down harm or evil on someone
x: The old woman muttered a malediction at the boys who had broken her window.
My boss let out a string of maledictions when the printer jammed again before the presentation.
Folklorists collected maledictions from village elders, recording curses passed down through generations.
According to legend, a malediction placed on the castle brought misfortune to every family that lived there.
She felt her mother-in-law's silence was worse than any malediction she could have spoken.
tc: Instead of blessing the newlyweds, the jealous sorceress pronounced the ______ that doomed their kingdom to a hundred years of drought.
'Instead of blessing' signals the opposite, and 'doomed their kingdom' shows the blank means a curse.
se: The furious old priest hurled the ______ at the soldiers, wishing ruin on them and all their descendants.
curse
Both 'malediction' and 'curse' mean words that wish harm on someone, as 'wishing ruin' confirms.

m: a person who commits a crime or does evil
x: Our neighbourhood watch was set up after a malefactor broke into three homes in one week.
The internal audit eventually identified the malefactor who had been leaking confidential files.
The criminology course examines why some malefactors reoffend while others reform completely.
Police appealed to the public for help in tracking down the malefactors behind the bank fraud.
In her eyes, the friend who had betrayed her was no better than a common malefactor.
tc: Far from being the town's benefactor, as everyone believed, the wealthy merchant turned out to be its worst ______, secretly poisoning the river with waste from his mills.
'Far from being the town's benefactor' sets up the opposite, and poisoning the river shows he was an evildoer.
se: The new law imposes heavy penalties on any ______ caught dumping toxic waste in public waterways.
offender
Both 'malefactor' and 'offender' mean a person who breaks the law.

m: an excessive, often short-lived enthusiasm or desire for something; a craze
x: During the World Cup, football mania takes over our neighbourhood, with flags on every rooftop.
The office has caught a strange mania for standing desks this year.
Psychologists studied the mania for collecting that drove some people to fill entire houses.
Tulip mania in seventeenth-century Holland is often cited as the first great financial bubble.
His mania for cleanliness began to strain his relationship with his easy-going roommate.
tc: Her interest in houseplants grew from a casual hobby into an all-consuming ______; soon every windowsill, shelf and stair held a pot.
'From a casual hobby into an all-consuming' and the pots everywhere show an excessive enthusiasm.
se: The ______ for cryptocurrency swept the city, with taxi drivers and teachers alike buying coins they barely understood.
craze
Both 'mania' and 'craze' mean a widespread, excessive enthusiasm, as everyone buying coins shows.

m: many and of various kinds
x: The benefits of a daily walk are manifold, from better sleep to a calmer mind.
The new manager quickly discovered that the department's problems were manifold.
Her essay explores the manifold ways in which colonialism shaped modern Bengali literature.
The causes of the economic crisis were manifold, and no single policy could have prevented it.
Despite his manifold faults, she still believed he was a good father.
tc: The reasons for the project's failure were not single but ______, ranging from poor planning to bad weather to staff shortages.
'Not single but' signals the opposite, and the list of causes shows the reasons were many and varied.
se: The advantages of learning a second language are ______, including better job prospects and a sharper memory.
numerous
Both 'manifold' and 'numerous' mean many, which fits the list of advantages that follows.

m: to spoil or damage the appearance or quality of something
x: A single coffee stain marred the otherwise perfect white tablecloth.
One careless typo can mar an otherwise impressive job application.
Several calculation errors marred her thesis, though her argument was strong.
Violent clashes between rival supporters marred the final day of the tournament.
He did not want an old argument to mar his sister's wedding day.
tc: The architect warned that the ugly new car park would ______ the elegant view of the old palace from the river.
An 'ugly' car park set against an 'elegant view' suggests the blank means to spoil.
se: Nobody wanted the bitter dispute between the two families to ______ the celebrations.
spoil
Both 'mar' and 'spoil' mean to damage the quality of something, here a happy occasion.

m: spoiled or damaged in appearance or quality
x: We stayed in a beautiful hotel, but the view was marred by a construction crane.
The product launch was marred by technical glitches during the live demonstration.
Critics said the study was marred by a small sample size and sloppy analysis.
The election was marred by allegations of vote-buying in several rural districts.
Their friendship, once marred by jealousy, grew stronger after they talked honestly.
tc: The surface of the antique desk, once smooth and flawless, was now ______ by deep scratches and water rings.
'Once smooth and flawless' contrasts with 'now', and 'deep scratches' shows the surface was damaged.
se: His otherwise brilliant performance was ______ by a nervous stumble in the final scene.
spoiled
Both 'marred' and 'spoiled' mean that one flaw damaged something otherwise good.

m: relating to war, soldiers or military life
x: My younger brother has practised martial arts every evening since he was eight.
The company's founder ran his office with almost martial discipline, demanding absolute punctuality.
Historians have studied the martial traditions of the Mughal court and its cavalry.
The government declared martial law after weeks of violent unrest in the capital.
Her father's martial bearing, a legacy of thirty years in the army, intimidated every boyfriend she brought home.
tc: Though he had left the army decades earlier, the old colonel still marched about the garden with ______ precision, as if on parade.
'Left the army', 'marched' and 'as if on parade' all point to a word meaning military.
se: The band played stirring ______ music as the troops paraded through the square.
military
Both 'martial' and 'military' describe music associated with soldiers, fitting the troops' parade.

m: a short statement expressing a general truth or rule of conduct
x: My grandmother lived by the maxim that you should never go to bed angry.
Our manager's favourite maxim is that the customer is always right, even when he is not.
Students of economics learn the old maxim that there is no such thing as a free lunch.
Doctors still follow the ancient maxim 'first, do no harm' when weighing risky treatments.
He repeated his father's maxim about honesty to himself before confessing the mistake to his wife.
tc: Every carpenter learns the ______ 'measure twice, cut once', a short rule that sums up generations of hard experience.
'A short rule that sums up generations of hard experience' defines a maxim.
se: She always quoted the ______ that honesty is the best policy, though she did not always follow it.
adage
Both 'maxim' and 'adage' mean a short, well-known saying that states a general truth.

m: to blend or combine into a single whole
x: The chef melds Bengali spices with French techniques to create surprising new dishes.
After the merger, management struggled to meld two very different company cultures.
Her research melds psychology and economics to explain why people save too little.
The city's architecture melds colonial buildings with gleaming modern glass towers.
Over the years, their separate lives slowly melded into one shared routine.
tc: Rather than keeping the two genres separate, the band tries to ______ jazz and folk into a single, seamless sound.
'Rather than keeping... separate' and 'into a single, seamless sound' show the blank means to blend.
se: The new curriculum attempts to ______ theory and practice so that students learn by doing.
blend
Both 'meld' and 'blend' mean to combine two things into one.

m: a confused, noisy fight or scuffle involving many people
x: I lost my sandal in the melee at the bus stop when everyone rushed for the last seat.
Several reporters were pushed to the ground in the melee outside the courthouse.
The history lecture described the chaotic melee that followed the cavalry charge.
Police said three people were injured in a melee that broke out after the football match.
In the melee of the wedding reception, she never got a chance to talk to her cousin.
tc: What began as a polite queue for concert tickets quickly turned into the kind of ______ in which people shoved, shouted and trampled each other.
'Began as a polite queue' contrasts with 'shoved, shouted and trampled', describing a chaotic crowd scuffle.
se: A police officer was injured in the ______ that erupted when rival fans spilled onto the pitch.
fracas
Both 'melee' and 'fracas' mean a noisy, disorderly fight among many people.

m: sweet, smooth and pleasant to hear
x: The radio presenter's mellifluous voice made even the traffic report sound soothing.
Our call centre hires people with mellifluous voices to calm angry customers.
The poet's mellifluous lines are best appreciated when read aloud in class.
Audiences adored the singer's mellifluous rendition of the old Tagore song.
She fell in love with his mellifluous laugh before she even saw his face.
tc: Unlike the harsh, grating tones of his predecessor, the new announcer's voice was ______, smooth and pleasing to the ear.
'Unlike the harsh, grating tones' signals a contrast, and 'smooth and pleasing to the ear' restates the meaning.
se: Listeners praised the narrator's ______ voice, which made the audiobook a pleasure to hear.
melodious
Both 'mellifluous' and 'melodious' describe a voice that is sweet and pleasant to listen to.

m: very rapid and dazzling, especially describing a rise to success
x: Her meteoric rise from intern to vice-president surprised even her closest friends.
The start-up's meteoric growth attracted investors from three continents within a year.
The young physicist's meteoric career began with a paper she wrote as an undergraduate.
