The cricketer's meteoric rise ended abruptly when a knee injury forced him to retire at twenty-five.
Their romance was meteoric: they met in March, married in June and separated by Christmas.
tc: Whereas most actors spend years in small roles, her ascent to stardom was ______, taking her from obscurity to fame in a single season.
'Whereas most actors spend years' signals a contrast, and 'in a single season' shows extreme speed.
se: The band's ______ rise to fame took them from local pubs to sold-out stadiums in under a year.
rapid
Both 'meteoric' and 'rapid' describe how fast the band rose, as 'in under a year' shows.

m: done in a systematic, orderly way; careful and well organised
x: My father is so methodical that he labels every jar in the kitchen.
A methodical approach to debugging saved us hours of pointless guesswork.
She prepared for the GRE in a methodical way, learning twenty new words every single day.
Investigators carried out a methodical search of the building, room by room.
Her methodical nature balanced his impulsiveness, which is perhaps why their marriage worked.
tc: Unlike his haphazard roommate, who studied whatever caught his eye, Imran was ______, working through each chapter in order and reviewing his notes every evening.
'Unlike his haphazard roommate' sets up a contrast, and working 'in order' shows a systematic approach.
se: The detective was slow but ______, checking every alibi before reaching a conclusion.
systematic
Both 'methodical' and 'systematic' mean following an orderly process, like checking every alibi.

m: a person's appearance or manner, especially as a sign of their character or mood
x: Despite her calm mien, she was terrified of giving the speech.
The new director's serious mien made the staff nervous on his first day.
The professor's gentle mien encouraged even the shyest students to ask questions.
The general's stern mien betrayed nothing as he announced the army's retreat.
Her grandfather's dignified mien hid the deep grief he felt after his wife's death.
tc: Although he was inwardly furious, the diplomat kept a composed ______, so that no one in the room could guess his true feelings.
'Although he was inwardly furious' contrasts his feelings with his outward manner, which is what the blank names.
se: The judge's stern ______ silenced the noisy courtroom before he spoke a word.
demeanour
Both 'mien' and 'demeanour' mean a person's outward manner, which here was stern enough to silence the room.

m: a person's social environment or setting
x: Growing up in a milieu of musicians, she could read sheet music before she could read books.
He found it hard to adjust to the competitive milieu of a large investment bank.
The novel vividly portrays the intellectual milieu of Calcutta in the 1920s.
Sociologists argue that a child's social milieu strongly shapes his or her ambitions.
After moving abroad, he missed the warm, noisy milieu of his family home.
tc: Having grown up surrounded by painters, poets and late-night debates about art, she felt out of place in the dull corporate ______ of her new employer.
The contrast between her artistic upbringing and the 'dull corporate' setting shows the blank means social environment.
se: Many immigrants struggle to adapt to the unfamiliar cultural ______ of their new country.
environment
Both 'milieu' and 'environment' mean the social surroundings a person lives in.

m: to be a strong factor that makes something less likely (usually 'militate against')
x: The heavy rain militated against our plans for a picnic by the river.
Tight deadlines militate against careful work, so mistakes are bound to creep in.
Several factors militate against a simple explanation of the experiment's results.
Widespread corruption continues to militate against foreign investment in the region, economists warn.
Their very different ambitions militated against a lasting relationship, however much they loved each other.
tc: The region's mountainous terrain and harsh winters ______ against any attempt to build a reliable railway there.
Difficult terrain and harsh winters are obstacles, so the blank means to act as a strong factor against.
se: The candidate's lack of experience is likely to ______ against him in the final round of interviews.
weigh
'Militate against him' and 'weigh against him' both mean to count as a strong disadvantage.

m: the act or skill of imitating someone or something, often to amuse or, in nature, for protection
x: My nephew's mimicry of our grumpy neighbour had the whole family laughing.
His mimicry of the CEO's accent at the office party was funny but risky.
In biology class, we learned how mimicry helps harmless snakes resemble venomous ones.
Researchers found that the parrot's mimicry included the sound of a ringing mobile phone.
She was hurt to discover that her friends' affectionate mimicry of her laugh had a mocking edge.
tc: The comedian was famous not for original jokes but for ______, copying the voices and gestures of celebrities so perfectly that audiences gasped.
'Not for original jokes but' and 'copying the voices and gestures' define the skill of imitation.
se: The lyrebird's ______ of chainsaws and car alarms astonished the documentary crew.
imitation
Both 'mimicry' and 'imitation' mean copying sounds, which is what the lyrebird does.

m: a servile follower or underling of a powerful person
x: I am tired of being treated like a minion who exists only to fetch tea.
The CEO rarely attends meetings himself and simply sends one of his minions instead.
In the novel, the dictator's minions spy on every citizen who dares to complain.
The gang leader's minions were arrested, but the man himself escaped abroad.
She refused to become her domineering brother's minion, even if it cost her the inheritance.
tc: The tyrant never dirtied his own hands; instead he relied on a trusted ______ to carry out every cruel order without question.
'Never dirtied his own hands' and 'carry out every... order without question' describe a servile follower.
se: The mob boss sent his most loyal ______ to collect the money from frightened shopkeepers.
henchman
Both 'minion' and 'henchman' mean a follower who does a powerful person's bidding.

m: small, precise or trivial details
x: I don't have the patience for the minutiae of planning a wedding.
A good manager delegates the minutiae and focuses on the bigger picture.
His dissertation got bogged down in the minutiae of medieval tax records.
The public lost interest as the debate descended into the minutiae of budget procedure.
She remembered all the minutiae of their first date, down to the colour of his shirt.
tc: The CEO cared about broad strategy and had no interest in the ______, such as which font the reports used or where the staplers were kept.
The contrast with 'broad strategy' and the trivial examples that follow show the blank means small details.
se: Lawyers spent hours arguing over the ______ of the contract while the main issue went unresolved.
details
Both 'minutiae' and 'details' mean the small points, which contrast with 'the main issue'.

m: an optical illusion caused by hot air; figuratively, something that seems real or attainable but is not
x: On the hot highway, we kept seeing a mirage of water that vanished as we approached.
The promised promotion turned out to be a mirage designed to keep him working overtime.
Our physics teacher explained how layers of hot air bend light to create a mirage.
Economists warn that the recent boom may be a mirage built on cheap credit.
For years, the dream of reconciling with his father remained a painful mirage.
tc: The lake the exhausted travellers saw shimmering ahead was the cruellest kind of ______: as they stumbled toward it, it simply vanished.
Something that appears ahead in the heat and then 'simply vanished' is an optical illusion.
se: Economists warned that rising house prices created only the ______ of prosperity, since wages had not grown at all.
illusion
Both 'mirage' and 'illusion' mean something that looks real but is not, as stagnant wages reveal.

m: to trap or entangle in difficulties, as if stuck in deep mud
x: Our car got mired in the mud on the way to the village during the monsoon.
The project has been mired in delays since the original contractor went bankrupt.
The research grant application was mired in bureaucracy for nearly a year.
The country remains mired in debt despite years of painful austerity.
He felt mired in self-doubt after his third rejection letter.
tc: The opposition hoped the corruption allegations would ______ the government in scandal for months, leaving it unable to pass any new laws.
'For months' and 'unable to pass any new laws' show the blank means to trap someone in difficulty.
se: Endless lawsuits threatened to ______ the company in costly legal battles for years.
embroil
Both 'mire' and 'embroil' mean to entangle someone in trouble they cannot easily escape.

m: amusement, especially when expressed in laughter
x: Our attempts to assemble the furniture without instructions caused great mirth among the neighbours.
The intern's spectacular spelling mistake in the company newsletter was a source of mirth for weeks.
The lecturer's dry jokes about statistics provoked surprising mirth in the exam-weary class.
The satirical cartoon caused mirth among readers and fury among the politicians it mocked.
She could barely contain her mirth when her husband tried to dance at the wedding.
tc: The sombre funeral reception unexpectedly dissolved into ______ when the grandfather's old parrot began singing a rude song.
'Sombre' and 'unexpectedly' set up a contrast, and a parrot singing a rude song would cause laughter.
se: The clown's clumsy tricks filled the children's party with ______ and laughter.
merriment
Both 'mirth' and 'merriment' mean cheerful amusement, which fits a clown at a children's party.

m: to interpret someone's words or actions wrongly
x: Please don't misconstrue my silence as agreement; I simply need time to think.
The manager misconstrued my email as a complaint, when I was really asking for advice.
Students often misconstrue the author's sarcasm as a sincere argument.
Officials claim journalists misconstrued the minister's remarks about raising fuel prices.
She misconstrued his shyness as arrogance and avoided him for months.
tc: Because the message was so brief and lacked any context, it was easy to ______ a friendly joke as a personal insult.
'Lacked any context' explains why a joke could be taken as an insult, so the blank means to interpret wrongly.
se: Foreign visitors sometimes ______ local customs, mistaking politeness for unfriendliness.
misinterpret
Both 'misconstrue' and 'misinterpret' mean to understand something wrongly, as 'mistaking politeness for unfriendliness' shows.

m: a minor wrongdoing; in law, a crime less serious than a felony
x: Forgetting my mother's birthday was a misdemeanor she has never quite let me forget.
In this office, arriving late is treated as a serious misdemeanor rather than a small slip.
Copying a friend's homework was regarded as a misdemeanor, but plagiarising a thesis meant expulsion.
He was charged with a misdemeanor for shoplifting and ordered to do community service.
She forgave her husband's small misdemeanors, but lying to her was another matter.
tc: Unlike a felony, which can bring years in prison, the ______ he committed carried only a small fine.
'Unlike a felony' and 'only a small fine' show the blank means a minor offence.
se: Teachers overlooked the occasional ______, such as talking in class, but cheating was punished severely.
infraction
Both 'misdemeanor' and 'infraction' mean a minor breach of rules, contrasting with serious cheating.

m: extremely unwilling to spend money; stingy
x: My miserly landlord refuses to fix the leaking tap because he says a plumber costs too much.
The company's miserly travel budget meant staff had to share cramped hotel rooms at conferences.
Researchers complained that the miserly grant barely covered the cost of their lab equipment.
Critics called the government's miserly flood relief package an insult to families who had lost everything.
She found it hard to love a man so miserly that he questioned every taka she spent on groceries.
tc: Although he had made a fortune in shipping, he remained so ______ that he reused tea bags and refused to heat his house.
'Although he had made a fortune' contrasts with reusing tea bags and not heating the house, so the blank must mean stingy.
se: Her ______ uncle gave her ten dollars as a wedding present, despite being one of the richest men in town.
stingy
Both 'miserly' and 'stingy' describe someone unwilling to spend money, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: feelings of doubt or worry about whether something is right or will turn out well
x: I had misgivings about lending my car to my cousin, and sure enough he returned it with a dent.
Several engineers voiced misgivings about the tight deadline, but management pushed ahead anyway.
Despite her misgivings about the course's heavy workload, she enrolled and ended up loving it.
Environmental groups expressed serious misgivings about the proposed coal plant near the Sundarbans.
His parents' misgivings about the marriage faded once they got to know his fiancée.
tc: Although she signed the contract, she had deep ______ about the vague clause on unpaid overtime.
'Although she signed' sets up a contrast, so the blank must mean doubts or worries about the deal.
se: Many voters had ______ about the candidate's lack of experience in government.
reservations
Both 'misgivings' and 'reservations' mean doubts, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: a minor accident or piece of bad luck
x: Apart from a small mishap with the cake, which slid off the plate, the party went perfectly.
A technical mishap delayed the online meeting by twenty minutes, so we had to rush the agenda.
The lab manual warns students that even a minor mishap with acid can cause painful burns.
Officials insisted the power outage was a one-off mishap rather than a sign of deeper problems.
We still laugh about the mishap on our honeymoon when we boarded a train going the wrong way.
tc: The rest of the journey passed without ______, a welcome change after the flat tyre and missed ferry of the first day.
The flat tyre and missed ferry are examples of small accidents, so the blank means a minor misfortune.
se: The parade went ahead without a single ______, much to the organizers' relief.
accident
Both 'mishap' and 'accident' refer to an unlucky incident, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: a person who dislikes, distrusts or is strongly prejudiced against women
x: Everyone at the dinner party winced when he made yet another joke that revealed him to be a misogynist.
The manager was exposed as a misogynist after female staff shared emails in which he mocked their abilities.
Literature students debated whether the novelist was a misogynist or simply depicting the attitudes of his era.
Online forums where misogynists gather to complain about women have drawn growing concern from researchers.
She ended the relationship once she realized her boyfriend was a misogynist who never respected her opinions.
tc: The playwright was no ______; on the contrary, his plays are full of strong, intelligent women whom he clearly admired.
'On the contrary' and his admiration for women show the blank means someone who dislikes women.
se: Colleagues described the retired judge as an unapologetic ______ who believed women did not belong in the legal profession.
sexist
Both 'misogynist' and 'sexist' name a person prejudiced against women, so the sentence means the same.

m: to make fun of someone or something, often by copying them unkindly
x: My little brother loves to mock my accent whenever I come back from a semester abroad.
It's unprofessional to mock a colleague's mistakes in front of the whole team.
The professor warned that students who mock others' questions would be asked to leave the seminar.
Satirists have long mocked politicians who promise new roads every election and deliver nothing.
She felt deeply hurt when her friends mocked her dream of becoming a writer.
tc: Rather than support his ambition to study astrophysics, his classmates chose to ______ it, laughing whenever he mentioned the stars.
'Rather than support' and 'laughing' show the blank means to ridicule.
se: Comedians were quick to ______ the minister's claim that the floods were caused by too much rain.
ridicule
Both 'mock' and 'ridicule' mean to make fun of, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: fashionable and stylish in a way that follows current trends
x: She showed up in a modish leather jacket that made the rest of us feel underdressed.
The startup's modish office, complete with bean bags and a coffee bar, impressed young job applicants.
Some scholars dismiss the theory as a modish idea that will be forgotten within a decade.
Gulshan has become a hub for modish cafés serving overpriced lattes to Dhaka's young professionals.
He felt out of place among his wife's modish friends, who talked only about fashion and gallery openings.
tc: Once considered ______, the restaurant's minimalist décor now looks dated and dull.
'Once' contrasts with 'now looks dated', so the blank must mean fashionable.
se: The magazine featured several ______ boutique hotels where every room is designed by a different artist.
stylish
Both 'modish' and 'stylish' mean fashionable, so the hotel is described the same way.

m: to shed old feathers, skin, hair or shell so that new growth can replace them
x: Our parrot molts every spring, leaving feathers scattered all over the living room floor.
The zookeeper explained that snakes often stop eating for a few days before they molt.
In biology class, we watched a time-lapse video of a crab molting its old shell.
Scientists have found that rising temperatures are changing when some Arctic birds molt.
Watching a cicada molt in the garden, the old man told his grandson it was a lesson in starting over.
tc: Like many reptiles, the lizard must periodically ______, leaving behind a papery shell of dead skin.
'Leaving behind a papery shell of dead skin' defines the blank as shedding.
se: Each summer, ducks ______ their flight feathers and cannot fly for several weeks.
shed
Both 'molt' and 'shed' mean to lose old feathers, so the meaning is the same.

m: of great importance, especially in its effect on the future
x: Moving to a new country is a momentous decision, so take your time before you sign anything.
Signing our first international client was a momentous day for the small software firm.
Getting an admission offer from a top university felt like the most momentous event of his life.
The discovery of penicillin was a momentous breakthrough that transformed modern medicine.
They knew their first child's birth would be momentous, but nothing prepared them for the joy it brought.
tc: Far from being trivial, the court's ruling proved ______, reshaping labor law for decades.
'Far from being trivial' and 'reshaping labor law for decades' show the blank means highly significant.
se: Historians agree that the fall of the Berlin Wall was one of the most ______ events of the twentieth century.
significant
Both 'momentous' and 'significant' mean very important, so the sentence means the same.

m: large, powerful and uniform throughout, with no variety or flexibility
x: It is a mistake to treat young voters as a monolithic group with identical opinions.
Working inside such a monolithic corporation, she felt her suggestions vanished into endless layers of approval.
The historian argues that medieval Christianity was far from monolithic, with fierce disagreements between regions.
The party's monolithic control of the media left little room for dissenting voices.
He realized that seeing his in-laws as a monolithic, disapproving clan was unfair, since each had a different view of him.
tc: Critics who describe the immigrant community as ______ ignore its enormous diversity of languages, religions and political views.
The contrast with 'enormous diversity' shows the blank means uniform and undivided.
se: The opposition is hardly ______; its members disagree on almost every major issue.
uniform
Both 'monolithic' and 'uniform' mean all the same throughout, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: the customs and moral standards accepted by a particular community
x: Moving from a village to Dhaka, she had to adjust to very different social mores about dating and dress.
New employees quickly learn the unwritten office mores, such as never leaving before the boss.
The anthropology course examines how marriage mores have changed across cultures over the past century.
Sexual mores in many Western countries shifted dramatically during the 1960s and 1970s.
His parents' traditional mores clashed with his own ideas about how a modern couple should live.
tc: The novel satirizes the ______ of Victorian high society, exposing its rigid rules about dress, courtship and manners.
'Rigid rules about dress, courtship and manners' restates the blank as a society's customs.
se: Foreign visitors should respect local ______ regarding modest clothing at religious sites.
customs
Both 'mores' and 'customs' mean accepted social practices, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: having an unhealthy interest in unpleasant subjects, especially death and disease
x: My sister has a morbid habit of reading about plane crashes the night before she flies.
Office chatter took a morbid turn when someone started ranking the worst ways to die.
Some readers find the poet's morbid fascination with graveyards unsettling rather than profound.
Journalists were criticized for feeding the public's morbid curiosity with graphic photos of the accident.
After his father's death, his thoughts grew so morbid that his friends urged him to see a counselor.
tc: Crowds gathered at the crash site not to help but out of ______ curiosity, staring at the wreckage and filming the victims.
'Not to help' and staring at victims point to an unhealthy interest in death and suffering.
se: The tour guide's ______ jokes about the castle's torture chamber made several visitors uncomfortable.
macabre
Both 'morbid' and 'macabre' describe a dwelling on death and horror, so the meaning is the same.

m: made up of many different, often mismatched, kinds of people or things
x: Our book club is a motley group of retired teachers, college students and a dentist.
The startup began with a motley team of engineers, designers and one very patient accountant.
The museum's archive holds a motley collection of letters, maps, coins and old photographs.
A motley coalition of farmers, students and shopkeepers marched together against the new tax.
At the wedding, our motley assortment of relatives somehow got along for an entire evening.
tc: Unlike the uniformed ranks of a professional army, the rebel force was distinctly ______, mixing farmers, students and former soldiers.
'Unlike the uniformed ranks' and the mixed list of members show the blank means made up of mismatched parts.
se: The garage was filled with ______ furniture collected from flea markets over thirty years.
assorted
Both 'motley' and 'assorted' mean of many different kinds, so the sentence means the same.

m: marked with irregular spots or patches of different colors
x: The old dog's mottled coat made him look like a walking patchwork quilt.
Years of water damage had left the office ceiling mottled with brown stains.
In the field guide, the bird is identified by its mottled brown and white breast.
Doctors noted that the patient's mottled skin was a sign of poor circulation.
She smiled at her grandmother's mottled hands, remembering how they had once braided her hair.
tc: The frog's ______ skin, patched with green and brown, helps it blend in among the fallen leaves.
'Patched with green and brown' defines the blank as spotted with different colors.
se: Sunlight filtering through the leaves cast ______ shadows across the lawn.
dappled
Both 'mottled' and 'dappled' mean marked with patches of light and color, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: rebellious; refusing to obey people in authority
x: The children grew mutinous when their parents announced there would be no television for a week.
After a third round of pay cuts, the factory workers were in a mutinous mood.
The teacher faced a mutinous class when she assigned extra homework on the last day of term.
Mutinous soldiers seized the national radio station and demanded the general's resignation.
His mutinous silence at dinner made it clear that he had not forgiven his father.
tc: Once loyal and obedient, the crew became ______ after weeks of short rations and brutal punishments.
'Once loyal and obedient' signals a change to the opposite, so the blank means rebellious.
se: Backbenchers grew increasingly ______ as the prime minister ignored their objections.
rebellious
Both 'mutinous' and 'rebellious' mean ready to defy authority, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to make someone feel sick or strongly disgusted
x: The smell of rotting fish in the bin nauseated everyone in the kitchen.
It nauseates me to see managers take credit for work their junior staff did.
Some patients find that the medication nauseates them unless they take it with food.
Graphic footage of the massacre nauseated viewers around the world and sparked calls for an inquiry.
After everything he did, her ex-boyfriend's fake apologies now only nauseate her.
tc: The gory scenes were meant to thrill the audience, but they only managed to ______ them, and several people left the cinema.
'But they only managed' contrasts with 'thrill', and people leaving shows the blank means sicken.
se: Violent videos like that ______ me, so I never watch them.
sicken
Both 'nauseate' and 'sicken' mean to make someone feel ill or disgusted, so the meaning is the same.

m: a long-standing rival or enemy; something that causes someone's downfall
x: Mathematics was my nemesis in school, no matter how many tutors my parents hired.
The rival firm became our nemesis after it poached three of our best engineers.
For many physics students, quantum mechanics is the nemesis that ends their hopes of a top grade.
India has long been Bangladesh's cricketing nemesis, though recent matches have been much closer.
He always saw his older brother as his nemesis, competing with him for their father's approval.
tc: The hero thought he had defeated his old ______ for good, but the villain returned in the sequel more dangerous than ever.
'Defeated' and 'the villain returned' show the blank means a long-standing enemy.
se: The challenger finally defeated his ______ in the championship final after five straight losses to him.
rival
Both 'nemesis' and 'rival' name a long-standing opponent, so the sentence means the same.

m: to irritate or annoy someone
x: It really nettled me that my roommate ate my leftovers without asking.
Her constant interruptions in meetings began to nettle her colleagues.
The student was nettled by the examiner's suggestion that he had copied parts of his thesis.
The minister was visibly nettled by reporters' questions about the missing funds.
His habit of correcting her grammar in front of friends nettled her more than she admitted.
tc: Although he tried to appear calm, the critic's sneering review managed to ______ him, and he replied angrily on social media.
'Although he tried to appear calm' contrasts with replying angrily, so the blank means irritate.
se: Small things like slow walkers on the pavement tend to ______ her more than real problems do.
irritate
Both 'nettle' and 'irritate' mean to annoy, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: a connection or link between things, or a central point where they meet
x: Our kitchen table is the nexus of family life, where we eat, argue and do homework.
Investigators uncovered a nexus between the contractor and several city officials.
The paper explores the nexus between poverty and poor health outcomes in rural areas.
Singapore has long served as a nexus of trade between East and West.
For their friend group, she was the nexus who kept everyone in touch after graduation.
tc: Because nearly every rail line in the region passes through it, the city serves as the ______ of the country's transport network.
Every rail line passing through the city shows the blank means a central connecting point.
se: Researchers studied the ______ between social media use and teenage anxiety.
link
Both 'nexus' and 'link' mean a connection between two things, so the meaning stays the same.

m: the belief that life has no meaning and that moral values have no real basis
x: After failing his exams twice, he drifted into a gloomy nihilism and stopped caring about anything.
Her manager's nihilism about the project, insisting nothing would ever change, dragged down the whole team.
Our philosophy seminar spent a week on Nietzsche's critique of nihilism.
Some commentators blame a growing political nihilism for the record number of citizens who no longer vote.
She worried that her son's teenage nihilism was more than just a passing phase.
tc: The novel's young hero rejects religion, family and every moral rule, embracing ______ as the only honest response to a meaningless world.
Rejecting every moral rule and seeing the world as meaningless defines the blank as nihilism.
se: His later essays reflect a bleak ______ that sees no value in tradition or morality.
cynicism
Both 'nihilism' and 'cynicism' describe a bleak rejection of accepted values, so the sentence means nearly the same.

m: existing in name only, not in reality; or very small compared with the real value
x: The museum charges only a nominal fee, so families can visit every weekend.
He is the nominal head of the department, but his deputy makes all the real decisions.
Students pay a nominal sum for the library card, mainly to cover printing costs.
The country's monarch holds nominal power, while parliament actually governs.
Their marriage had become nominal; they shared a house but lived completely separate lives.
tc: Although she is the ______ leader of the party, real authority rests with a small committee behind the scenes.
'Although' contrasts her title with 'real authority' elsewhere, so the blank means in name only.
se: The president's role is largely ______; the prime minister runs the government.
symbolic
Both 'nominal' and 'symbolic' mean having a title without real power, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: a person or thing of no importance or influence
x: At the glamorous party, he felt like a complete nonentity among the famous guests.
She refused to remain a nonentity in the office and volunteered to lead the next big project.
The professor dismissed the author as a literary nonentity, yet her novel later became a classic.
The candidate was a political nonentity until a viral debate clip made him famous overnight.
In her husband's family, she was treated as a nonentity whose opinions never mattered.
tc: Before her best-selling memoir, she was a literary ______; afterward, every publisher in town wanted her next book.
'Before' and 'afterward' contrast her later fame, so the blank means a person of no importance.
se: Surrounded by famous relatives, he felt he was a mere ______ at family gatherings.
nobody
Both 'nonentity' and 'nobody' mean an unimportant person, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: the state of being famous for something bad
x: The café gained unwanted notoriety after a food critic found a cockroach in his soup.
The firm achieved notoriety for firing employees by text message.
The scientist's fabricated data brought him notoriety rather than the fame he wanted.
The bridge has earned notoriety as one of the city's worst accident spots.
Her brief notoriety as the bride who fled her own wedding still embarrasses her.
tc: Rather than earning the respect he craved, the hacker won only ______ for leaking thousands of private medical records.
'Rather than earning the respect' and the harmful leak show the blank means fame for wrongdoing.
se: The dictator's ______ for brutality spread well beyond his country's borders.
infamy
Both 'notoriety' and 'infamy' mean being well known for something bad, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: deep respect or submission, often shown by bowing
x: The children made a playful obeisance to their grandfather, bowing low before asking for sweets.
Junior staff were expected to show obeisance to the chairman, standing whenever he entered the room.
Medieval vassals paid obeisance to their lord in an elaborate public ceremony.
Critics accused the newspaper of paying obeisance to the ruling party instead of questioning it.
She was tired of the obeisance her husband demanded from everyone in the family.
tc: Courtiers entering the throne room were required to bow low in ______ before the king.
'Bow low' before a king shows the blank means a show of deep respect.
se: Every candidate felt obliged to pay ______ to the party's founder in their speeches.
homage
Both 'pay obeisance' and 'pay homage' mean to show public respect, so the sentence means the same.

m: extremely unpleasant, rude or offensive
x: The man next to me on the bus played obnoxious music on his phone without headphones.
His obnoxious habit of replying to all on every email irritates the whole department.
One obnoxious student kept interrupting the lecture with irrelevant questions.
Fans criticized the club for allowing obnoxious chants aimed at the opposing players.
She couldn't understand why her sister kept dating such an obnoxious man.
tc: Though his guests were polite and charming, he himself was loud, rude and utterly ______ throughout the dinner.
'Though' contrasts him with polite guests, and 'loud, rude' points to extremely unpleasant.
se: The tourists' ______ behavior in the temple drew angry looks from the worshippers.
offensive
Both 'obnoxious' and 'offensive' describe rude, unpleasant behavior, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: an idea or interest that fills someone's mind constantly, often to an unhealthy degree
x: My father's obsession with cricket means our television is never free during a series.
Her obsession with perfection makes her a brilliant editor but a slow one.
His obsession with grades left him little time to enjoy university life.
Psychologists warn that an obsession with social media likes can damage teenagers' self-esteem.
What began as a crush became an unhealthy obsession, and he could think of nothing but her.
tc: What began as a casual hobby turned into ______; she now spends every evening and weekend restoring antique clocks.
The shift from 'casual hobby' to spending every evening and weekend shows the blank means a consuming fixation.
se: The detective's ______ with the unsolved case eventually cost him his marriage.
fixation
Both 'obsession' and 'fixation' mean a constant, consuming focus, so the meaning is the same.

m: noticeable in an unwelcome or intrusive way
x: The new hotel's obtrusive neon sign ruins the view of the old fort.
Good managers keep an eye on their team's progress without being obtrusive or controlling.
The footnotes in this edition are so obtrusive that they distract from the poems themselves.
Residents complained that the obtrusive security cameras made the street feel like a prison.
Her mother-in-law's obtrusive questions about when they would have children upset her.
tc: The waiter was attentive but never ______, refilling our glasses so quietly that we hardly noticed him.
'Hardly noticed him' shows the blank means noticeable in an unwelcome way, which he was not.
se: The architect hid the air-conditioning units so they would not look ______ against the historic facade.
conspicuous
Both 'obtrusive' and 'conspicuous' mean sticking out unpleasantly, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: relating to supernatural or magical powers, or to secret knowledge of them
x: My aunt keeps a shelf of occult books on astrology, tarot and palm reading.
The office joked that occult forces controlled the printer because it only jammed on Mondays.
The historian studies occult societies that flourished in Victorian London.
Police found candles and occult symbols painted on the walls of the abandoned house.
She grew uneasy when her new boyfriend confessed his fascination with occult rituals.
tc: The village healer claimed ______ powers, insisting that spirits told him which herbs would cure each illness.
Spirits telling him which herbs to use shows the blank means supernatural.
se: The cult's leader claimed to possess ______ knowledge that ordinary people could not understand.
esoteric
Both 'occult' and 'esoteric' describe secret knowledge known only to a few, so the meaning is the same.

m: casual or careless in a way that can seem rude; said without preparation
x: His offhand remark about her cooking hurt her more than he realized.
The manager's offhand response to our safety concerns made us feel ignored.
The professor made an offhand comment in class that later inspired my entire thesis.
Critics condemned the official's offhand treatment of the flood victims' complaints.
She was stung by her father's offhand manner when she told him about her promotion.
tc: Instead of warmly congratulating her, he responded in an almost ______ way and went straight back to reading his newspaper.
'Instead of warmly congratulating' and returning to his paper show the blank means careless and casual.
se: Her ______ reply to the reporter's serious question caused a storm on social media.
casual
Both 'offhand' and 'casual' describe an unthinking, careless reply, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: a small group of people who control a country or organization
x: Our housing society is run by a small oligarchy of residents who never consult anyone else.
Employees complained that the company had become an oligarchy of three senior partners.
In political science class, we compared Sparta's oligarchy with Athenian democracy.
Critics warn that concentrated wealth is slowly turning the democracy into an oligarchy.
Her extended family functioned like an oligarchy in which two uncles decided everything.
tc: Although the country holds elections, real power lies with the ______ of a few wealthy families who control its banks and media.
'Real power lies with... a few wealthy families' defines rule by a small group.
se: A tiny ______ of military officers ruled the country for two decades.
clique
Both 'oligarchy' and 'clique' here mean a small group holding power, so the sentence means the same.

m: suggesting that something bad is going to happen
x: Dark, ominous clouds gathered over Dhaka, warning of the first monsoon storm.
There was an ominous silence in the meeting room after the CEO announced a restructuring.
The professor's ominous warning that the final exam would be 'challenging' kept us studying all night.
Economists see the steady fall in exports as an ominous sign for the coming year.
When her husband said 'we need to talk', the words sounded ominous.
tc: The doctor's long pause before speaking struck the family as ______, and they braced themselves for bad news.
Bracing for bad news shows the blank means suggesting that something bad is coming.
se: The ______ rumble of distant thunder sent picnickers hurrying to their cars.
menacing
Both 'ominous' and 'menacing' describe something that threatens trouble, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: a duty or responsibility, especially the burden of proving something
x: Since I suggested the trip, the onus is on me to book the hotel.
The new policy places the onus on managers to report safety violations.
In a research paper, the onus is on the author to cite every source properly.
In criminal trials, the onus of proof lies with the prosecution, not the accused.
She felt the whole onus of caring for her ailing parents fell on her, while her brothers did nothing.
tc: Because the company made the claim, the ______ is on it, not the public, to prove that its product is safe.
'To prove' and 'not the public' show the blank means the responsibility or burden of proof.
se: The ______ of finding a solution now rests with the government.
responsibility
Both 'onus' and 'responsibility' mean a duty that someone must carry, so the meaning is the same.

m: sounding wise or prophetic but often mysterious and hard to interpret
x: When I asked my grandmother about my future husband, she gave an oracular smile and said, 'You'll know.'
The CEO's oracular memos, full of vague hints, left employees guessing about the merger.
Students struggled with the poet's oracular style, which seems profound but resists clear interpretation.
Markets hang on the central bank chief's oracular statements, parsing every word for clues.
His oracular advice about love, 'follow the river,' baffled me more than it helped.
tc: Followers treated the guru's ______ sayings as prophecies, even though no one could agree on what they actually meant.
'Prophecies' plus 'no one could agree on what they meant' shows the blank means prophetic but obscure.
se: The investor is famous for ______ remarks that hint at future trends without stating anything plainly.
cryptic
Both 'oracular' and 'cryptic' describe mysterious remarks that hint rather than state, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to order or decree something officially
x: As if fate had ordained it, I missed every bus that morning and reached the interview hall just as it closed.
The new regulations ordain that all employees must complete safety training every year.
The university statutes ordain that no student may sit an exam more than three times.
The constitution ordains that general elections must be held every five years.
Her parents believed heaven had ordained their marriage, so divorce was unthinkable to them.
tc: The king chose to ______ a day of national mourning, commanding that all shops close in honor of the fallen soldiers.
'Commanding that all shops close' restates the blank as officially decree.
se: The ancient law would ______ that every son inherit an equal share of the family land.
decree
Both 'ordain' and 'decree' mean to order officially, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: showing too much confidence or pride; arrogant
x: His overweening confidence led him to skip the practice test, and he paid for it on exam day.
The manager's overweening ambition alienated everyone who worked under him.
The scholar's overweening pride kept him from admitting the flaw in his theory.
Historians often blame the empire's collapse on the overweening ambition of its rulers.
Her overweening sense of entitlement made her friends gradually drift away.
tc: His ______ pride would not allow him to admit, even privately, that his rival's plan had been better.
Being unable to admit fault even privately shows the blank means excessive and arrogant.
se: The general's ______ self-confidence led him to underestimate the enemy.
excessive
Both 'overweening' and 'excessive' describe confidence that goes too far, so the meaning is the same.

m: extremely nervous, upset or agitated
x: She was so overwrought after the car accident that she couldn't remember her own phone number.
Don't send that overwrought email to your boss tonight; read it again in the morning.
Reviewers found the novel's prose overwrought, crammed with adjectives and melodramatic speeches.
Overwrought parents crowded outside the school after hearing rumors of a fire.
He became overwrought whenever his girlfriend didn't answer her phone.
tc: Though she had been calm during the crisis, she became ______ afterward, crying and shaking for hours.
'Though she had been calm' contrasts with crying and shaking, so the blank means extremely agitated.
se: The ______ passengers shouted at the airline staff after the third flight delay.
agitated
Both 'overwrought' and 'agitated' mean very upset and excited, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: very small or meager; too little to matter
x: After a full day of work, the delivery rider earned a paltry three hundred taka.
Management offered a paltry two percent raise despite record profits.
The survey's paltry sample of twenty people made its conclusions unreliable.
Critics said the paltry fine would do nothing to stop companies from polluting the river.
She felt insulted by his paltry apology after he forgot her birthday.
tc: Considering the risks the miners take every day, their wages are ______, barely enough to feed a family.
'Barely enough to feed a family' shows the blank means pitifully small.
se: The injured workers received only ______ compensation from the company.
meager
Both 'paltry' and 'meager' mean too small, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to satisfy someone's weak or unworthy desires in order to please them
x: Some parents pander to their children's every whim and then wonder why they are spoiled.
Our marketing team refused to pander to clickbait trends, even when competitors' sensational headlines drew more traffic.
The professor accused textbook publishers of pandering to students who want summaries instead of ideas.
Politicians often pander to voters' fears instead of offering real solutions.
He realized he had pandered to his friend's ego for years just to avoid arguments.
c: pander to the lowest common denominator
tc: Rather than challenge their viewers, many reality shows simply ______ to their taste for scandal and humiliation.
'Rather than challenge' sets up a contrast, so the blank means to indulge unworthy tastes.
se: The newspaper refuses to ______ to readers' appetite for celebrity gossip.
cater
Both 'pander to' and 'cater to' mean to supply what people crave, so the meaning is the same.

m: a complete or impressive range or collection of things
x: The market offered a dazzling panoply of spices, fabrics and street food.
New hires receive a panoply of benefits, from health insurance to free gym membership.
The library holds a panoply of resources for graduate students, including rare manuscripts.
The ceremony featured the full panoply of state power: soldiers, flags and a twenty-one-gun salute.
Their wedding included the whole panoply of Bengali traditions, from the gaye holud to the reception.
tc: The museum's exhibition displays the full ______ of medieval warfare, from swords and shields to siege engines.
'The full' and 'from swords and shields to siege engines' show the blank means a complete range.
se: Doctors can now draw on an entire ______ of treatments for the disease.
array
Both 'panoply' and 'array' mean a wide range, so the sentence means the same.

m: the theft of money entrusted to one's care, especially public funds; embezzlement
x: The club treasurer's peculation came to light when members noticed the fund was nearly empty.
An audit uncovered years of peculation by the finance manager.
The historian's book documents the widespread peculation by colonial administrators that drained the provinces' treasuries.
The minister resigned amid accusations of peculation from the flood relief fund.
She could not forgive her brother's peculation from their late father's estate.
tc: Auditors discovered that the trusted accountant had been quietly diverting public money into his own account, a clear case of ______.
Diverting public money into his own account defines the blank as embezzlement.
se: The mayor was jailed for ______ after millions vanished from the city budget.
embezzlement
Both 'peculation' and 'embezzlement' mean stealing entrusted funds, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: relating to or involving money
x: My uncle helps me with advice, but never with any pecuniary support.
Employees must declare any pecuniary interest in companies that bid for our contracts.
The scholarship offers pecuniary assistance as well as mentoring for first-generation students.
In many countries, lawmakers face penalties for failing to disclose their pecuniary interests in private firms.
Their friendship cooled once pecuniary matters, like who owed whom, came between them.
tc: She volunteered at the clinic for years with no thought of ______ reward, caring only about the patients.
'Volunteered' implies working without pay, so the blank means relating to money.
se: The court ordered the company to pay damages for the ______ losses suffered by customers.
financial
Both 'pecuniary' and 'financial' mean involving money, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: a teacher, especially one who is strict or overly formal
x: My piano teacher was an old-school pedagogue who rapped my knuckles for every wrong note.
Our new trainer is a born pedagogue who can explain complex software in simple terms.
The university honored the retiring pedagogue for forty years of inspiring students.
Educational reformers criticized pedagogues who relied entirely on rote memorization.
He resented his father, who behaved more like a stern pedagogue than a loving parent.
tc: Rather than inspire curiosity, the stern ______ insisted that students copy his notes word for word and never ask questions.
Insisting that students copy his notes shows the blank is a strict teacher.
se: The school's founder was a gifted ______ who trained a whole generation of teachers.
educator
Both 'pedagogue' and 'educator' mean a teacher, so the meaning is the same.

m: in a rushed, confused and disorderly way
x: When the rain started, the picnickers ran pell-mell for their cars.
Staff rushed pell-mell into the meeting room when they heard the CEO had arrived early.
Students dashed pell-mell to the notice board when the admission results were posted.
Investors fled pell-mell from the stock market after the bank collapsed.
Clothes, books and letters were thrown pell-mell into boxes when she moved out of his apartment.
tc: Hearing the fire alarm, the children abandoned all order and ran ______ toward the exits, pushing past one another.
'Abandoned all order' and 'pushing past one another' show the blank means in a disorderly rush.
se: The crowd surged ______ through the gates the moment they opened.
headlong
Both 'pell-mell' and 'headlong' mean in a hasty, uncontrolled rush, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: eternal punishment after death; complete and utter ruin
x: My grandmother always warned us that gambling was the road to perdition.
The company's reckless borrowing sent it straight to financial perdition.
The seminar examined how medieval preachers described the torments of perdition.
Some commentators predicted that the policy would lead the economy to perdition.
He felt that his affair had dragged both of them toward perdition.
tc: The preacher warned sinners that only repentance could save them from eternal ______.
'Repentance could save them' points to the blank as eternal damnation.
se: Without a rescue loan, the struggling airline seemed headed for ______.
ruin
Both 'perdition' and 'ruin' mean complete destruction, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: a long journey or period of wandering, especially through foreign lands
x: After months of peregrination across South America, she finally returned home with a backpack full of souvenirs.
His career has been a peregrination through six companies in four countries.
The biography traces the poet's peregrinations through Europe in search of inspiration.
Scientists tracked the long peregrinations of migratory birds from Siberia to the wetlands of Bangladesh.
Their peregrinations as young lovers, hitchhiking from town to town, are a story they still love to tell.
tc: After decades of ______ from port to port, never settling anywhere, the old sailor finally bought a small house by the sea.
'Never settling anywhere' shows the blank means long wandering travel.
se: The novel follows the hero's long ______ across the deserts of North Africa.
journey
Both 'peregrination' and 'journey' mean long travel, so the meaning is the same.

m: to carry out or commit a harmful, illegal or immoral act
x: Someone in our building has been perpetrating petty thefts from the mailboxes.
The audit revealed that a small group of employees had perpetrated a massive fraud.
The professor warned that students who perpetrate plagiarism face expulsion.
Investigators are still trying to identify who perpetrated the bombing.
She refused to forgive the cruelty he had perpetrated against her during their marriage.
tc: Police believe the same gang went on to ______ a series of bank robberies across three provinces.
'Gang' and 'bank robberies' show the blank means to commit a crime.
se: Prosecutors say the defendant helped ______ one of the largest frauds in the country's history.
commit
Both 'perpetrate' and 'commit' mean to carry out a wrongful act, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: the state of being confused or puzzled
x: I stared in perplexity at the flat-pack instructions, which showed parts I didn't seem to have.
To my perplexity, my boss praised the report he had criticized the day before.
The students' perplexity over the new calculus topic showed clearly on their faces.
Scientists expressed perplexity at the unusual radio signals coming from the distant star.
She looked at him in perplexity, unable to understand why he was suddenly so cold.
tc: The tourist stared at the map in complete ______, unable to work out which of the five identical streets led to the hotel.
'Unable to work out' which street to take shows the blank means confusion.
se: His sudden resignation caused great ______ among his colleagues.
confusion
Both 'perplexity' and 'confusion' mean puzzlement, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: pleasant and friendly in manner and appearance
x: Our new neighbor is a personable young man who greets everyone in the stairwell.
Recruiters look for personable candidates who can deal with clients easily.
The personable teaching assistant made even the shyest students feel comfortable asking questions.
The candidate's personable style won over voters who had found his rival cold.
She was drawn to his personable manner long before she noticed his good looks.
tc: Unlike his cold and aloof predecessor, the new manager was warm and ______, chatting easily with everyone on the shop floor.
'Unlike his cold and aloof predecessor' and 'chatting easily' show the blank means friendly and pleasant.
se: Hotel staff are trained to be ______ and helpful to every guest.
affable
Both 'personable' and 'affable' mean friendly and pleasant, so the meaning is the same.

m: deliberately unreasonable or contrary; showing a stubborn wish to act wrongly
x: My brother takes a perverse pleasure in spoiling the endings of films.
It seemed perverse to cut the training budget just as the company was hiring new staff.
The study found a perverse effect: the anti-smoking ads actually made some teenagers want to smoke.
Critics argue the subsidy creates perverse incentives that end up rewarding polluters.
Out of some perverse pride, she refused to call him even though she missed him terribly.
tc: With ______ stubbornness, the child refused every dessert simply because his parents wanted him to choose one.
Refusing simply because his parents wanted him to choose shows the blank means deliberately contrary.
se: It would be ______ to reject an offer that gives you everything you asked for.
unreasonable
Both 'perverse' and 'unreasonable' describe going against good sense, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: a tendency to expect the worst or to see the bad side of things
x: Her pessimism about the weather made her pack an umbrella even on sunny days.
A mood of pessimism spread through the office after the second round of layoffs.
His pessimism about passing the GRE faded once his practice scores began to rise.
Economic pessimism has led many families to postpone buying homes.
Her husband's constant pessimism wore her down until she stopped sharing her plans with him.
tc: Despite the encouraging test results, the patient clung to his ______, convinced that he would never fully recover.
'Despite the encouraging test results' contrasts with expecting never to recover, so the blank means expecting the worst.
se: Investor ______ deepened as the currency fell to a record low.
gloom
Both 'pessimism' and 'gloom' describe a negative outlook, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to frighten someone so much that they cannot move or think
x: Thunderstorms used to petrify my little sister, who would hide under the bed.
Public speaking petrifies him, so he rehearses every presentation a dozen times.
The thought of her thesis defense petrified her more than writing the thesis itself.
Reports of a man-eating tiger near the village petrified residents on the edge of the Sundarbans.
He was petrified that she would say no, so he waited a whole year before proposing.
tc: The roar from the darkness seemed to ______ the hikers, who stood frozen, unable to run or even scream.
'Stood frozen, unable to run or even scream' shows the blank means to terrify into stillness.
se: Heights ______ me, so I never go near the edge of a cliff.
terrify
Both 'petrify' and 'terrify' mean to frighten badly, so the meaning is the same.

m: a person who is indifferent or hostile to art, culture and intellectual pursuits
x: My uncle calls himself a philistine and happily admits he would rather watch cricket than visit any museum.
Only a philistine would suggest tearing down the old library to build another parking garage.
The professor dismissed anyone who skipped the poetry seminar as a philistine, which seemed a little unfair.
Critics accused the city council of behaving like philistines when it cut all funding for public theatre.
I felt like a complete philistine at the gallery opening, nodding at paintings I didn't understand at all.
tc: Far from being a lover of the arts, the new owner proved to be the kind of ______ who saw the gallery's paintings only as items to sell.
'Far from being a lover of the arts' signals the opposite: a person with no regard for culture.
se: Members of the music society regard anyone who calls opera a waste of time as the worst kind of ______.
barbarian
In this context both 'philistine' and 'barbarian' describe someone with no appreciation for culture.

m: the act of presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own
x: The university uses software to check every thesis for plagiarism before it can be submitted.
After the plagiarism was discovered, the journalist lost her column and issued a public apology.
Copying a paragraph from Wikipedia without citing it counts as plagiarism, even in a school assignment.
Our manager was furious when a rival agency's pitch turned out to be outright plagiarism of our campaign.
He felt betrayed when his closest friend was accused of plagiarism and never denied it.
tc: Because the essay reproduced whole pages from a published book without any citation, the committee had no choice but to treat it as ______.
Reproducing pages from someone else's book without citation is the definition of the missing word.
se: The editor withdrew the article after readers pointed out clear signs of ______ from an earlier blog post.
copying
Both words mean taking another writer's work without credit, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: sounding sad and mournful, often as if pleading
x: The plaintive cry of a stray kitten kept us awake for most of the night.
Her plaintive emails asking for an extension went unanswered until the deadline had passed.
The documentary opens with the plaintive call of a loon echoing across an empty lake.
A plaintive melody drifted from a flute player on the riverbank as the monsoon clouds gathered.
He looked at me with plaintive eyes, silently begging me not to leave so soon.
tc: Unlike the cheerful tunes of the festival, the old woman's song was slow and ______, full of grief for her lost son.
The contrast with 'cheerful' and the phrase 'full of grief' show the blank means sad and mournful.
se: From somewhere down the hall came the ______ wail of a child who had lost his mother in the crowd.
mournful
Both 'plaintive' and 'mournful' describe a sad, sorrowful sound, giving the same meaning.

m: loud, deep and resonant, with a sad or mournful quality
x: The plangent tolling of the church bell announced the funeral to the whole village.
Critics praised the cellist's plangent tone, which seemed to fill every corner of the concert hall.
In the lecture, the musicologist explained how minor keys give folk ballads their plangent quality.
A plangent foghorn sounded across the harbor as the ferry crept into port.
Her plangent voice on the phone told me something terrible had happened before she said a word.
tc: The guitarist's ______ chords, both deep and sorrowful, rang through the silent hall long after he had stopped playing.
'Both deep and sorrowful' and 'rang through the hall' define a sound that is resonant and mournful.
se: The ______ notes of the bagpipes echoed across the cemetery as the coffin was lowered.
mournful
At a funeral, both 'plangent' and 'mournful' describe the sad, echoing music in the same way.

m: easily shaped or molded; capable of being changed or influenced
x: Young children's minds are remarkably plastic, which is why they pick up new languages so quickly.
Clay stays plastic only as long as it is kept damp and covered.
Neuroscientists once believed the adult brain was fixed, but research shows it remains plastic throughout life.
Our startup's culture is still plastic enough that a few new hires could reshape it completely.
At nineteen my opinions were plastic, and every persuasive friend seemed to reshape them a little.
tc: Wax is useful to sculptors because, unlike hard stone, it remains soft and ______ enough to be reshaped again and again.
The contrast with 'hard stone' and the phrase 'reshaped again and again' point to a word meaning easily molded.
se: When heated, the glass becomes ______ and the artisan can stretch it into delicate shapes.
malleable
Both words mean soft enough to be shaped, so the sentence means the same either way.

m: belonging to ordinary people; common, unrefined or lacking sophistication
x: My aunt considers instant noodles a plebeian meal, but I eat them happily three times a week.
The club's members looked down on anything they thought plebeian, from football to fast food.
Historians note that plebeian citizens in ancient Rome eventually won the right to hold high office.
Some colleagues sneered at his plebeian accent, yet he became the most respected manager in the firm.
She worried her parents would find her new boyfriend too plebeian, so she delayed introducing them.
tc: The duchess, who prided herself on her refined tastes, dismissed the fairground's cheap snacks and loud music as hopelessly ______.
Someone proud of 'refined tastes' would dismiss cheap, loud entertainment as common and unrefined.
se: Although he became a wealthy banker, he never lost his fondness for ______ pleasures like street food and cheap cinema.
lowbrow
Both 'plebeian' and 'lowbrow' describe simple, unsophisticated pleasures of ordinary people.

m: an abundance; the condition of being full or plentiful
x: The farmers' market offers a plenitude of fresh vegetables every Saturday morning.
During the monsoon, Bangladesh enjoys a plenitude of rain that keeps its rice paddies green for months.
The new archive gives researchers a plenitude of letters and diaries to study.
Despite a plenitude of job applicants, the company struggled to find anyone with the right skills.
She spoke of her childhood as a time of plenitude, full of love, laughter and long summer afternoons.
tc: After years of drought and scarcity, the village finally enjoyed a season of ______, with granaries filled to the brim.
The contrast with 'drought and scarcity' and 'filled to the brim' show the blank means abundance.
se: The reef's ______ of marine life amazes every diver who visits.
abundance
Both words mean a great quantity, so the reef's rich marine life is described the same way.

m: easily bent or shaped; also easily influenced or persuaded
x: Soak the willow branches overnight so they become pliable enough to weave into a basket.
The new manager hoped the junior staff would be pliable and accept his changes without complaint.
Engineers have developed a pliable plastic that can bend thousands of times without cracking.
Leather becomes more pliable with wear, so my shoes are finally comfortable after a month.
He chose a pliable partner who rarely argued, but he soon grew bored of always getting his way.
tc: The dough had dried out and cracked, so the baker added water until it was soft and ______ again.
Dough that had 'dried out and cracked' needs to become easy to bend and shape again.
se: Copper wire is ______ enough to be twisted into almost any shape by hand.
flexible
Both words mean easily bent, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: bending easily; also readily yielding to the will or influence of others
x: Young bamboo shoots are pliant and sway in even the gentlest breeze.
Critics said the board had become too pliant, approving whatever the chief executive proposed.
Gymnasts train for years to keep their muscles strong yet pliant.
Dictators often prefer a pliant press that repeats the official version of events.
She was no longer the pliant teenager who did whatever her older brother told her.
tc: The general wanted his deputy to be ______, following orders without question rather than challenging him.
'Following orders without question' restates the meaning of the blank: easily yielding to others.
se: Investors worried that the regulator had grown ______ and would no longer stand up to the big banks.
compliant
Both words describe someone who gives in easily, so 'no longer stand up to' fits either.

m: government by the wealthy, or a society ruled by a small rich class
x: Many voters feel their country has drifted toward plutocracy, with billionaires shaping every major policy.
In our political science seminar, we debated whether huge campaign donations turn democracy into plutocracy.
The novel depicts a future plutocracy where only property owners are allowed to vote.
My grandfather used to joke that the housing society committee was a plutocracy run by the three richest families.
Critics warn that unlimited lobbying will slowly transform the government into a plutocracy.
tc: Since only the richest landowners could vote or hold office, historians describe the city-state's system as ______, not democracy.
Power held only by 'the richest landowners' defines rule by the wealthy.
se: When a handful of wealthy families control both the media and the parliament, the result is ______ disguised as democracy.
oligarchy
Both words describe rule by a small, powerful (here wealthy) group, giving the same meaning.

m: graceful calm and self-control, especially under pressure
x: Even when the microphone failed, the young speaker handled the moment with remarkable poise.
Interviewers look for candidates who show poise when faced with difficult questions.
The batsman's poise under pressure helped Bangladesh chase down the target in the final over.
She regained her poise after stumbling on the stairs and carried on as if nothing had happened.
Ballet teaches children not only graceful movement but also poise and confidence.
tc: Though the audience heckled him loudly, the comedian never lost his ______ and calmly finished his set.
'Though ... heckled' sets up a contrast, and 'calmly finished' shows he kept his self-control.
se: The pilot's ______ during the emergency landing reassured the frightened passengers.
composure
Both words mean calm self-control, which is what would reassure frightened passengers.

m: wise and shrewd in practical matters; tactful and prudent
x: It seemed politic to say nothing about the burnt rice at my mother-in-law's dinner.
She decided it would be more politic to raise her concerns privately rather than in the meeting.
The professor thought it politic to praise the reviewer's comments before rejecting most of them.
Given the tense negotiations, the minister made the politic choice of delaying the announcement.
Telling your partner exactly what you think of their friends is not always the most politic thing to do.
tc: Rather than openly contradicting her boss in front of the clients, she thought it more ______ to wait and discuss the error privately.
Choosing to wait and speak privately instead of contradicting openly shows tactful, prudent judgment.
se: With the election only weeks away, the senator judged it ______ to avoid commenting on the controversial bill.
prudent
Both words mean wise and sensible in the circumstances, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: an utter coward
x: In the old adventure novel, the villain is revealed as a poltroon who flees at the first sign of danger.
My grandfather called anyone who backed away from a challenge a poltroon, a word that made us children laugh.
Historians have unfairly painted the general as a poltroon, ignoring the impossible odds he faced.
He felt like a poltroon for not standing up to the bully who mocked his little brother.
Refusing to be seen as a poltroon, the team captain went out to face the angry fans himself.
tc: Far from being the brave knight he claimed to be, Sir Robin turned out to be the worst kind of ______, running away from every battle.
'Far from being brave' and 'running away from every battle' point to a coward.
se: The soldiers despised their officer, calling him the worst ______ in the regiment for hiding during the attack.
coward
Both words mean a person lacking courage, which matches hiding during an attack.

m: self-important and showing off in a grand, solemn or affected way
x: Our neighbor gives pompous speeches about his garden as if he had won a national prize.
The new director's pompous memos, full of jargon and grand claims, quickly became an office joke.
Students groaned whenever the pompous lecturer quoted his own books for the third time in an hour.
Nobody in the flooded villages was impressed by the minister's pompous statement about 'historic achievements'.
I love my cousin, but he gets a bit pompous whenever he talks about his time at Oxford.
tc: Unlike his modest predecessor, the new mayor was ______, filling every speech with grand phrases about his own importance.
The contrast with 'modest' and 'his own importance' show the blank means self-important.
se: The critic's ______ review, stuffed with long words and references to his own expertise, irritated many readers.
pretentious
Both words describe showy self-importance, so the review is characterized the same way.

m: to put forward or assume something as a fact or basis for argument
x: Some economists posit that remote work will permanently lower office rents in big cities.
In her thesis, she posits a link between childhood bilingualism and later problem-solving skills.
Physicists posited the existence of the particle decades before anyone was able to detect it.
Our consultant posited that customer complaints, not prices, were driving people away.
My friend posits that every argument with his wife starts because someone is hungry.
tc: Lacking direct evidence, the astronomers could only ______ the existence of the unseen planet, assuming it was there to explain the star's wobble.
'Lacking direct evidence' and 'assuming it was there' show they could only propose it as a premise.
se: Some scientists ______ that life on Earth began near deep-sea volcanic vents.
hypothesize
Both verbs mean to put forward an idea as a basis for reasoning, giving the same meaning.

m: to assume or claim something as true, as the basis for reasoning or a theory
x: Einstein postulated that the speed of light is the same for every observer.
The researchers postulate that rising sea temperatures are driving the fish northward.
Our marketing team postulated that younger customers would prefer the app to the website.
Philosophers have long postulated a fundamental difference between mind and body.
My mother postulated, quite correctly, that I had eaten the last mango while she was out.
tc: Without any way to observe dark matter directly, scientists can only ______ its existence to explain how galaxies hold together.
'Without any way to observe' shows they must assume it exists as the basis of a theory.
se: Early geologists began to ______ that the continents had once been joined together.
theorize
Both verbs mean to put forward an idea as a theory, so the sentence means the same.

m: a ruler with great power, especially an autocratic monarch
x: The museum displays jewels that once belonged to a powerful Mughal potentate.
Our chief executive acts like a potentate, issuing decrees and expecting everyone to obey without question.
The history course examines how ancient potentates used grand monuments to display their power.
Foreign potentates arrived for the summit in long motorcades of black cars.
My father rules the dinner table like a little potentate, deciding who speaks and when.
tc: The old king was the kind of ______ whose word was law, ruling without parliament or courts to check his power.
'Whose word was law' and 'without ... courts to check his power' describe an all-powerful ruler.
se: The ______ of the desert kingdom held absolute power over his subjects.
monarch
Both words name a powerful ruler of a kingdom, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to talk at length in a foolish, childish or trivial way
x: My little niece prattled happily about her new kitten all the way to school.
He prattled on about his holiday for twenty minutes while the meeting fell behind schedule.
During his viva, the nervous student prattled about irrelevant details instead of answering the examiner's question.
Talk-show hosts prattle endlessly about celebrity gossip while serious news goes unreported.
She liked to prattle about nothing in particular, and I found that oddly comforting after long days.
tc: Rather than get to the point, my seatmate would ______ for hours about his cats, his diet and his dreams.
'Rather than get to the point' and the list of trivial topics show the blank means to talk foolishly at length.
se: The children began to ______ excitedly about the circus the moment they climbed into the car.
chatter
Both verbs mean to talk rapidly about trivial things, which fits excited children.

m: an earlier event or decision used as an example or guide for later cases
x: Letting one student submit late would set a precedent that the others would expect to follow.
The court's ruling established an important precedent for future cases of online defamation.
There is no precedent in our company for promoting an intern straight to manager.
The pandemic created challenges without precedent for hospitals around the world.
If you lend your brother money once, you set a precedent he will certainly remember.
tc: Since nothing similar had ever happened before, the judges had no ______ to guide their decision.
'Nothing similar had ever happened before' means there was no earlier case to serve as a guide.
se: The landmark decision became an important ______ for later civil rights cases.
model
Both words mean an earlier case that later ones follow, so the meaning is the same.

m: a very steep cliff; figuratively, the brink of disaster
x: We stopped at the edge of the precipice and looked down at the river far below.
Economists warn that the country is standing on the precipice of a severe recession.
The geologist explained how centuries of erosion had carved the sheer precipice.
Our company was teetering on the precipice of bankruptcy until a new investor stepped in.
After the breakup, she felt as if she were standing on a precipice, unsure what came next.
tc: One wrong step on the narrow mountain path would send a climber over the ______ and hundreds of meters down to the rocks.
Falling 'hundreds of meters down' from a mountain path points to a steep cliff.
se: With debts mounting and sales collapsing, the firm stood on the ______ of ruin.
brink
'On the brink of ruin' and 'on the precipice of ruin' both mean very close to disaster.

m: exact and accurate in every detail; careful about details
x: Please give me the precise time your flight lands so I can pick you up.
Our client wants precise figures, not rough estimates, in the final report.
Scientific instruments must be precise enough to measure changes of a fraction of a millimeter.
At that precise moment, the power went out and the whole stadium fell dark.
He is precise in everything he does, from folding his shirts to writing birthday cards.
tc: Unlike the vague estimates in his first draft, the engineer's final calculations were ______ down to the last millimeter.
The contrast with 'vague estimates' and 'down to the last millimeter' signal exactness.
se: The recipe calls for ______ measurements, so don't just guess the amount of flour.
exact
Both words mean accurate in detail, the opposite of guessing.

m: an idea or opinion formed beforehand without adequate knowledge or experience
x: I had a preconception that Dhaka would be unbearable, but I quickly fell in love with the city.
Good interviewers try to set aside their preconceptions about a candidate's background.
The study challenges common preconceptions about how teenagers use social media.
Travel has a way of breaking down our preconceptions about other cultures.
She came to the first date without any preconceptions, which made it easier to enjoy.
tc: The documentary forced viewers to abandon every ______ they had about prison life by showing a reality they had never imagined.
Ideas that must be abandoned when faced with an unimagined reality were opinions formed beforehand.
se: Try to approach the case with no ______ about who is guilty until you have heard all the evidence.
assumption
Both words mean a belief formed in advance, which the evidence should come before.

m: present as the strongest or main element; most common or influential
x: Rice is the predominant crop in the fertile delta regions of Bangladesh.
The predominant view in the office is that the new software creates more problems than it solves.
Researchers found that anxiety, not laziness, was the predominant cause of students missing deadlines.
Rising prices remain the predominant concern of voters in this year's election.
Relief was the predominant feeling when I finally heard my sister's voice on the phone.
tc: Although several dialects are spoken in the region, English remains the ______ language of business, used in nearly every company.
'Used in nearly every company' shows English is the main, most common language.
se: Fear was the ______ emotion among residents in the days after the earthquake.
dominant
Both words mean the strongest or most widespread, so the sentence means the same.

m: surpassing all others; most distinguished or outstanding
x: She is the preeminent expert on tropical diseases in the entire country.
Our firm has become the preeminent supplier of solar panels in the region.
Students hoping to study law often apply to the preeminent universities in Britain and America.
The city was once the preeminent trading port on the Bay of Bengal.
For my grandmother, family loyalty was the preeminent value, more important than wealth or success.
tc: Surpassing all her rivals in every competition, the young pianist quickly became the ______ performer of her generation.
'Surpassing all her rivals' defines being above everyone else.
se: He was regarded as the ______ authority on medieval manuscripts, consulted by scholars from around the world.
foremost
Both words mean leading or most distinguished, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to take action to prevent something expected from happening; to forestall
x: I booked the restaurant early to preempt any argument about where to celebrate.
The company cut prices to preempt a rival's expected entry into the market.
Good teachers preempt confusion by explaining common mistakes before students make them.
The government released the report itself, hoping to preempt damaging leaks to the press.
