She apologized quickly to preempt a fight, knowing how sensitive her husband was about money.
tc: Hoping to ______ criticism before it began, the author addressed the most obvious objections in her book's opening chapter.
'Before it began' shows she acted in advance to prevent the expected criticism.
se: The coach changed tactics at halftime to ______ the opponent's expected counterattack.
forestall
Both verbs mean to act first to prevent something anticipated.

m: to think out or plan an action, especially a crime, beforehand
x: The jury had to decide whether the defendant had premeditated the attack or acted in sudden anger.
Her resignation wasn't impulsive; she had premeditated every step for months.
Criminology students learn how prosecutors prove that a killer premeditated the crime.
Police said the robbers had clearly premeditated the heist, studying the bank's routines for weeks.
I didn't premeditate my outburst at dinner; it simply burst out of me after a long, frustrating day.
tc: The theft was no spur-of-the-moment act; the evidence showed the thieves had taken weeks to ______ every detail.
'No spur-of-the-moment act' and 'taken weeks' show the crime was planned in advance.
se: Investigators believe the gang began to ______ the kidnapping long before it took place.
plan
Both verbs mean to work out an action in advance, so the sentence means the same.

m: the quality of being greater in number, weight or importance
x: There is a preponderance of young people in the city's tech industry.
The judge ruled on the preponderance of the evidence rather than on a single witness's account.
A preponderance of studies suggests that regular exercise improves mood.
Given the preponderance of complaints about the canteen, management finally changed the caterer.
Despite a preponderance of happy memories, she still thought of their marriage with some sadness.
tc: Although a few studies found no effect, the ______ of research points clearly to a link between sleep and memory.
The contrast with 'a few studies' shows the blank means the greater part of the research.
se: The ______ of the evidence suggested that the fire had started in the kitchen.
bulk
Both words mean the greater part, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: completely absurd, unreasonable or ridiculous
x: It's preposterous to expect anyone to cross Dhaka in twenty minutes during rush hour.
The vendor quoted a preposterous price for fixing a single cracked screen.
Early critics called the theory of continental drift preposterous, but evidence later proved it right.
Voters rejected the preposterous claim that the new bridge would cost taxpayers nothing.
Their friends found it preposterous that the couple had met while stuck together in an elevator.
tc: The claim that the ancient pyramids were built in a single summer is so ______ that no serious historian has ever considered it.
A claim no serious historian would consider must be completely absurd.
se: She laughed at the ______ suggestion that her cat had learned to open the refrigerator.
absurd
Both words mean ridiculous and unbelievable, which is why she laughed.

m: a special right or privilege belonging to a particular person or group
x: It's a host's prerogative to decide whether guests take off their shoes at the door.
Setting the team's budget is the manager's prerogative, not ours.
Granting pardons is traditionally the prerogative of the head of state.
Choosing a research topic is every doctoral student's prerogative, though advisors often have strong opinions.
Changing her mind about the wedding venue was her prerogative, and her fiancé knew better than to argue.
tc: Because the constitution grants the president alone the power to dissolve parliament, that decision is his ______ and no one else's.
A power granted to 'the president alone' is a special right belonging only to him.
se: Whether to accept the job offer is entirely your ______; nobody else can make the decision for you.
right
Both words mean something you alone are entitled to decide, so the meaning is the same.

m: to be a sign or warning that something, usually bad, will happen
x: Dark clouds over the Bay of Bengal often presage a cyclone.
Falling orders presaged the layoffs that came later that year.
Some economists argue that the current housing boom presages a painful crash.
Her sudden silence at dinner presaged the difficult conversation we had later that night.
In the novel, a dead bird on the doorstep presages the tragedy that will strike the family.
tc: Sailors believed that a red sky at dawn would ______ a storm later in the day.
A sign seen at dawn of something 'later in the day' means a warning of what is to come.
se: Analysts fear the sudden drop in exports may ______ a wider economic slowdown.
portend
Both verbs mean to be a sign of something bad to come, so the sentence means the same.

m: to state with authority what must be done, such as a rule, course of action or medical treatment
x: The doctor prescribed antibiotics and told me to rest for a week.
Company policy prescribes exactly how expense claims must be submitted.
The syllabus prescribes three novels that every student must read before the exam.
The law prescribes a heavy fine for anyone caught littering in public parks.
My grandmother prescribed hot ginger tea for every illness, from colds to heartbreak.
tc: Tradition continues to ______ exactly how the ceremony must be performed, leaving the priests no room to improvise.
'Exactly how ... must be performed' and 'no room to improvise' show that tradition lays down the rules.
se: The regulations ______ that all food handlers wear gloves and hairnets.
stipulate
Both verbs mean to lay down as a requirement, giving the same meaning.

m: an intuitive feeling that something, especially something bad, is about to happen
x: I had a presentiment that the trip would go wrong, and our flight was cancelled that morning.
Several employees had a presentiment of layoffs long before management announced anything.
Psychologists study why people sometimes report presentiments shortly before disasters.
Villagers spoke of a strange presentiment in the air the night before the flood.
She couldn't shake a presentiment that her father was ill, so she called home immediately.
tc: Though nothing had gone wrong yet, she could not shake the ______ that something terrible was about to happen.
'Nothing had gone wrong yet' plus 'about to happen' describe a feeling of coming trouble.
se: The old sailor's ______ of danger made him refuse to go out to sea that morning.
premonition
Both words mean an intuitive feeling that something bad will happen.

m: beyond what is normal or natural; extraordinary, sometimes seemingly supernatural
x: Our cat has a preternatural ability to appear the moment anyone opens the fridge.
The new analyst showed a preternatural talent for spotting errors in long spreadsheets.
The young mathematician solved the problem with preternatural speed, astonishing her professors.
A preternatural calm settled over the city in the hours before the hurricane arrived.
He had a preternatural sense of when his mother was upset, even over the phone.
tc: Her memory was so far beyond anything ordinary that her teachers described it as almost ______.
'So far beyond anything ordinary' restates the meaning of the blank.
se: The goalkeeper's ______ reflexes allowed him to stop shots that seemed impossible to save.
uncanny
Both words describe abilities so remarkable they seem beyond normal explanation.

m: a false reason given to hide the real reason for an action
x: He called me on the pretext of returning a book, but he really wanted to apologize.
The company used the downturn as a pretext for cutting staff it had wanted to fire anyway.
She went to the library on the pretext of studying, though she mostly chatted with friends.
Historians agree that the border incident was merely a pretext for invasion.
My cousin invented a pretext to leave the family dinner early so he could meet his girlfriend.
tc: Claiming to check the gas meter was just the ______ he used to get inside; his real aim was to steal.
'His real aim was to steal' shows the stated reason was false cover for the true one.
se: The dictator used a minor protest as the ______ for imposing martial law.
excuse
Both words mean a false justification for an action, so the meaning is the same.

m: to prove more powerful or successful; to win out over opposition
x: After a long debate about where to eat, my sister's choice prevailed as usual.
Common sense prevailed, and the board decided not to launch the product before proper testing.
In the end, the defending champions prevailed over Sri Lanka by just two runs.
Scientists hope that evidence will prevail over rumor in the public debate about vaccines.
Their love prevailed despite years of distance and disapproving relatives.
tc: Although the rebels were heavily outnumbered, their courage helped them ______ against the much stronger army.
'Although ... outnumbered' sets up a contrast: despite the odds, they won.
se: In a close vote, the reformers managed to ______ over the old guard.
triumph
Both verbs mean to win against opposition, so the sentence means the same.

m: stiffly formal and proper, and easily shocked by anything improper
x: My prim aunt sat upright on the sofa and refused to laugh at any of the jokes.
Her prim email reminding everyone about the dress code made the whole office roll its eyes.
The prim headmistress insisted that girls' skirts reach well below the knee.
Victorian novels often mock prim characters who are shocked by any mention of romance.
He found her a little prim at first, but she turned out to have a wicked sense of humor.
tc: Unlike her easygoing sister, who laughed at every joke, Margaret was so ______ that she blushed at the mildest innuendo.
The contrast with 'easygoing' and blushing at mild innuendo point to someone stiffly proper.
se: The ______ librarian frowned at the teenagers holding hands in the reading room.
prudish
Both words describe someone easily offended by anything improper.

m: relating to the earliest stage or most basic instincts; fundamental
x: Fear of the dark seems to be a primal instinct that many adults never fully outgrow.
Some advertisers deliberately appeal to primal urges like hunger and the desire for status.
The anthropologist argued that rhythm and dance satisfy a primal human need for connection.
A primal roar rose from the crowd as the home team scored in the final minute.
Holding her newborn son, she felt a primal urge to protect him from everything.
tc: Hunger, fear and the urge to protect our young are ______ drives, rooted in the earliest stages of human evolution.
'Rooted in the earliest stages of human evolution' defines the blank as basic and original.
se: The horror film plays on our ______ fear of being hunted in the dark.
instinctive
Both words describe a deep, inborn fear rather than a learned one.

m: existing at or from the very beginning of time; original and earliest
x: Scientists believe life first emerged from a primordial soup of simple chemicals.
Astronomers study the faint radiation left over from the primordial universe.
The forest felt primordial, as if no human had ever walked beneath its giant trees.
In our office, the rivalry between sales and engineering seems almost primordial, older than anyone can remember.
She felt a primordial bond with the ocean, as though she had always belonged there.
tc: Billions of years before the first cells appeared, the young Earth was covered by ______ oceans rich in simple chemicals.
'Billions of years before the first cells appeared' points to the very earliest times.
se: The explorers hiked through dense, ______ forests that had stood untouched since the last ice age.
primeval
Both words mean existing from the earliest times, so the forest is described the same way.

m: a state of lacking basic necessities such as food, warmth or shelter
x: My grandparents rarely spoke about the privation they endured during the 1971 war.
Many refugees suffered years of privation before finally being resettled abroad.
The study tracks how childhood privation affects health and income in later life.
Workers at the remote mining camp endured harsh privation during the long winter.
Having known privation as a boy, he never wasted food and always helped those in need.
tc: During the siege, the citizens lived in such ______ that they had neither food nor fuel to survive the winter.
'Neither food nor fuel' describes a lack of basic necessities.
se: The explorers endured great ______ on their journey across the frozen continent.
hardship
Both words mean suffering caused by a lack of basic needs.

m: to hold out or offer something for someone to accept
x: The waiter proffered a plate of sweets as we sat down.
She proffered her resignation, but the board refused to accept it.
Students proffered several theories during the seminar, but none convinced the professor.
The government proffered emergency aid to the flood victims within hours of the disaster.
He proffered his hand in reconciliation, and after a long pause his brother shook it.
tc: Eager to make peace, the general decided to ______ an olive branch to his former enemies rather than withhold it.
'Eager to make peace' and the contrast with 'withhold' show the blank means to offer.
se: Several colleagues tried to ______ advice, but she preferred to solve the problem herself.
offer
Both verbs mean to present something for someone to accept.

m: so high, especially in cost, as to prevent people from buying or doing something
x: The rent in that neighborhood is prohibitive for most young families.
We abandoned the project because the cost of the new software was prohibitive.
For many talented students, the prohibitive fees at foreign universities make scholarships essential.
Prohibitive import taxes have made electric cars a rarity in the country.
Long-distance calls used to be so prohibitive that my father phoned his brother only once a month.
tc: The treatment works well, but its ______ cost means only the very wealthy can afford it.
'Only the very wealthy can afford it' shows the cost is high enough to keep most people out.
se: The airline's ______ baggage fees have driven many travelers to cheaper rivals.
exorbitant
Both words mean unreasonably high, which explains why travelers left.

m: relating to the working class, especially industrial wage earners
x: He was proud of his proletarian roots and often talked about his father's years in the jute mill.
The union leader's plain, proletarian way of speaking won him support on the factory floor.
Marxist historians have devoted much of their research to proletarian movements in nineteenth-century Europe.
The restaurant serves proletarian dishes like fish and chips at very bourgeois prices.
Despite her wealth, she kept her proletarian habits and still took the bus to work.
tc: Unlike the wealthy landowners who ruled the town, the strikers came from ______ families who had worked in the factories for generations.
The contrast with 'wealthy landowners' and 'worked in the factories' point to the working class.
se: The novel portrays ______ life in the industrial towns of northern England.
working-class
Both words describe the lives of industrial workers, so the meaning is the same.

m: nearness in place, time or relationship; proximity
x: The propinquity of the school to our flat means my children can walk there in five minutes.
Sociologists have found that propinquity is one of the strongest predictors of friendship.
Office propinquity often leads to romance between colleagues who sit side by side.
The two nations' geographic propinquity has made trade between them natural for centuries.
Their constant propinquity during the long lockdown either strengthened couples or drove them apart.
tc: Because the two families lived next door for decades, their friendship grew less from shared interests than from simple ______.
'Lived next door for decades' shows the friendship grew from physical nearness.
se: The hotel's main selling point is its ______ to the beach, just a two-minute walk away.
proximity
Both words mean nearness, and 'a two-minute walk away' confirms it.

m: a person who argues in favor of an idea, cause or policy
x: My father is a strong proponent of eating dinner together as a family every night.
Proponents of the four-day work week say it boosts productivity and morale.
She is a leading proponent of teaching coding in primary schools.
Proponents of the new dam argue it will reduce flooding, while critics fear for local fisheries.
As a proponent of open communication, he always told his partner exactly how he felt.
tc: While critics call the policy reckless, its most enthusiastic ______ insists that it will create thousands of jobs.
'While critics call it reckless' sets up a contrast with someone who supports the policy.
se: She has long been the most vocal ______ of renewable energy on the city council.
advocate
Both words mean a person who publicly supports a cause.

m: to try to convert people to one's religion, beliefs or opinions
x: My vegan roommate proselytizes about plant-based diets at every single meal.
Some employees complained that the new manager proselytized constantly about his favorite productivity app.
Laws in several countries forbid foreign missionaries from proselytizing in public places.
The professor never proselytized for her own theory, preferring students to reach their own conclusions.
He used to proselytize about running until his friends begged him to talk about anything else.
tc: Rather than practice his faith quietly, the new neighbor seemed determined to ______, knocking on every door to win converts.
'Rather than ... quietly' and 'to win converts' show the blank means to try to convert others.
se: Ever since discovering yoga, my aunt has started to ______ to anyone who will listen.
preach
Both verbs mean to urge one's beliefs on others, giving the same meaning.

m: lying stretched out face down; or completely overcome and helpless, as with grief or exhaustion
x: After the marathon, several runners lay prostrate on the grass, too tired to move.
Worshippers lay prostrate on the mosque floor during the evening prayer.
Half the office was prostrate with flu during the first week of January.
The economy lay prostrate after years of war and sanctions.
She was prostrate with grief after her mother's sudden death.
tc: After hearing of his son's death, the old man was ______ with grief, unable to eat, speak or rise from his bed.
'Unable to eat, speak or rise' describes someone completely overcome and helpless.
se: Weeks of drought left the farmers ______ with despair, unsure how they would survive the year.
overcome
Both words mean completely overwhelmed by an emotion, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: able to change frequently or easily; versatile and adaptable
x: My friend is a protean cook who can switch from Thai curries to French pastries with ease.
The company needs protean employees who can handle sales, design and customer support.
Scholars still discuss the protean career of an artist who painted, sculpted and wrote poetry.
Viruses are protean enemies, constantly mutating to escape our vaccines.
Her protean moods made it hard for her friends to predict how she would react.
tc: An actor of extraordinary range, she was ______ enough to play a queen one night and a beggar the next.
'Extraordinary range' and playing opposite roles show the blank means versatile and changeable.
se: The ______ musician moved easily between jazz, classical and rock.
versatile
Both words mean able to adapt to many different forms or styles.

m: the place of origin or the documented history of ownership of something
x: Before buying the antique chair, ask the dealer about its provenance.
Our supplier must prove the provenance of every bale of cotton it sells us.
Archivists spent months tracing the provenance of the medieval manuscript.
The museum returned the statue after investigators discovered its provenance had been faked.
My grandmother's necklace has a romantic provenance: my grandfather bought it with his first salary.
tc: Because no one could document where the painting came from or who had owned it, its ______ remained a mystery to experts.
'Where the painting came from or who had owned it' defines the blank as origin and ownership history.
se: Customers increasingly want to know the ______ of the food they eat, from farm to plate.
origin
Both words mean where something comes from, as 'from farm to plate' shows.

m: referred to in a well-known saying; or so widely known as to be legendary
x: I was like the proverbial kid in a candy store when I walked into that huge bookshop.
Finding the bug in a million lines of code was like searching for the proverbial needle in a haystack.
The professor's absent-mindedness was proverbial; students joked that he once lectured to an empty room.
Rising fuel prices were the proverbial last straw for many struggling families.
When the baby finally slept through the night, we felt we had reached the proverbial light at the end of the tunnel.
c: the proverbial needle in a haystack
tc: His stinginess was so famous across the village that it had become ______, the subject of countless jokes and sayings.
'So famous' and 'the subject of countless jokes and sayings' show the trait had become legendary.
se: Her generosity was ______ among her friends, who could all tell stories of her kindness.
legendary
Both words mean so well known that it is talked about by everyone.

m: making careful preparation for the future, especially by saving money
x: A provident shopper, my mother always kept extra rice and lentils in case prices rose.
The company's provident decision to build cash reserves helped it survive the downturn.
In our personal finance course, we learned why provident savers enjoy a more comfortable retirement.
Provident governments set aside revenue in good years to cushion the impact of future crises.

tc: Unlike his improvident brother, who spent every paycheck at once, Karim was ______ and put money aside each month for emergencies.
The contrast with 'improvident' and 'put money aside for emergencies' point to careful planning for the future.
se: It was ______ of the town council to store grain before the long winter arrived.
prudent
Both words mean wisely preparing for the future, so the meaning is the same.

m: a condition or qualification attached to an agreement or statement
x: My parents let me borrow the car, with the proviso that I fill the tank before returning it.
The contract was signed with one important proviso: the supplier must deliver within thirty days.
The professor accepted late essays, but only with the proviso that students explain the delay in writing.
Parliament passed the bill with a proviso that it be reviewed after five years.
She agreed to move in with him on the proviso that they would share every household chore equally.

'Agreed... but he added one' followed by a requirement shows the blank means a condition attached to the agreement.
se: The board approved the merger with the ______ that no staff would be laid off for a year.
stipulation
Both 'proviso' and 'stipulation' mean a condition attached to the approval, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: having or encouraging an excessive or unhealthy interest in sexual or scandalous matters
x: Tabloids thrive on prurient gossip about the private lives of actors and athletes.
The editor rejected the photographs, saying they would appeal only to readers' prurient interest.
In her lecture, the historian argued that many Victorian moralists were secretly prurient themselves.
Critics accused the documentary of exploiting a tragic scandal to satisfy the public's prurient curiosity.
He felt uneasy about his friend's prurient questions concerning his new girlfriend.

'Rather than serious analysis' and 'lurid details' point to an unhealthy, sensational interest.
se: The judge ruled that the film's main purpose was to arouse ______ interest rather than to tell a story.
salacious
Both 'prurient' and 'salacious' describe an unhealthy sexual interest, so the sentence means the same either way.

m: having great power or influence; mighty (literary)
x: In the old legends, a puissant king could raise an army of thousands with a single command.

Medieval scholars wrote admiringly of the puissant lords who controlled entire provinces.

Her grandmother rarely raised her voice, yet she remained the most puissant figure in the family.

'Far from being a feeble power' signals the opposite, so the blank must mean powerful.
se: In the novel, the most ______ warlord in the land commands armies that no one dares to challenge.
mighty

m: physical beauty, especially of a person

In his essay, the art historian traced how ideals of pulchritude changed across the centuries.
The pageant claimed to celebrate talent, but the judges seemed interested mainly in pulchritude.
He was dazzled at first by her pulchritude, but it was her wit that made him fall in love.
tc: Though she was admired for her ______, she wanted to be known for her intelligence rather than her looks.
'Rather than her looks' restates the blank, so it must mean physical beauty.
se: The poet devoted dozens of sonnets to praising the ______ of his beloved.
beauty
Both 'pulchritude' and 'beauty' refer to physical attractiveness, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to crush into powder or dust; figuratively, to defeat completely

After the breakup, he felt as if his confidence had been completely pulverized.
tc: The machine is designed to ______ the hard grain until nothing remains but a fine flour.
'Nothing remains but a fine flour' shows the blank means to grind into powder.
se: The champion expected to ______ his inexperienced opponent within three rounds.
crush
Both 'pulverize' and 'crush' mean to defeat completely, giving the same meaning.

m: to strike repeatedly, especially with the fists
x: The toddler laughed as he pummeled the sofa cushions with his tiny fists.
Critics pummeled the company's new phone for its weak battery and high price.
In our first boxing class, we learned to pummel the heavy bag without hurting our wrists.
Heavy rain pummeled the tin roofs all night during the first storm of the monsoon.
She was so angry that she wanted to pummel him, but she simply turned and walked away.

'Instead of gently patting' and 'furiously with both fists' signal repeated hard blows.
se: The waves continued to ______ the small boat until its hull began to crack.
batter
Both 'pummel' and 'batter' mean to strike again and again with force, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: an expert who regularly gives opinions to the public, especially in the media

The company hired a well-known technology pundit to speak at its annual conference.

Economic pundits disagreed sharply about whether interest rates would rise next year.

'Self-styled' and 'offered confident forecasts on every news channel' describe someone who gives expert opinions in the media.
se: On election night, every ______ on television tried to explain the surprising result.
commentator
Both 'pundit' and 'commentator' mean a media figure who offers expert opinions, so the meaning stays the same.

m: to steal, often something small or in a sneaky way

Hackers purloined the personal data of millions of customers last year.
She smiled when she realized he had purloined her favorite sweater and never given it back.

'Rather than buying' and 'hiding it in his bag' show the blank means to steal secretly.
se: The spy managed to ______ secret documents from the embassy without being noticed.
steal
Both 'purloin' and 'steal' mean to take something dishonestly, so the meaning is the same.

m: to claim or appear to be or do something, often falsely

A video purporting to show a dramatic rescue during the floods turned out to be fake.
He purports to be my best friend, yet he never calls when I need help.

The contrast with 'were forged' shows the blank means to claim falsely.
se: These websites ______ to offer free medical advice, but most of them simply sell supplements.
claim
Both 'purport' and 'claim' mean to present oneself as doing something, possibly falsely, so the sentence means the same.

m: to supply or provide goods, services or information, especially as a business

My grandmother purveyed advice to anyone who would listen, whether they wanted it or not.

'Supplying them fresh every morning' restates the blank, so it means to supply as a trade.
se: The company was founded to ______ high-quality tea to hotels and restaurants.
supply
Both 'purvey' and 'supply' mean to provide goods commercially, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: generally believed or assumed to be, though not proven

The court ordered the putative father to take a DNA test before deciding on support payments.
Everyone praised his putative charm, but I found him rather rude when we finally met.

'No one had yet proven that it actually worked' shows the blank means supposed but unconfirmed.
se: Scientists are still debating whether the ______ cause of the disease is truly to blame.
supposed
Both 'putative' and 'supposed' mean assumed but not proven, so the meaning stays the same.

m: to drink something heartily and in large amounts
x: After the long hike, we quaffed cold water straight from the bottles.
At the office party, a few colleagues quaffed too much punch and began singing loudly.
Students quaffed cup after cup of strong tea while revising for their final exams.
Researchers found that people who quaff sugary drinks every day face a higher risk of diabetes.
He quaffed his wine nervously while waiting for her to answer his proposal.
tc: Rather than sipping his drink politely, the thirsty traveler began to ______ it in great gulps.
'Rather than sipping' and 'in great gulps' show the blank means to drink heartily.
se: After the match, the players loved to ______ cold lemonade in the dressing room.
guzzle
Both 'quaff' and 'guzzle' mean to drink eagerly in large amounts, so the meaning is the same.

m: a difficult, complicated situation that is hard to escape; literally, a bog
x: Our attempt to renovate the kitchen turned into a quagmire of delays and rising costs.

Her thesis slowly sank into a quagmire of conflicting data and unanswered questions.
Many historians describe the long war as a military quagmire that no government could end.
After years of bitter quarrels, their marriage had become an emotional quagmire for both of them.
tc: What was meant to be a quick military operation turned into the kind of ______ from which an army cannot withdraw for a decade.
The contrast with 'quick' and the phrase 'cannot withdraw for a decade' show the blank means a situation that is hard to escape.
se: The tax dispute turned into a bureaucratic ______ that took years to resolve.
morass
Both 'quagmire' and 'morass' mean a complicated situation that traps people, so the sentence means the same.

m: an uneasy feeling of doubt, especially about whether one is doing the right thing
x: I had a few qualms about leaving my dog with a stranger for the weekend.
She had no qualms about telling her manager that the plan would fail.
Some students feel no qualms about copying answers from the internet.
Scientists have raised ethical qualms about editing the genes of human embryos.
Despite his qualms, he agreed to meet his estranged father for dinner.
tc: He felt not the slightest ______ about lying to his boss, which shocked his more scrupulous colleagues.
The contrast with 'more scrupulous colleagues' shows the blank means a feeling of moral unease.
se: She signed the contract without a single ______, confident that the deal was fair.
misgiving
Both 'qualm' and 'misgiving' mean a feeling of doubt, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: (of a voice) to shake or tremble, usually because of emotion
x: Her voice quavered slightly as she thanked everyone at her retirement party.
During his first presentation to the board, the intern's voice began to quaver.
The young student's voice quavered as she read her poem aloud to the class.
The old man's voice quavered as he told reporters how the flood had swept away his home.
My voice quavered when I finally told my parents that I wanted to study abroad.
tc: Although she tried to sound calm, her voice began to ______ when she mentioned her late mother.
'Although she tried to sound calm' signals a contrast, so the blank means to tremble with emotion.
se: His voice started to ______ with emotion as he described his son's recovery.
tremble
Both 'quaver' and 'tremble' describe a voice shaking with feeling, giving the same meaning.

m: the most perfect or typical example of a quality or type

Our manager was the quintessence of professionalism, calm even when every deadline collapsed.
Many critics regard this novel as the quintessence of Victorian realism.
With its noise, color and crowds, the old market is the quintessence of the city's character.
To her, his small daily acts of kindness were the quintessence of true love.
tc: With his perfect manners and tailored suits, he seemed the very ______ of the English gentleman.
'Perfect manners and tailored suits' show he is the most typical example, so the blank means the perfect embodiment.
se: Many people consider the Taj Mahal the ______ of Mughal architecture.
epitome
Both 'quintessence' and 'epitome' mean the most perfect example, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: a short, clever and witty remark

The CEO opened the meeting with a quip about the broken coffee machine.
Our physics teacher's quips made even the hardest lessons enjoyable.
The candidate's clever quip during the debate quickly spread across social media.
She answered his awkward question with a playful quip, and they both laughed.
tc: Known for his sharp wit, the host greeted each guest with a clever ______ that made everyone smile.
'Known for his sharp wit' and 'made everyone smile' show the blank means a witty remark.
se: The speaker eased the tension in the room with a well-timed ______ about his own mistakes.
witticism
Both 'quip' and 'witticism' mean a clever, funny remark, so the sentence means the same.

m: a peculiar habit or feature; also, a strange accident or chance

tc: Her habit of reading the last page first is just a harmless ______, not a sign of anything serious.
'Harmless' and 'not a sign of anything serious' show the blank means an odd personal habit.
se: His only ______ was insisting that every pencil on his desk point in the same direction.
eccentricity
Both 'quirk' and 'eccentricity' mean an odd personal habit, so the meaning is the same.

m: good-humored teasing or joking

The professor accepted the students' gentle raillery about his old-fashioned slides with a smile.
Political cartoons have long relied on raillery to expose the vanity of those in power.
Their friendship survived years of raillery and only grew stronger with time.
tc: The friends' ______ was never meant to hurt; it was simply the playful teasing of people who knew each other well.
'Playful teasing' after the semicolon restates the blank.
se: Over coffee, the old classmates exchanged affectionate ______ about each other's gray hair.
banter
Both 'raillery' and 'banter' mean friendly teasing, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: dashing and stylish in a carefree, slightly disreputable way
x: He wore his cap at a rakish angle, which made him look like a film star.
The new marketing director had a rakish charm that won over clients quickly.
In the novel, a rakish young lord gambles away his family's entire fortune.
Car magazines praised the rakish lines of the new sports coupe.
She was drawn to his rakish smile, though her friends warned her he was unreliable.
tc: Unlike his staid and serious brother, Arif was ______, with a crooked smile, a tilted hat and a taste for late nights.
'Unlike his staid and serious brother' signals a contrast, and the details describe a dashing, carefree manner.
se: With his tilted hat and confident swagger, the actor looked ______ at the premiere.
dashing
Both 'rakish' and 'dashing' describe a stylish, confident appearance, so the meaning is the same.

m: a consequence of an action or event, especially a complex or unwelcome one
x: Before quitting your job, think carefully about the financial ramifications.
The legal team is still studying the ramifications of the new data protection law.
In the seminar, students discussed the ethical ramifications of using artificial intelligence in research.
Rising sea levels could have serious ramifications for low-lying countries such as Bangladesh.
She had not considered the emotional ramifications of moving so far from her family.
tc: Though the change seemed trivial, its most serious ______ was the loss of thousands of jobs.
'Though the change seemed trivial' contrasts with a serious result, so the blank means a consequence.
se: Few voters understood every ______ of the new tax law until they filed their returns.
implication
Both 'ramification' and 'implication' mean a resulting effect, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: to cause lasting annoyance or bitterness
x: It still rankles me that my neighbor never apologized for denting my car.
The decision to promote a newcomer over her rankled several senior staff.
A low mark on an essay she had worked hard on rankled her for weeks.
The unfair peace treaty continued to rankle the defeated nation for several generations.
His careless remark at our wedding still rankles, even though it was years ago.
tc: Although he pretended to forget the insult, it continued to ______ long after everyone else had moved on.
'Pretended to forget' and 'long after everyone else had moved on' show the blank means to cause lasting resentment.
se: Being left off the invitation list began to ______ her more than she would admit.
irk
Both 'rankle' and 'irk' mean to annoy or irritate, so the meaning stays the same.

m: to make thinner or less dense; also, to make more refined or exclusive
x: At high altitudes the air is rarefied, so climbers often struggle to breathe.

Years in academia had rarefied his tastes until he could enjoy only obscure foreign films.
Some critics complain that modern poetry has become so rarefied that ordinary readers feel shut out.
Life in the rarefied world of high fashion left her feeling lonely and cut off from old friends.
tc: As the balloon climbed higher, the air began to ______, becoming so thin that the passengers felt dizzy.
'Becoming so thin' restates the blank, so it means to become less dense.
se: Climbers know that higher altitudes ______ the air, so every step demands more effort.
thin
Both 'rarefy' and 'thin' mean to make the air less dense, so the sentence means the same.

m: to formally approve an agreement or decision, making it officially valid
x: Members of our housing society met on Friday to ratify the new parking rules.
The union voted overwhelmingly to ratify the pay deal offered by management.
The student council must ratify any change to the debate club's constitution.
Several countries have yet to ratify the climate treaty signed last year.
Their engagement was ratified only when both families met and gave their blessing.
tc: The treaty cannot take effect until each nation's parliament votes to ______ it.
'Cannot take effect until... votes' shows the blank means to formally approve.
se: Shareholders are expected to ______ the board's decision at the annual meeting.
approve
Both 'ratify' and 'approve' mean to formally accept the decision, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: the process of exact, logical reasoning
x: Solving this kind of puzzle requires patient ratiocination, not lucky guesses.
Her report impressed the board with its clear ratiocination and well-supported conclusions.
Philosophy students spend years practicing the demanding art of ratiocination in seminars.
Science advances through ratiocination and careful experiment rather than through superstition.
In matters of the heart, ratiocination rarely helps; he simply knew that he loved her.
tc: The detective solved the case not by luck or intuition but by patient ______, moving step by step from clue to conclusion.
'Not by luck or intuition' and 'step by step from clue to conclusion' point to logical reasoning.

tc: The quiet village, usually asleep by nine, was transformed during the harvest festival by days of music, dancing and ______.
The contrast with 'usually asleep by nine' and the list 'music, dancing' show the blank means noisy celebration.
se: Neighbors complained that the students' late-night ______ made it impossible to sleep.
merrymaking
Both 'revelry' and 'merrymaking' mean noisy, lively celebration.

m: so absurd or foolish that it deserves to be laughed at
x: His excuse that the dog had eaten his passport was so risible that even the officer smiled.
The consultant's risible sales forecast assumed we would triple revenue in six months.
Reviewers found the paper's conclusions risible, since its sample included only twelve people.
The minister's claim that Dhaka's traffic problem had been solved seemed risible to anyone who drove to work that morning.
She found his attempt to look tough on their first date more risible than impressive.
tc: Far from being taken seriously, the candidate's promise to abolish all taxes was considered ______ by every economist.
'Far from being taken seriously' signals that the blank means laughable.
se: The defense lawyer's argument was so ______ that several jurors had to hide their smiles.
laughable
Both 'risible' and 'laughable' mean absurd enough to provoke laughter.

m: plump and round in shape
x: Our rotund old cat struggles to jump onto the sofa these days.
The rotund manager of the canteen always slipped extra sweets to the night-shift workers.
The rotund figures in Botero's paintings are a favorite topic in our art history class.
The town's famous rotund statue of a merchant has become a popular spot for selfies.
She smiled fondly at her rotund grandfather, who still insisted on a second helping of rice.
tc: Years of rich food had turned the once-slender chef into someone so ______ that he could barely tie his apron.
The contrast with 'once-slender' and the trouble tying his apron show the blank means plump.
se: The ______ innkeeper, with his round belly and red cheeks, greeted every traveler warmly.
portly
Both 'rotund' and 'portly' describe someone pleasantly plump, giving the same meaning.

m: to bitterly regret something one has done
x: You'll rue the day you skipped breakfast before a four-hour exam.
He rued his decision to quit a stable job once the startup ran out of money.
Many students rue not starting their GRE preparation earlier, when they still had plenty of time.
Fans will long rue the missed chance when the captain dropped an easy catch in the final over.
She came to rue the harsh words she had said to her mother before leaving home.
tc: He laughed off his friends' warnings about the investment, but he would soon ______ ignoring them when he lost his savings.
Losing his savings after ignoring warnings shows the blank means bitterly regret.
se: Voters may ______ their choice once they see how the new government handles the economy.
regret
Both 'rue' and 'regret' mean to feel sorry about a past decision.

m: a trick or scheme intended to deceive someone
x: The phone call from 'the bank' was a ruse to get my mother's PIN.
Her sudden headache was just a ruse to leave the boring meeting early.
The researchers used a clever ruse, telling participants the study was about memory when it was really about honesty.
Police said the burglars used the ruse of posing as gas inspectors to enter elderly people's homes.
He invited her for coffee, but it was only a ruse to ask about her roommate.
tc: The 'emergency' that called him away from dinner turned out to be the latest ______ he used to avoid paying the bill.
The fake 'emergency' used to avoid paying shows the blank means trick.
se: Detectives eventually saw through the ______ and realized the kidnapping had been staged by the 'victim' himself.
ploy
Both 'ruse' and 'ploy' mean a deceptive scheme, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: excessively sweet or sentimental in a false or sickly way
x: I couldn't finish the movie because its saccharine ending made me cringe.
Her saccharine emails to clients often hide how frustrated she actually is.
Critics dismissed the novel as saccharine, full of perfect families and easy happy endings.
The campaign ad was so saccharine, with smiling children and soft piano music, that many viewers mocked it online.
He wrote her a saccharine love poem that embarrassed them both when she read it aloud.
tc: Unlike his earlier films, which were gritty and unsentimental, the director's latest work is ______, full of tearful reunions and syrupy music.
'Unlike... gritty and unsentimental' plus 'syrupy music' show the blank means overly sweet.
se: The greeting card's verses were so ______ that my teenage son refused to sign it.
syrupy
Both 'saccharine' and 'syrupy' mean excessively sweet and sentimental.

m: regarded as too important or sacred to be changed, questioned, or interfered with
x: In our house, Sunday lunch with the whole family is sacrosanct.
My manager treats the weekly deadline as sacrosanct, even when the work isn't ready.
No scientific theory should be sacrosanct; every claim must remain open to new evidence.
The finance minister insisted that pensions were sacrosanct and would not be touched by budget cuts.
For him, the evening hour he spent talking with his wife was sacrosanct, no matter how busy work became.
tc: Although the company has cut almost every expense, the research budget remains ______; no executive dares to touch it.
'No executive dares to touch it' explains the blank, which means untouchable.
se: In this school, the principal's rule that students must arrive on time is considered ______ and is never relaxed.
inviolable
Both 'sacrosanct' and 'inviolable' mean something that must never be broken or changed.

m: having an excessive or improper interest in sexual matters; lewd or scandalous
x: The tabloid filled its front page with salacious gossip about a celebrity divorce.
HR warned staff that sharing salacious jokes in the group chat could lead to disciplinary action.
The professor cautioned us not to judge the medieval poem only by its few salacious passages.
Editors debated whether publishing the salacious details of the scandal served the public interest.
She was hurt to discover that her ex had been spreading salacious rumors about her.
tc: The serious newspaper refused to print the photographs, judging them ______ rather than newsworthy.
'Serious newspaper' and 'rather than newsworthy' suggest the photos were indecent and scandalous.
se: Readers bought the magazine mainly for its ______ stories about the private lives of film stars.
lurid
Both 'salacious' and 'lurid' describe sensational, sexually suggestive stories.

m: of the skin, having an unhealthy pale or yellowish color
x: After a week of flu, his face looked sallow and thin.
Months of night shifts under fluorescent lights had left the nurses sallow and exhausted.
By the end of exam season, most students in the library looked sallow from lack of sleep and sunlight.
The report described the factory workers' sallow complexions as a sign of chronic malnutrition.
She worried about her father's sallow skin and finally persuaded him to see a doctor.
tc: Once rosy-cheeked and lively, the patient had grown ______ and thin after months in the hospital.
The contrast with 'once rosy-cheeked' shows the blank means unhealthily pale.
se: His ______ complexion suggested that he had spent far too long indoors without proper food.
sickly
Both 'sallow' and 'sickly' describe skin that looks pale and unhealthy.

m: to save something from loss, damage, or destruction
x: After the flood, we salvaged a few photo albums from the waterlogged cupboard.
The new manager tried to salvage the project by cutting its scope in half.
Desperate to salvage her grade, she asked the professor for an extra-credit assignment.
Divers spent weeks salvaging cargo from the ship that sank off the coast.
They went on holiday together in a last attempt to salvage their marriage.
tc: Although the first half of the match had gone disastrously, the team scored twice late on to ______ a draw.
'Although... disastrously' and the late goals show the team rescued something from a bad situation.
se: The firefighters managed to ______ only a few paintings from the burning gallery.
rescue
Both 'salvage' and 'rescue' mean to save something from destruction.

m: involving much bloodshed; eager to shed blood
x: The film's sanguinary battle scenes were too much for my younger brother.
The new editor cut my article with sanguinary enthusiasm, slashing nearly half of it.
Our history teacher described the sanguinary war in such detail that half the class lost their appetite.
Historians call it one of the most sanguinary conflicts of the century, with millions killed.
She couldn't understand her husband's love of sanguinary crime novels full of murders.
tc: Unlike the bloodless coup that preceded it, the civil war that followed was ______, leaving hundreds of thousands dead.
The contrast with 'bloodless' and 'hundreds of thousands dead' show the blank means bloody.
se: The ______ dictator ordered the execution of anyone suspected of disloyalty.
bloodthirsty
Both 'sanguinary' and 'bloodthirsty' describe someone eager to shed blood.

m: using humor, irony, or exaggeration to mock and criticize
x: My uncle loves satiric cartoons that mock politicians of every party.
At the office party, the interns performed a satiric sketch about our endless meetings.
We studied Swift's satiric essay "A Modest Proposal" in our first-year literature class.
The satiric news website was briefly blocked after its articles angered government officials.
She has a satiric streak, so her friends are never sure whether she is joking.
tc: Although readers first took the article as sincere advice, it was actually ______, using mock praise to ridicule the government's policies.
'Although... sincere' and 'mock praise to ridicule' show the blank means mocking through irony.
se: The magazine is famous for its ______ cartoons, which poke fun at the rich and powerful.
satirical
'Satiric' and 'satirical' are variant forms with the same meaning.

m: gloomy, sullen, and dark in mood or manner
x: Our saturnine neighbor rarely says more than a gruff hello when we meet on the stairs.
Despite his saturnine manner in meetings, the director is actually kind to junior staff.
The professor's saturnine expression made students nervous about asking questions.
The novel's saturnine hero broods over the loss of his family throughout the story.
She fell for his saturnine good looks, though his moodiness later wore her down.
tc: Her brother is cheerful and talkative, whereas she is ______, seldom smiling and often lost in dark thoughts.
'Whereas' contrasts her with her cheerful brother, and 'seldom smiling' confirms the blank means gloomy.
se: The ______ old fisherman rarely smiled and spoke to no one in the village.
morose
Both 'saturnine' and 'morose' mean gloomy and sullen.

m: to walk in a slow, relaxed, unhurried way
x: We sauntered along the beach at sunset, in no hurry to get back to the hotel.
He sauntered into the meeting twenty minutes late, holding a cup of coffee.
Students sauntered across the campus lawn as if the exam had already been cancelled.
Tourists sauntered through the old quarter, stopping to photograph every doorway.
She sauntered over to his table and asked, with a smile, whether the seat was free.
tc: While everyone else rushed to the train, Karim continued to ______ down the platform as though he had all the time in the world.
The contrast with 'rushed' and 'all the time in the world' show the blank means walk slowly.
se: On Friday evenings, couples like to ______ along the lakeside path, chatting and eating ice cream.
stroll
Both 'saunter' and 'stroll' mean to walk in a leisurely way.

m: a person of great learning or exceptional knowledge
x: My grandfather was something of a savant who could quote Tagore and explain physics at the dinner table.
The company hired a data savant to make sense of its chaotic sales figures.
Scholars from around the world came to consult the elderly savant on ancient manuscripts.
The article profiled a self-taught savant who had predicted the financial crisis years earlier.
She admired him as a savant, but she found it hard to talk to him about ordinary feelings.
tc: Although he never attended university, the old librarian was a true ______ whose knowledge of history astonished visiting professors.
Knowledge that astonished professors, despite no university education, shows the blank means a learned person.
se: The village children brought every difficult question to the old ______, who seemed to know everything.
sage
Both 'savant' and 'sage' mean a wise, deeply learned person.

m: to enjoy something slowly and fully
x: I like to savor my morning tea on the balcony before the Dhaka traffic starts honking.
After closing the deal, the team took a moment to savor their success before the next project.
She savored her last weeks of university life, knowing she would soon be working full time.
The winning party is savoring its landslide victory in the general election.
He savored every word of her letter, reading it again and again.
tc: Rather than gulping down the expensive wine, he paused to ______ each sip slowly.
'Rather than gulping down' and 'slowly' show the blank means enjoy fully.
se: Having trained for years, the athlete wanted to ______ the moment she stood on the podium.
relish
Both 'savor' and 'relish' mean to take great pleasure in something.

m: small or insufficient in quantity or amount
x: Our dinner was scanty because I had forgotten to go to the market.
With scanty information from the client, the designers had to guess what she wanted.
The evidence for the theory is scanty, so most scientists remain skeptical.
Scanty rainfall this year has left farmers in the north worried about the rice harvest.
His scanty replies to her messages made her wonder if he was losing interest.
tc: Although the explorers expected plentiful supplies at the base camp, they found only ______ rations that would last barely two days.
The contrast with 'plentiful' and 'barely two days' show the blank means insufficient.
se: Historians know little about the poet's childhood because the surviving records are ______.
sparse
Both 'scanty' and 'sparse' mean too few or too little.

m: a split or division between opposing groups, often within an organization
x: An argument over the inheritance caused a schism in the family that lasted for years.
The dispute over remote work created a schism between senior managers and younger employees.
Our history lecturer explained how the Great Schism of 1054 divided the Christian church.
The vote exposed a deep schism within the ruling party over economic reform.
What began as a small disagreement between the two friends grew into a schism neither could repair.
tc: Once united behind their leader, the movement suffered a bitter ______ when members disagreed over whether to use violence.
'Once united' contrasted with members disagreeing shows the blank means split.
se: The debate over the new constitution caused a lasting ______ between the two wings of the party.
rift
Both 'schism' and 'rift' mean a serious division between groups.

m: a tiny trace or amount of something
x: If you have even a scintilla of doubt about the contract, don't sign it.
The auditors found not a scintilla of evidence that money had been stolen.
The researcher admitted there was not a scintilla of data to support her original hypothesis.
There isn't a scintilla of truth in the rumor that the government plans to close all village schools.
After everything he had done, she no longer felt a scintilla of affection for him.
tc: Although the lawyer spoke for hours, he could not produce the slightest ______ of proof that his client had been elsewhere.
'The slightest' signals that the blank means a tiny amount.
se: His story was so far-fetched that it did not contain a single ______ of truth.
shred
Both 'scintilla' and 'shred' mean the smallest possible amount.

m: to sparkle or flash; to be brilliantly lively and witty
x: The diamonds in the display case scintillated under the jewellery shop's bright lights, catching every customer's eye.
At the conference dinner, our new colleague scintillated, charming everyone with sharp stories.
The professor's lectures scintillate with wit, so students rarely skip them.
Astronomers explained that stars scintillate because their light passes through turbulent air.
On their first date she seemed to scintillate, and he was too charmed to touch his food.
tc: Usually shy and dull in company, the novelist would ______ once she began talking about books, dazzling everyone with her wit.
The contrast with 'shy and dull' and 'dazzling everyone with her wit' show the blank means sparkle brilliantly.
se: In the moonlight, the frost on the grass seemed to ______ like scattered jewels.
sparkle
Both 'scintillate' and 'sparkle' mean to give off flashes of light.

m: a person or thing that causes great suffering or trouble
x: Mosquitoes are the scourge of every summer picnic in our backyard, no matter how much repellent we use.
Spam emails have become the scourge of our customer service inbox.
Malaria remains a scourge in many tropical countries despite decades of research.
The monsoon floods are a recurring scourge for farmers in northern Bangladesh.
For years, his drinking was the scourge of the family, ruining every holiday.
tc: Far from being a boon to the region, the new dam proved to be a real ______, flooding villages and destroying crops.
'Far from being a boon' signals a contrast, so the blank means a cause of suffering.
se: Drug addiction has become the ______ of many poor neighborhoods, destroying families and careers.
bane
Both 'scourge' and 'bane' mean a source of great harm and misery.

m: a moral doubt or feeling that makes one hesitate to do something wrong
x: He has no scruples about borrowing money and never paying it back.
She had scruples about inflating the sales figures, so she refused to sign the report.
Our ethics professor argued that a good scientist must have scruples about manipulating data, even under pressure to publish.
Investigators found that the company's directors had shown no scruple in dumping waste into the river.
Despite his scruples, he finally agreed to lie to his parents about where he was going.
tc: The swindler felt no ______ about cheating elderly widows out of their savings; he slept soundly every night.
'He slept soundly every night' shows he had no moral hesitation, which is what the blank means.
se: The journalist had no ______ about publishing the leaked documents, believing the public deserved the truth.
compunction
Both 'scruple' and 'compunction' mean a moral hesitation, so the sentence means the same.

m: to formally withdraw from a union, federation, or organization
x: After the quarrel, my cousins half-jokingly declared that they would secede from the family WhatsApp group.
Unhappy with the union's leadership, the nurses voted to secede and form an independent association.
In history class, we learned why eleven southern states seceded from the United States in 1861.
The region held a referendum on whether to secede from the federation.
Several members threatened to secede from the club if the new fees were approved.
tc: Rather than remain part of a country that ignored its language and culture, the province decided to ______ and declare independence.
'Rather than remain part of' and 'declare independence' show the blank means withdraw formally.
se: Several states threatened to ______ from the federation if the new tax law was passed.
withdraw
Both 'secede' and 'withdraw' mean to leave the federation formally.

m: the state of being private and away from other people
x: After the noise of the city, I enjoyed the seclusion of my aunt's village home.
The CEO retreated into seclusion for a week to plan the company's future.
To finish her dissertation, she worked in near seclusion, seeing almost no one for months.
The former star now lives in seclusion on a remote island, refusing all interviews.
After the divorce, he withdrew into seclusion and stopped answering his friends' calls.
tc: After decades in the public eye, the actress chose a life of ______, moving to a remote farm and refusing to see visitors.
'Remote farm' and 'refusing to see visitors' explain the blank, which means isolation.
se: The monks spend months in ______, cut off from the outside world, to devote themselves to prayer.
isolation
Both 'seclusion' and 'isolation' mean being cut off from other people.

m: relating to divisions between religious or political groups, often narrow-mindedly
x: My grandmother always warned us never to let sectarian differences divide our neighborhood.
The office banned political and sectarian debates after a heated argument between colleagues.
Her research examines how sectarian identities shaped voting patterns in the region.
The city has been tense since sectarian violence broke out last month.
He ended the friendship when he realized how sectarian and intolerant his old classmate had become.
tc: Instead of uniting the country's many religious groups, the leader's speeches were ______, favoring his own community and attacking all others.
'Instead of uniting' and 'favoring his own community' show the blank means narrowly devoted to one group.
se: The town's schools remain divided along ______ lines, with children of each faith studying separately.
denominational
Both 'sectarian' and 'denominational' refer to divisions between religious groups.

m: to be filled with intense anger that is barely held in
x: I seethed in silence as the bus driver skipped my stop for the third time.
She seethed when her manager took credit for her proposal in front of the board.
Students seethed over the sudden fee increase but feared speaking out.
The capital seethed with anger after the election results were announced.
He was still seething about their argument when his wife called to apologize.
tc: Although he smiled politely throughout the meeting, inside he began to ______ at the insults directed at his team.
'Although he smiled politely' signals that inside he felt the opposite, intense hidden anger.
se: Fans continued to ______ over the referee's decision long after the match had ended.
fume
Both 'seethe' and 'fume' mean to feel intense, simmering anger.

m: an outward appearance of something, often hiding a different reality
x: After the storm, it took us a week to restore some semblance of order to the house.
The new manager brought a semblance of discipline to a team that had missed every deadline.
The study lacks even a semblance of scientific rigor, since it has no control group.
The election was held with only a semblance of fairness, as opposition candidates were barred.
She kept up a semblance of cheerfulness at the party, though she was heartbroken inside.
tc: Behind the ______ of calm she showed her guests, she was frantically worried about her missing son.
The contrast between what she 'showed her guests' and her real worry shows the blank means outward appearance.
se: Although the trial had the ______ of justice, everyone knew the verdict had been decided in advance.
appearance
Both 'semblance' and 'appearance' mean an outward show that hides the truth.

m: relating to or richly pleasing the senses
x: We sat in the garden, enjoying the sensuous scent of jasmine after the evening rain.
The new office cafe was designed to feel sensuous, with warm lighting, soft music and the smell of fresh bread.
Our literature professor praised Keats for the sensuous imagery of his odes.
Critics described the exhibition's sensuous textiles as a feast for the eyes and fingertips.
She loved the sensuous pleasure of walking barefoot on cool grass with her children.
tc: Unlike the austere, abstract poems of his youth, his late work is richly ______, full of colors, scents and textures.
The contrast with 'austere, abstract' and the list of colors, scents and textures show the blank means appealing to the senses.
se: The chef aims to create a richly ______ dining experience, with dishes that delight the eye and nose as much as the tongue.
sensory
Both 'sensuous' and 'sensory' describe an experience that appeals to the senses.

m: able to perceive and feel things
x: Anyone who has owned a dog knows that animals are sentient creatures with real emotions.
Our team joked that the office printer was sentient, since it always broke down before deadlines.
Philosophy students debated whether a computer could ever become truly sentient.
New laws in some countries recognize octopuses and crabs as sentient beings that can feel pain.
After the accident, the family took comfort in knowing he was still sentient and could recognize their voices.
tc: Unlike a rock or a plant, which cannot feel anything, a dog is ______ and can experience both pain and pleasure.
The contrast with things that 'cannot feel anything' shows the blank means able to feel.
se: Scientists are still debating whether insects are truly ______ and capable of suffering.
conscious
Both 'sentient' and 'conscious' mean aware and able to experience feelings.

m: to isolate or set apart from others
x: Every Friday evening, I sequester myself in my room to study without distractions.
The executives sequestered themselves in a hotel for three days to finalize the merger.
Forests help fight climate change because trees sequester large amounts of carbon.
The jury was sequestered throughout the trial to prevent exposure to media coverage.
After their quarrel, he sequestered himself in the study and refused to come down for dinner.
tc: To keep jurors from hearing news reports about the case, the judge decided to ______ them in a hotel until the verdict.
Keeping jurors away from news reports shows the blank means isolate.
se: The scientist chose to ______ herself in a remote lab, far from colleagues and distractions, to finish her experiments.
isolate
Both 'sequester' and 'isolate' mean to cut oneself off from others.

m: to restrain or limit someone's freedom of action
x: Don't let old fears shackle you when a new opportunity comes along.
Endless paperwork shackles our engineers and slows down every project the company takes on.
Many researchers feel shackled by funding rules that discourage risky ideas.
Critics say heavy regulation has shackled the country's small businesses.
She refused to be shackled by her family's expectations about marriage and career.
tc: Rather than freeing the economy as promised, the new rules seemed designed to ______ entrepreneurs with taxes and permits.
'Rather than freeing' signals a contrast, so the blank means restrain.
se: Excessive student debt can ______ a young graduate's choices for years.
hamper
Both 'shackle' and 'hamper' mean to restrict or hold back.

m: something that is not what it pretends to be; a fake
x: The 'free' holiday offer turned out to be a sham designed to sell overpriced timeshares.
Employees realized the consultation was a sham when management announced the decision before the meeting ended.
The journal retracted the study after investigators showed that its data were a sham.
Observers called the election a sham, since the main opposition party had been banned.
Their marriage had become a sham, kept up only for the sake of the children.
tc: The company praised its factory as a model of green technology, but inspectors exposed the claim as a complete ______ after finding toxic waste behind the walls.
Finding toxic waste contradicts the 'green' claim, so the blank means fake.
se: The so-called public inquiry was merely an elaborate ______ whose conclusions had been written before any witnesses testified.
farce
Both 'sham' and 'farce' mean a pretense that only looks genuine.

m: a long-held belief, slogan, or custom that marks a group, often now outdated
x: In my family, knowing all the words to the old village songs was a kind of shibboleth.
Jargon like 'synergy' has become a shibboleth that marks you as a true corporate insider.
The young economist challenged the old shibboleth that higher taxes always slow growth.
For decades, support for the policy was a party shibboleth that no candidate dared question.
Using the right slang was a shibboleth among my teenage friends, and I never quite mastered it.
tc: Once accepted without question by every party member, the slogan has become an empty ______ that younger activists openly mock as outdated.
A slogan once accepted without question but now mocked as outdated fits the meaning of shibboleth.
se: The new finance minister challenged the long-held ______ that a strong currency is always good for the economy.
dogma
Both 'shibboleth' and 'dogma' mean a belief accepted without question by a group.

m: to avoid a duty, task, or responsibility
x: My brother always finds an excuse to shirk washing the dishes after dinner.
Managers noticed that a few employees shirked their duties whenever the boss was traveling.
Group projects are frustrating when one member shirks his share of the research.
The report accused officials of shirking responsibility for the collapse of the garment factory.
She never shirked caring for her elderly parents, even while working full time.
tc: Unlike his hardworking sister, who volunteered for every task, Rafi tried to ______ any chore his parents gave him.
The contrast with a sister who 'volunteered for every task' shows the blank means avoid.
se: A good leader does not ______ responsibility when things go wrong.
evade
Both 'shirk' and 'evade' mean to avoid a duty, so the meaning is the same.

m: badly made or done; of poor quality
x: The shoddy umbrella I bought on the street broke in the first monsoon storm.
Clients complained about the agency's shoddy work and refused to pay the final invoice.
The professor returned my essay with a note criticizing its shoddy research.
Investigators blamed shoddy construction for the collapse of the eight-storey building.
He felt ashamed of the shoddy way he had treated his friend after their argument.
tc: Although the builder charged premium prices, his work was ______, with cracked walls and leaking pipes within months.
'Although... premium prices' and the cracks and leaks show the blank means poorly made.
se: Customers stopped buying from the factory after receiving one batch of ______ goods after another.
inferior
Both 'shoddy' and 'inferior' mean of poor quality.

m: to deliberately avoid or keep away from someone or something
x: She shunned sweets for a month before her wedding, much to her mother's dismay.
The startup shuns traditional offices, letting employees work from anywhere.
Scientists who shunned the new theory at first later accepted it as the evidence grew.
Many young voters now shun mainstream parties in favor of independent candidates.
After the scandal, many of his old friends began to shun him at the club.
tc: Although she was once the center of every party, after her divorce she began to ______ social gatherings entirely.
'Although she was once the center of every party' signals a contrast, so the blank means avoid.
se: The reclusive author continued to ______ publicity, refusing all interviews even after winning the prize.
avoid
Both 'shun' and 'avoid' mean to keep away from something deliberately.

m: to smile in a silly, affected, or falsely shy way
x: The waiter simpered at the wealthy guests but ignored everyone else.
I can't stand the way he simpers whenever the director walks into the room.
The student simpered at the examiner, hoping charm would make up for his lack of preparation.
At the awards ceremony, the young actor simpered for the cameras while clutching his trophy.
She simpered and fluttered her eyelashes, which only made him more suspicious.
tc: Instead of answering the question honestly, the flattering assistant would only ______ and nod at everything his boss said.
'Flattering' and nodding at everything suggest the blank means smile in a silly, ingratiating way.
se: The courtiers would ______ at the king's feeble jokes, hoping to win his favor.
titter
Both 'simper' and 'titter' describe a silly, affected show of amusement meant to please.

m: a paid position that requires little or no real work
x: My uncle's job at the trade board was a sinecure; he read newspapers all morning and went home after lunch.
Critics argued that the new advisory post was nothing more than a sinecure for the minister's loyal friends.
Some honorary professorships are sinecures, offering a title and a salary but almost no teaching.
She turned down the sinecure because she wanted work that would actually challenge her.
After years of exhausting labour, he secretly hoped for a comfortable sinecure where nobody would bother him.
tc: Far from being the ______ everyone imagined, the chairman's role demanded twelve-hour days and constant travel.
'Far from' signals a contrast with 'twelve-hour days and constant travel', so the blank must mean a job with almost no work.
se: The ambassadorship was regarded as the juiciest ______ in the government's gift, handed to loyal donors as a reward.
plum
Both 'sinecure' and 'plum' describe a desirable, well-paid post handed out as a reward, so the meaning stays the same.

m: giving the impression that something harmful or evil is happening or will happen
x: There was something sinister about the way the stranger kept watching the children in the park.
Investigators suspect a more sinister motive behind the sudden deletion of the company's financial records.
In the novel, the kindly old headmaster gradually reveals a sinister side that shocks his students.
A sinister silence fell over the village after the armed men rode through at midnight.
I assumed his late-night phone calls were sinister until I learned he was planning my surprise party.
tc: Although the old house looked charming by day, at night its creaking shutters and dark windows gave it an air that was distinctly ______.
'Although' contrasts 'charming by day' with the night-time mood, so the blank must mean threatening or evil.
se: Police were worried that the anonymous letters pointed to something more ______ than a simple prank.
menacing
Both 'sinister' and 'menacing' suggest a real threat of harm, as opposed to a harmless prank.

m: to become or make slower, looser, or less intense
x: Once the monsoon rains slackened, the streets of Dhaka slowly began to drain.
Demand for office space has slackened since many companies switched to remote work.
Don't slacken your effort in the final week before the exam; that is when revision counts most.
Economists expect inflation to slacken next year as fuel prices fall.
Their friendship never really ended; it simply slackened as they moved to different cities.
tc: The coach warned that if the players began to ______ their effort now, the lead they had built so carefully would vanish.
The warning that the lead 'would vanish' shows the blank means to reduce or relax effort.
se: By late afternoon the wind began to ______, and the fishing boats finally headed out to sea.
abate
Both 'slacken' and 'abate' mean the wind grew weaker, which is why the boats could leave.

m: lazy and unwilling to work or make any effort
x: After a slothful Sunday on the sofa, I felt guilty about the pile of unread emails.
The manager blamed the delay on slothful contractors who rarely arrived before noon.
Professors complained that slothful students copied assignments rather than doing their own reading.
Critics accused the slothful bureaucracy of letting permit applications gather dust for months.
She loved him, but his slothful habits, especially leaving dishes for days, drove her mad.
tc: Unlike her industrious sister, who rose at dawn to study, Rina was so ______ that she rarely left her bed before noon.
'Unlike her industrious sister' sets up a contrast, so the blank must mean lazy.
se: The new director vowed to shake up the ______ department, where staff routinely took two-hour lunches.
indolent
Both 'slothful' and 'indolent' mean lazy, matching the staff's two-hour lunches.

m: messy and careless in appearance, habits, or work
x: His slovenly appearance, with a stained shirt and uncombed hair, did not impress the interviewers.
The report was so slovenly, full of typos and missing figures, that my boss sent it straight back.
By the end of term our hostel room was slovenly, with clothes and textbooks strewn everywhere.
Inspectors blamed slovenly record-keeping for the hospital's failure to trace infected patients.
She stopped visiting her brother because his slovenly flat made her feel uncomfortable.
tc: Though the chef was meticulous about her dishes, her kitchen staff were so ______ that crumbs and grease covered every counter.
'Though' contrasts the chef's meticulousness with her staff, and the crumbs and grease confirm the blank means messy and careless.
se: The editor rejected the article because of its ______ writing, riddled with spelling errors and half-finished sentences.
sloppy
Both 'slovenly' and 'sloppy' describe careless work full of errors.

m: a habitually lazy, slow-moving person
x: My roommate is a real sluggard who sleeps through every alarm and misses morning lectures.
The foreman warned that sluggards would be dropped from the crew before the next contract.
In the old proverb, the sluggard is told to watch the ant and learn the value of hard work.
Commentators called the reform committee a gathering of sluggards that had produced nothing in two years.
I felt like a sluggard next to my grandmother, who was up at five every morning tending her garden.
tc: Everyone dismissed Kamal as the office ______, but in fact he worked night shifts and simply slept during the day.
'But in fact he worked night shifts' contrasts with how he was seen, so the blank must mean a lazy person.
se: The coach had no patience for the team's lone ______, who skipped drills and arrived late to every practice.
slacker
Both 'sluggard' and 'slacker' name a lazy person who avoids effort, as the skipped drills show.

m: a small amount of something, or a slight, superficial knowledge of a subject
x: I have only a smattering of French, enough to order coffee but not to hold a conversation.
The conference drew a smattering of investors, far fewer than the organizers had hoped.
His essay showed a smattering of economic theory but no real grasp of the subject.
Only a smattering of voters turned up at the polling station because of the heavy rain.
She picked up a smattering of Bangla from her in-laws and loved surprising them with it.
tc: Rather than a deep knowledge of Japanese, he had only the barest ______ of the language, enough to read a menu.
'Rather than a deep knowledge' and 'enough to read a menu' show the blank means a slight, superficial knowledge.
se: The concert attracted nothing more than the thinnest ______ of fans, most of them relatives of the band.
scattering
Both 'smattering' and 'scattering' mean a small number spread thinly, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: completely soaked with water
x: After walking home through the downpour without an umbrella, my shoes were sodden and my books ruined.
She draped her sodden coat over the office radiator and hoped it would dry before the meeting.
The researchers' field notebooks were sodden after a week of constant rain in the rainforest.
Groundstaff covered the sodden pitch, but the cricket match was eventually abandoned.
He sat on the sodden bench in the rain, too heartbroken to care that he was getting wet.
