Both 'utopia' and 'paradise' mean an ideal, perfect place, giving the same meaning.

m: an unpredictable or erratic change, action, or idea
x: Farmers in Bangladesh are at the mercy of the vagaries of the monsoon.
Anyone who takes the bus to work soon learns to live with the vagaries of the timetable.
The study examines the vagaries of human memory, showing how easily details are distorted.
Small exporters struggle to cope with the vagaries of the currency market.
She had grown used to the vagaries of her husband's moods, which changed without warning.
tc: Each sudden ______ of the market, from unexpected crashes to wild rallies, left investors more confused than before.
'Sudden', 'unexpected crashes' and 'wild rallies' describe unpredictable changes.
se: The farmers' income depends on every ______ of the weather, which can destroy a crop overnight.
caprice
Both 'vagary' and 'caprice' mean an unpredictable change, so the sentence means the same.

m: excessively proud of oneself and boastful
x: My vainglorious neighbor reminds everyone at every dinner party about his expensive new car.
The vainglorious chief executive named the new headquarters after himself and hung his portrait in the lobby.
Critics called the professor's memoir vainglorious, since it barely mentioned his co-researchers.
The general's vainglorious boasts of a quick victory proved disastrously wrong.
She eventually left him, tired of his vainglorious stories in which he was always the hero.
tc: Unlike her humble predecessor, the new mayor was ______, constantly boasting about her achievements and putting her name on every public building.
The contrast with 'humble' and 'constantly boasting' point to excessive pride.
se: The athlete's ______ claims that he was the greatest player in history annoyed even his own fans.
boastful
Both 'vainglorious' and 'boastful' describe excessive bragging, giving the same meaning.

m: to boast about or praise something excessively
x: My uncle loves to vaunt his cooking, though his curries are always too salty.
The company vaunted its new software as revolutionary, but users found it full of bugs.
Universities often vaunt their rankings in brochures aimed at international students.
The government vaunted its record on job creation, yet unemployment had actually risen.
He kept vaunting his new girlfriend's accomplishments until his friends grew tired of hearing about her.
tc: Rather than quietly letting his work speak for itself, the new manager preferred to ______ every small success at staff meetings.
'Rather than quietly letting his work speak for itself' signals the opposite: loud boasting.
se: Politicians love to ______ their achievements in the weeks just before an election.
trumpet
Both 'vaunt' and 'trumpet' mean to proclaim one's successes boastfully.

m: to change direction suddenly; to shift abruptly in course or opinion
x: A rickshaw veered into our lane, and the driver slammed on the brakes just in time.
The meeting veered off topic, and we spent twenty minutes discussing office parking.
Halfway through the lecture, the professor veered into a long story about his student days.
The party has veered sharply to the right since losing the last election.
Their conversation veered from light-hearted teasing to a painful argument about money.
tc: Instead of continuing straight down the highway, the truck began to ______ wildly from one lane to another.
'Instead of continuing straight' signals sudden changes of direction.
se: The driver was forced to ______ off the road to avoid hitting a cow.
swerve
Both 'veer' and 'swerve' mean to change direction suddenly, giving the same meaning.

m: a superficially attractive appearance that hides someone's or something's true, less pleasant nature
x: Beneath his veneer of politeness, he was furious that nobody had asked for his opinion.
The company's glossy annual report offered a veneer of stability while its debts quietly piled up.
Her research exposes the thin veneer of objectivity in many early studies of intelligence.
After the election, the veneer of civility between the two parties cracked almost immediately.
I could tell that his cheerful veneer was hiding real disappointment about the breakup.
tc: Behind the ______ of calm that she showed the reporters, the mayor was deeply worried about the flooding.
'Behind the ... that she showed the reporters' signals a surface appearance hiding her true worry.
se: His charming manners were merely the ______ behind which he hid a ruthless ambition.
facade
Both 'veneer' and 'facade' mean a pleasing outward show that conceals the truth.

m: of a fault or sin: minor and easily forgiven
x: Forgetting to reply to a birthday message is a venial mistake, not a sign that you don't care.
The auditor treated the rounding errors as venial, but the missing invoices worried her.
In Catholic theology, venial sins are distinguished from mortal sins, which are considered far graver.
The committee decided the senator's late filing was a venial lapse rather than deliberate fraud.
Arriving ten minutes late to dinner seemed venial to me, but my mother saw it as disrespect.
tc: Compared with the embezzlement uncovered later, his habit of taking office pens home seemed entirely ______.
The comparison with serious embezzlement shows the pen-taking was a small, forgivable fault.
se: The teacher overlooked the student's ______ errors in spelling and focused on the strength of the argument.
excusable
Both 'venial' and 'excusable' describe small faults that can easily be forgiven.

m: in exactly the same words as were originally used; word for word
x: She repeated my instructions verbatim, which proved she had been listening after all.
The intern copied whole paragraphs verbatim from a competitor's website, so the report had to be rewritten.
Students who reproduce lecture notes verbatim in exams rarely score the highest marks.
The newspaper printed the minister's statement verbatim, without adding any commentary of its own.
During our argument, he quoted my old text messages back to me verbatim, which felt unsettling.
tc: Rather than paraphrasing the witness's testimony, the clerk recorded it ______, every hesitation included.
'Rather than paraphrasing' and 'every hesitation included' show the testimony was recorded word for word.
se: The software flags any essay that reproduces published sources ______ without using quotation marks.
exactly
Both 'verbatim' and 'exactly' mean copied in precisely the original words.

m: the appearance of being true or real
x: The film's careful attention to period costumes gives it remarkable verisimilitude.
To add verisimilitude to the training exercise, the managers staged a realistic fire alarm.
Historians praised the novel's verisimilitude, though they noted several invented characters.
The fake news site copied the layout of real newspapers to lend its stories verisimilitude.
His story about missing the bus lacked verisimilitude, since I had seen him at the café that morning.
tc: The director filmed in real Dhaka neighborhoods and cast local residents, hoping that such ______ would make the story more convincing.
Using real locations and residents to make the story convincing points to an appearance of reality.
se: Critics admired the ______ of the war scenes, which felt disturbingly close to real combat.
realism
Both 'verisimilitude' and 'realism' mean the quality of seeming true to life.

m: a true principle or belief, especially one of fundamental importance; truth
x: My grandmother's household ran on a few simple verities: work hard, eat together, and never waste rice.
The consultant challenged the old verity that customers always prefer the cheapest option.
Science advances by questioning accepted verities rather than protecting them.
The election shook many of the political verities that commentators had relied on for decades.
Over the years she came to doubt the verity of everything he had told her about his past.
tc: Many readers accepted the ______ of the memoir without question, until a journalist proved that several chapters were invented.
The contrast with chapters proven to be invented shows the blank means truth.
se: No one in the room doubted the ______ of her account, since several witnesses confirmed every detail.
truth
Both 'verity' and 'truth' refer to the account being accurate, as the witnesses confirm.

m: a brief, vivid description, account, or scene
x: Her blog is full of charming vignettes about life in a crowded Dhaka apartment building.
The presentation opened with a short vignette about a customer whose order went missing.
Each chapter of the textbook begins with a clinical vignette describing a real patient's symptoms.
The documentary is a series of vignettes showing how ordinary families cope with rising prices.
He wrote her a little vignette of their first date, and she kept it in her wallet for years.
tc: Rather than a full biography, the essay is only the briefest ______: twelve pages describing the poet's last summer.
'Rather than a full biography' and 'twelve pages' indicate a short, vivid sketch.
se: The novel's best moment is the short ______ in which the grandfather teaches his grandson to fish.
scene
Both 'vignette' and 'scene' describe a brief, self-contained episode in the story.

m: physical strength, energy, and enthusiasm
x: Even at eighty, my grandfather walks to the market every morning with remarkable vigor.
The new manager tackled the backlog with such vigor that the team finished a week early.
She defended her thesis with vigor, answering every tough question from the panel.
The government has promised to pursue tax evaders with renewed vigor this year.
After the long illness, he slowly regained his vigor and his old sense of humor.
tc: Though the old coach had seemed tired all season, he led the final practice with surprising ______.
'Though ... seemed tired' sets up a contrast, so the blank must mean energy.
se: The campaign was launched with great ______, but enthusiasm faded within a month.
energy
Both 'vigor' and 'energy' describe the strong enthusiasm that later faded.

m: to spoil or weaken the quality or effectiveness of something; to make legally invalid
x: A single rude comment can vitiate an otherwise pleasant evening with friends.
Sloppy data entry vitiated the whole quarterly analysis, so we had to start again.
The researchers admitted that a small sample size vitiated their conclusions.
Lawyers argued that the contract was vitiated by fraud and was therefore unenforceable.
His constant jealousy gradually vitiated the trust that their marriage depended on.
tc: One biased question in the survey was enough to ______ the results, making the whole study worthless.
'Making the whole study worthless' shows the blank means to spoil or invalidate.
se: The scientists feared that contamination in the lab would ______ months of careful experimentation.
undermine
Both 'vitiate' and 'undermine' mean to weaken or ruin the value of the work.

m: to give, grant, or reveal something, often reluctantly or as a special favor
x: My teenage son rarely vouchsafes more than a grunt when I ask about his day.
The CEO vouchsafed only a brief comment to staff about the rumored merger.
The archive finally vouchsafed scholars access to letters that had been sealed for a century.
The spokesperson declined to vouchsafe any details about the ongoing investigation.
She vouchsafed me a rare smile when I finally apologized for my behavior.
tc: Despite hours of questioning, the suspect refused to ______ even his name, staring silently at the wall.
'Refused' and 'staring silently' show he would not give or reveal anything.
se: The reclusive author would not ______ any information about her next novel.
disclose
Both 'vouchsafe' and 'disclose' mean to reveal information that is being held back.

m: humorous in a playful, mischievous way
x: My waggish uncle always hides the remote control and pretends he has no idea where it went.
A waggish colleague renamed the office printer 'Out of Order' as a joke.
The professor's waggish footnotes made a dry textbook surprisingly fun to read.
One waggish reporter asked whether the minister's promise came with a money-back guarantee.
I fell for his waggish charm the moment he joked about the terrible restaurant service.
tc: Unlike his solemn brother, Rafiq was ______, always ready with a prank or a teasing remark.
'Unlike his solemn brother' and 'a prank or a teasing remark' point to playful humor.
se: The guide's ______ comments about the museum's stuffy portraits kept the schoolchildren entertained.
jocular
Both 'waggish' and 'jocular' describe joking, playful remarks.

m: to indulge in an unpleasant emotion, especially self-pity, without trying to recover
x: After failing his driving test, he spent the whole weekend wallowing on the sofa.
Instead of wallowing in last quarter's losses, the team began planning the next campaign.
There's no point wallowing in self-pity after a bad exam; just study harder for the next one.
Critics say the documentary wallows in misery without offering any solutions.
She allowed herself one evening to wallow in sadness after the breakup, then called her friends.
tc: Rather than ______ in self-pity after losing the election, she immediately began organizing for the next one.
'Rather than' contrasts the blank with taking action, so it must mean dwelling on unhappiness.
se: After the defeat, the players were allowed to ______ for one night before training resumed.
mope
Both 'wallow' and 'mope' mean to sit around feeling sorry for oneself.

m: pale and looking ill or exhausted; of a smile, weak and faint
x: She looked wan after the long overnight bus journey from Chittagong.
Several wan employees dragged themselves into the office after the all-night product launch.
After weeks of exam revision, the students' faces were wan and tired.
Doctors noted that many patients appeared wan and underweight after the outbreak.
He gave me a wan smile, but I could tell the news had hurt him.
tc: After a week in hospital, the once ruddy-cheeked boy looked thin and ______.
The contrast with 'once ruddy-cheeked' and the hospital stay point to a pale, sickly look.
se: Her face was ______ from lack of sleep, and dark circles ringed her eyes.
pale
Both 'wan' and 'pale' describe a face drained of color from exhaustion.

m: a wasteful or good-for-nothing person, especially one who squanders money
x: Her father worried she would marry some wastrel who would gamble away the family savings.
The company's founder refused to hand the business to his son, whom he considered a wastrel.
In the novel, a young wastrel squanders his inheritance on horses and card games.
Tabloids portrayed the heir as a wastrel, though he actually ran several successful charities.
I was a bit of a wastrel in my twenties, spending every paycheck within a week.
tc: Unlike his thrifty sisters, who saved every taka, Kamal was the family ______, spending his salary on gadgets within days.
'Unlike his thrifty sisters' and spending his salary within days show he is a wasteful person.
se: Everyone in town knew him as the ______ who had wasted his father's fortune in less than five years.
spendthrift
Both 'wastrel' and 'spendthrift' mean a person who recklessly wastes money.

m: to grow gradually larger, stronger, or more intense
x: Her interest in gardening seems to wax and wane with the seasons.
Support for the proposal waxed as more managers saw how much money it would save.
Students observed the moon wax from a thin crescent to a full disc over two weeks.
The party's influence waxed during the economic boom and faded after the crash.
His affection for her waxed slowly over many long conversations.
tc: Public interest in the scandal began to ______ as new details emerged each day, until it dominated every front page.
Interest that ends up dominating every front page must be growing, so the blank means increase.
se: As the evening went on, his confidence seemed to ______, and by midnight he was dancing in front of everyone.
grow
Both 'wax' and 'grow' mean his confidence steadily increased.

m: to sharpen or stimulate an appetite, interest, or desire
x: The smell of frying onions from the kitchen whetted my appetite long before dinner.
A short demo at the conference whetted investors' interest in the new software.
The introductory lecture whetted her curiosity about astrophysics, and she changed her major.
The trailer only whetted fans' appetite for the film, which sold out on opening night.
Their first date whetted his desire to learn everything about her.
tc: The museum hoped the free sample tour would ______ visitors' interest enough that they would buy a full ticket.
The goal of getting visitors to buy a full ticket shows the tour should stimulate their interest.
se: The first chapter is designed to ______ readers' curiosity without revealing too much of the plot.
pique
Both 'whet' and 'pique' mean to arouse or stimulate curiosity.

m: playfully quaint or fanciful behavior, humor, or style
x: The café's mismatched teacups and painted ceilings give it a charming sense of whimsy.
Our designer added a touch of whimsy to the dull annual report with hand-drawn illustrations.
Children's literature often combines serious lessons with a large dose of whimsy.
Critics complained that the city's new public sculpture was all whimsy and no substance.
She loved his whimsy, like the time he planned a picnic on their rooftop in the rain.
tc: The architect's earlier buildings were sober and functional, but her latest design is full of ______: curving staircases, bright colors, and a slide instead of stairs.
The contrast with 'sober and functional' and the playful details point to fanciful humor.
se: The film's ______ delighted children, who loved its talking teapots and flying bicycles.
playfulness
Both 'whimsy' and 'playfulness' describe the film's fanciful, light-hearted quality.

m: to remove unwanted people or things from a group until only the best remain
x: I need to winnow my wardrobe before moving into the smaller flat.
Recruiters winnowed three hundred applications down to a shortlist of ten.
Good researchers learn to winnow reliable sources from the flood of material online.
The primary elections will winnow the crowded field of candidates down to just two.
Over the years she winnowed her circle of friends to the few she could truly trust.
c: winnow the wheat from the chaff
tc: The admissions committee had to ______ thousands of applicants down to just two hundred places.
Reducing thousands to two hundred shows the blank means to sift out all but the best.
se: Editors must ______ the useful details from the mass of rumor that floods in after a disaster.
sift
Both 'winnow' and 'sift' mean to separate what is valuable from what is not.

m: a clever and funny remark
x: Dinner with my aunt always comes with a steady supply of witticisms about the neighbors.
His witticism about the broken coffee machine eased the tension in the meeting.
The professor peppered her lecture on thermodynamics with witticisms that kept students awake.
The columnist is famous for witticisms that skewer politicians of every party.
She tried to hide her nervousness behind a quick witticism, but her hands were shaking.
tc: Everyone expected a dull speech, but the retiring judge opened with the sharpest ______ anyone had heard all year, and the whole hall burst out laughing.
The contrast with 'a dull speech' and the laughter show the blank is a clever, funny remark.
se: His best ______ of the evening, about the host's legendary cooking disasters, drew applause from every table.
quip
Both 'witticism' and 'quip' mean a short, clever, amusing remark.

m: to argue or quarrel noisily or at length
x: My brother and I wrangled for an hour over who would get the window seat.
Department heads wrangled over the budget until the meeting ran well past six.
Scholars have wrangled for decades about who actually wrote the play.
Lawmakers continue to wrangle over the details of the new climate bill.
They wrangled so often about money that they eventually saw a counselor.
tc: Instead of reaching a quick agreement, the two sides continued to ______ over every clause for months.
'Instead of reaching a quick agreement' and 'for months' show the blank means to argue at length.
se: The heirs began to ______ over the house even before the funeral was over.
quarrel
Both 'wrangle' and 'quarrel' mean to argue angrily about something.

m: to cause or inflict a large amount of damage or harm
x: Our new puppy managed to wreak havoc on the living room in just ten minutes.
A single software bug wreaked chaos on the company's payroll system.
Invasive species can wreak serious damage on fragile island ecosystems.
The cyclone wreaked destruction across the coastal districts of southern Bangladesh last May.
He swore to wreak revenge on the friend who had betrayed him.
tc: Forecasters warned that the storm could ______ havoc on coastal towns, so thousands of people were evacuated.
The warning and the evacuation show the storm was expected to cause great damage.
se: Unchecked inflation can ______ serious damage on the savings of ordinary families.
inflict
Both 'wreak' and 'inflict' mean to cause harm, and both pair naturally with 'damage on'.

m: great energy or enthusiasm in pursuit of a cause or goal
x: She cleaned the whole flat with unusual zeal before her parents arrived.
The new recruit's zeal impressed everyone, though he sometimes worked too fast to be careful.
His zeal for mathematics led him to spend weekends solving olympiad problems.
Reformers pursued the anti-corruption campaign with almost religious zeal, refusing every compromise.
His early zeal for the relationship faded once the long-distance calls became a chore.
tc: Far from showing the ______ of a true believer, the new volunteer seemed bored and kept checking his phone.
'Far from' contrasts the blank with boredom, so it must mean intense enthusiasm.
se: The young activists campaigned with such ______ that even their opponents admired their dedication.
fervor
Both 'zeal' and 'fervor' mean intense, passionate enthusiasm for a cause.

m: to be next to or share a boundary with something
x: Our garden abuts a busy road, so we planted a hedge to block the noise.
The new office tower abuts the old train station, which makes the commute easy for staff.
The university's research park abuts a protected wetland, which limits further expansion.
Farmers whose land abuts the national park often clash with wildlife officials.
Their flats abut each other, so the two sisters see each other almost every day.
tc: Because the two properties ______ each other with no fence in between, the neighbors often argue about where one garden ends.
'With no fence in between' and the dispute over where one garden ends show the properties share a boundary.
se: The school playground will ______ the new highway, which worries many parents.
adjoin
Both 'abut' and 'adjoin' mean to lie directly next to something.

m: to accumulate or increase gradually over time, especially as a payment or benefit
x: If you don't pay your credit card bill on time, interest will accrue every single day.
Employees accrue two days of paid leave for each month they work.
Benefits accrue slowly to students who read a little every day rather than cramming.
Economists warn that the costs of climate inaction will continue to accrue for decades.
Over years of small kindnesses, trust accrued between the two families.
tc: Because she never paid the parking fines, penalties continued to ______ until she owed more than the car was worth.
'Continued to' and owing more than the car's value show the penalties kept building up.
se: Unpaid interest will ______ on the loan until the full balance is cleared.
accumulate
Both 'accrue' and 'accumulate' mean to build up gradually over time.

m: the highest point of achievement, success, or excellence; the peak
x: For my mother, a perfectly cooked pot of biryani is the acme of hospitality.
Winning the industry award was the acme of her career in advertising.
Many scholars regard this symphony as the acme of the composer's late style.
At the acme of its power, the empire stretched from the Mediterranean to the Indus.
Looking back, he realized that their first year together had been the acme of his happiness.
tc: After years of mediocre reviews, the restaurant finally reached the ______ of its fame when it won three national awards in one year.
The contrast with 'years of mediocre reviews' and winning three awards point to the highest point.
se: Critics agree that her third novel marks the ______ of her literary achievement.
pinnacle
Both 'acme' and 'pinnacle' mean the highest point of achievement.

m: to declare someone officially not guilty of a criminal charge
x: My cousin was relieved when the traffic court acquitted him of reckless driving.
The company's lawyers expect the jury to acquit the manager of all fraud charges.
In our law class, we studied why juries sometimes acquit defendants despite strong evidence.
After a two-year trial, the court acquitted the journalist of defamation.
Even after the jury acquitted her, some old friends never spoke to her again.
tc: Because the prosecution's key witness admitted she had lied, the jury had little choice but to ______ the defendant.
Once the key witness is shown to have lied, the case collapses, so the jury must find the defendant not guilty.
se: New DNA evidence led the appeals court to ______ the man who had spent ten years in prison.
exonerate
Both 'acquit' and 'exonerate' mean to officially clear someone of guilt.

m: to cite or offer something as evidence or proof in an argument
x: When I asked why we needed a new car, my husband adduced the rising cost of repairs.
The analyst adduced three years of sales data to support her proposal.
Students must adduce evidence from primary sources rather than relying on opinion.
The prosecution adduced phone records that placed the suspect near the scene.
He adduced countless reasons for missing her birthday, but none of them convinced her.
tc: Since the reviewer could not ______ a single example to support his claim of plagiarism, the editors dismissed it.
'To support his claim' shows the blank means to offer something as evidence.
se: In her essay, she was careful to ______ statistics from several independent studies to back up her thesis.
cite
Both 'adduce' and 'cite' mean to put forward facts as evidence for an argument.

m: to make a formal judgment or decision about a dispute or contest
x: My mother usually has to adjudicate when my brothers fight over the television remote.
An independent panel will adjudicate complaints about unfair hiring practices.
Three senior professors were asked to adjudicate the national debate competition.
The international court will adjudicate the border dispute between the two countries.
I refuse to adjudicate every argument between my two best friends.
tc: Because neither side trusted the other, they asked a retired judge to ______ the dispute impartially.
Calling in a retired judge to act impartially shows the blank means to formally decide the dispute.
se: A special tribunal was set up to ______ claims from workers injured in the factory fire.
judge
Both 'adjudicate' and 'judge' mean to examine claims and make a formal decision on them.

m: an opponent or enemy in a contest, conflict, or dispute
x: My little sister is a fierce adversary at carrom, and she rarely loses.
In negotiations, try to treat the other company as a partner rather than an adversary.
The two physicists were bitter adversaries but cited each other's work constantly.
Former political adversaries joined forces to pass the flood-relief bill.
After the divorce, they stopped being adversaries and became something like friends.
tc: Though she had once been his fiercest ______ on the debate team, she became his closest ally in law school.
'Though' contrasts the blank with 'closest ally', so it must mean opponent.
se: The champion respected her ______, knowing she had trained just as hard for the final.
opponent
Both 'adversary' and 'opponent' mean the person she competes against.

m: filled with horror or shock
x: I was aghast when I saw how much the plumber charged for a ten-minute repair.
Staff were aghast to learn that the bonus scheme had been cancelled without warning.
Parents were aghast at the exam results after the board changed the marking scheme.
Scientists looked on aghast as satellite images revealed the scale of the deforestation.
She stood aghast in the doorway, unable to believe what her boyfriend had just said.
tc: Expecting a modest bill, the tourists were ______ when the waiter charged them nearly a month's wages for one lunch.
The gap between 'a modest bill' and a month's wages shows the tourists were shocked.
se: Residents were ______ at the council's plan to cut down the city's oldest trees.
appalled
Both 'aghast' and 'appalled' mean shocked and horrified.

m: to make someone feel isolated, unfriendly, or no longer supportive

The party risks alienating rural voters with its latest proposal on fuel taxes.

tc: Rather than winning over new customers, the rude advertising campaign managed to ______ even loyal ones.

se: Raising prices yet again could ______ the company's oldest and most loyal customers.
antagonize
Both 'alienate' and 'antagonize' mean to turn customers against the company.

m: loyalty or commitment to a person, group, country, or cause

Employees' allegiance shifted to the new CEO after she raised everyone's salary.
Historians debate whether the soldiers' allegiance was to the king or to the nation.
New citizens take an oath of allegiance at a formal ceremony.
Torn between her parents during the divorce, she refused to declare allegiance to either.
tc: The defector's sudden switch of ______ shocked his former comrades, who had considered him utterly loyal.
'Defector' and 'considered him utterly loyal' show the blank means loyalty.
se: Voters in the region have shown unwavering ______ to the same party for three generations.
loyalty
Both 'allegiance' and 'loyalty' mean faithful support for the party.

m: a story, poem, or picture whose characters and events symbolize a deeper moral or political meaning

In literature class, we read Animal Farm as an allegory of the Russian Revolution.
Some critics see the film as an allegory for climate change and human denial.
He wrote her a short allegory about two birds building a nest together, and she understood.
tc: Though it appears to be a simple tale about animals on a farm, the book works on another level as political ______, with each creature representing a real historical figure.
'Works on another level' and each creature 'representing' a real figure define a symbolic story.

fable
Both 'allegory' and 'fable' mean a symbolic story that teaches a moral lesson.

m: to give or assign a share of something, such as time, money, or space

Candidates are allotted three hours to complete the written section of the exam.

In our marriage, we allot Sundays to family, with no phones at the table.

Dividing one hour into five-minute shares shows the blank means to assign portions.
se: The committee will ______ the remaining tickets to students who applied earliest.
allocate
Both 'allot' and 'allocate' mean to distribute shares to particular people.

m: to refer to something indirectly or briefly
x: My mother kept alluding to my cousin's wedding, hinting that I should get married too.
In his email, the manager alluded to possible layoffs without giving any details.
The poem alludes to Greek mythology in nearly every stanza.
The minister alluded to difficult decisions ahead, which many read as a sign of tax increases.
She never mentioned her ex by name, but she often alluded to a painful past.
tc: Never willing to name the scandal directly, the speaker would only ______ to 'recent unfortunate events.'
'Never willing to name the scandal directly' shows the blank means to mention indirectly.
se: The author chose to ______ to the family's tragedy only in passing, never describing it in full.
refer
Both 'allude' and 'refer' work with 'to ... only in passing' to mean mention briefly.

m: relating to or expressing romantic or sexual love
x: My aunt loves gossiping about the amatory adventures of the neighbors' grown-up children.
Office gossip about the director's amatory life distracted everyone from the quarterly report.
The seminar examined amatory poetry from medieval Persia to Elizabethan England.
The tabloid specializes in the amatory scandals of film stars and athletes.
He sent her an amatory letter so full of flowery phrases that she burst out laughing.
tc: Although the poet wrote mostly about war and politics, his early notebooks are filled with ______ verses addressed to a young woman he adored.
Verses 'addressed to a young woman he adored', contrasted with war and politics, must be about love.
se: Scholars have catalogued hundreds of ______ letters exchanged between the composer and his secret lover.
amorous
Both 'amatory' and 'amorous' describe letters expressing romantic love.

m: a word or phrase formed by rearranging the letters of another word or phrase
x: My daughter loves puzzles and quickly saw that 'listen' is an anagram of 'silent.'
Our team-building quiz included anagrams of colleagues' names, which caused a lot of laughter.

The setter hid an anagram of the city's name in the newspaper's Saturday crossword.
He proposed to her with an anagram that rearranged into 'Will you marry me?'
tc: Puzzle fans love the word 'dormitory' because its letters can be rearranged to form 'dirty room'; few English words have such a fitting ______.
'Its letters can be rearranged to form' defines a word made by reordering letters.
se: The word 'vile' is a simple ______ of 'evil,' formed by moving just one letter.
rearrangement
Both 'anagram' and 'rearrangement' describe a word made by reordering another word's letters.

m: a medicine that relieves pain without causing loss of consciousness
x: I always keep a mild analgesic in my bag in case a headache strikes during class.
Workers on the night shift reported taking analgesics regularly for back pain.
The study compared the effectiveness of two common analgesics after dental surgery.
Overuse of strong analgesics has become a serious public health problem in several countries.
After the accident, she relied on analgesics but found her family's support even more healing.
tc: The doctor prescribed a strong ______ to dull the pain from the patient's broken leg.
'To dull the pain' defines a pain-relieving medicine.
se: Aspirin, the world's most widely used ______, was first derived from willow bark.
painkiller
Both 'analgesic' and 'painkiller' mean a drug that relieves pain.

m: to add explanatory notes or comments to a text or diagram
x: I like to annotate recipes with my own changes so I remember them next time.
Please annotate the draft contract with your questions before Friday's meeting.
Our literature professor asked us to annotate every poem we read in the margins.
Researchers annotated thousands of satellite images to train the flood-detection model.
She found an old novel her late father had annotated, and reading his notes made her cry.
tc: To help later readers understand the obscure references, the editor decided to ______ the poem with detailed explanatory notes.
Adding 'explanatory notes' to help readers understand defines the act of annotating.
se: Medieval monks would often ______ difficult manuscripts, explaining obscure words in the margins.
gloss
Both 'annotate' and 'gloss' mean to add explanatory notes to a text.

m: showing no interest, enthusiasm, or concern
x: My teenage nephew is completely apathetic about anything that doesn't involve his phone.
Staff have grown apathetic since management ignored their last three suggestions.
Many students become apathetic when lectures feel irrelevant to their future careers.
Turnout was low because young voters felt apathetic about both candidates.
She wanted a fight, but his apathetic shrug hurt her more than any angry words.
tc: Organizers expected an eager crowd, but the audience was so ______ that many left before the speeches even began.
'But' contrasts the blank with 'eager', and leaving early shows a lack of interest.
se: Years of broken promises have left many citizens ______ about politics.
indifferent
Both 'apathetic' and 'indifferent' mean having no interest or concern.

m: a name or title given to a person, place, or thing
x: Our neighbor earned the appellation 'the Mango King' because of the huge tree in his yard.
In the office, she carries the unofficial appellation of 'Excel Queen.'
Botanists sometimes argue over the correct appellation for a newly discovered species.
Wines from the region may use the protected appellation only if they meet strict rules.
He hated the childish appellation his ex had given him, but secretly missed hearing it.
tc: Because he was always the first to arrive and the last to leave, the young clerk earned the ______ 'the Night Owl' from his coworkers.
The quoted nickname 'the Night Owl' that he 'earned' shows the blank means a name or title.
se: The city's old ______, 'the Venice of the East,' still appears in tourist brochures.
epithet
Both 'appellation' and 'epithet' mean a descriptive name given to the city.

m: to add something to the end of a written document or text
x: Remember to append your phone number to the bottom of the email.
Please append the signed invoices to the monthly expense report.
Authors should append a full list of references to the end of their thesis.
The council appended a note to the report warning that the figures were provisional.
She appended a short, heartfelt message to the formal wedding invitation.
tc: Rather than rewrite the whole agreement, the lawyers decided simply to ______ a new clause at the end.
'Rather than rewrite' and 'at the end' show the blank means to add on at the end.
se: Applicants must ______ copies of their certificates to the online form before submitting it.
attach
Both 'append' and 'attach' mean to add documents to the form.

m: an accessory or object associated with a particular activity, role, or way of life
x: My father bought a fishing rod, a tackle box, and every other appurtenance of his new hobby.

The museum displays the appurtenances of a nineteenth-century scholar's study, from quill pens to brass globes.
Critics argue that luxury watches have become appurtenances of power for politicians and executives.
Even after the divorce, she kept the small appurtenances of their life together: mugs, photos, and a worn blanket.
tc: Though he rarely took pictures, he had bought every ______ of the professional photographer: tripods, filters, and light meters.
The list of tripods, filters and light meters shows the blank means an accessory belonging to that role.
se: For that family, a grand piano in the living room was the most important ______ of respectability.
accessory
Both 'appurtenance' and 'accessory' mean an object that goes with a certain status.

m: to settle a dispute as an impartial judge chosen by both sides
x: When my sister and I fought over the car, our grandfather was called in to arbitrate.
An independent expert will arbitrate the pay dispute between the union and management.
The university asked a senior professor to arbitrate between two researchers claiming the same discovery.
A neutral country offered to arbitrate the fishing dispute before it escalated.
I refuse to arbitrate your arguments anymore; you two need to talk directly.
tc: Since both companies distrusted the courts, they agreed to let a neutral panel ______ their disagreement.
A 'neutral panel' chosen instead of the courts points to settling the dispute impartially.
se: The league appointed a retired judge to ______ the contract dispute between the club and its star player.
adjudicate
Both 'arbitrate' and 'adjudicate' mean to judge and settle the dispute formally.

m: the special jargon or slang used by a particular group
x: My younger cousins speak an argot of gaming terms that I can barely follow.
New employees take months to learn the argot of the trading floor.
Medical students quickly pick up the argot of the hospital wards.
The journalist spent a year learning the argot of street gangs for her investigation.
Couples often develop a private argot of nicknames and inside jokes.
tc: Outsiders struggle to follow conversations among surfers, whose ______ is full of words like 'gnarly' and 'barrel.'
Outsiders struggling with special words like 'gnarly' indicates a group's private slang.
se: The novel captures the ______ of 1920s jazz musicians, full of expressions that have since disappeared.
lingo
Both 'argot' and 'lingo' mean the special vocabulary of a particular group.

m: extremely dry from lack of rain; figuratively, dull and lacking interest or imagination
x: After months without rain, the vegetable patch behind our house was arid and cracked.
The meeting was an arid hour of budget figures that nobody in the room cared about.
Students complained that the textbook's arid prose made a fascinating subject seem dull.
Farmers in arid regions of the country are experimenting with drought-resistant crops.
Their conversations had become arid and polite, with none of the old warmth.
tc: Unlike the lush, rain-soaked coast, the interior of the country is ______, receiving barely ten centimeters of rain a year.
The contrast with 'lush, rain-soaked' and the tiny rainfall show the blank means extremely dry.
se: The professor's lectures were so ______ that even the most dedicated students struggled to stay awake.
dull
Both 'arid' and 'dull' describe lectures lacking any interest.

m: free from germs or contamination; figuratively, lacking warmth or feeling
x: We boiled the baby's bottles every morning to keep them aseptic.
The new packaging line uses aseptic techniques to keep juice fresh without preservatives.
Lab students must learn aseptic technique before they handle bacterial cultures.
Hospitals that enforce strict aseptic procedures report far fewer surgical infections.
Their once passionate letters had become aseptic, as if they were written by strangers.
tc: Because even a few bacteria could ruin the experiment, all samples were handled under strictly ______ conditions.
The fear that 'even a few bacteria' could ruin the work shows the conditions must be germ-free.
se: Surgical instruments must be kept ______ to prevent infections during operations.
sterile
Both 'aseptic' and 'sterile' mean free from germs.

m: extremely stupid or foolish
x: It was an asinine idea to drive to the airport in Dhaka's rush hour with only thirty minutes to spare.
Management's asinine new rule requires staff to request permission before using the stapler.
The reviewer dismissed the paper's central argument as asinine and unsupported by evidence.
Commentators called the proposal to ban umbrellas in public parks utterly asinine.
I regret the asinine things I said to her when I was jealous.
tc: Rather than offering a sensible solution, the committee came up with the ______ plan of painting the potholes so drivers could see them.
'Rather than ... sensible' signals a contrast, so the blank means extremely foolish.
se: Everyone laughed at his ______ suggestion that we cancel the trip because of a bad forecast for a different city.
foolish
Both 'asinine' and 'foolish' describe a stupid, senseless suggestion.

m: harshness or sharpness of tone or manner
x: When I asked my landlord about the leaking roof, he replied with obvious asperity.
The manager's asperity in meetings made junior staff afraid to speak.
The reviewer criticized the book with an asperity that surprised even its harshest detractors.
Diplomats noted the unusual asperity of the minister's remarks about the trade deal.
She spoke with such asperity that he realized she was still angry about the forgotten anniversary.
tc: Though she usually spoke gently to her students, there was unmistakable ______ in her voice when she found the cheating notes.
'Though she usually spoke gently' sets up a contrast, so the blank means harshness.
se: His reply to the complaint was written with such ______ that the customer felt insulted.
harshness
Both 'asperity' and 'harshness' describe a sharp, unkind tone.

m: to test or analyze something to determine its quality, purity, or composition
x: Before buying the gold necklace, my mother had a jeweler assay its purity.
The procurement team assayed each supplier's samples before signing any contracts.
Chemistry students assayed the water samples for lead and arsenic.
Geologists will assay the ore to see whether the mine is worth reopening.
Before committing to the relationship, she quietly assayed his character over many months.
tc: Before paying a fortune for the old coins, the collector hired an expert to ______ their silver content.
Checking 'their silver content' before paying shows the blank means to test or analyze.
se: Inspectors will ______ the samples to determine whether the medicine contains the correct dose.
analyze
Both 'assay' and 'analyze' mean to test the samples to find their composition.

m: sharp, severe, and harshly critical in manner or style
x: My aunt's astringent comments about my cooking were hard to swallow at dinner.
The editor's astringent feedback stung, but it made my report much sharper.
Her astringent review of the conference papers became the talk of the department.
The columnist is known for astringent critiques of government spending.
He hid his warm heart behind an astringent wit that kept most people at a distance.
tc: Fans expecting gentle praise were stung by the critic's ______ review, which called the album lazy and derivative.
The contrast with 'gentle praise' and calling the album 'lazy and derivative' show the review was harshly critical.
se: Her ______ remarks about the proposal left the young designer close to tears.
caustic
Both 'astringent' and 'caustic' describe sharply critical, hurtful remarks.

m: relating to the stars or outer space
x: Ancient astronomers kept careful records of astral movements to predict the changing seasons.
The planetarium's astral display drew more visitors to the company's open day than any of the engineering exhibits.
In our first-year physics course, we spent a week studying astral bodies far beyond our solar system.
Scientists announced that the new telescope had captured unusually clear images of astral dust clouds near the galactic center.
Lying on the roof during a power cut in Dhaka, we gazed at an astral glow the city haze usually hides.
tc: Unlike terrestrial phenomena, which we can study up close, ______ events must be observed from millions of miles away.
'Unlike terrestrial phenomena' signals a contrast, so the blank must mean relating to the stars.
se: Sailors once relied on ______ navigation, using the positions of the stars to find their way across the ocean.
celestial
Both 'astral' and 'celestial' mean relating to the stars, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: the return of a trait or behavior typical of distant ancestors; a reversion to an earlier type
x: My grandfather called my love of farming an atavism, since no one in the family had worked the land for three generations.
Some colleagues see the manager's insistence on paper memos as an atavism in an otherwise digital office.
The biology lecturer explained that hind-leg bones occasionally found in whales are a classic example of atavism.
Commentators described the rise of tribal politics as a dangerous atavism in a supposedly modern society.
She worried that her sudden fierce jealousy was some kind of atavism inherited from her grandmother.
tc: Far from being a modern innovation, the senator's rhetoric was a kind of ______, a throwback to the clan loyalties of centuries past.
'A throwback to the clan loyalties of centuries past' restates the blank, which must mean a reversion to an ancestral type.
se: Historians regarded the brief revival of duelling among young aristocrats as a curious ______, not a new fashion.
throwback
Both 'atavism' and 'throwback' mean a return to the ways of an earlier age.

m: gradual reduction in strength or numbers caused by sustained pressure or loss
x: Our book club has shrunk through simple attrition, as members move away and nobody new joins.
Rather than lay people off, the company plans to cut costs through natural attrition.
The graduate program has a high attrition rate, with nearly a third of students leaving before their final year.
The long war of attrition exhausted both armies and left the border towns in ruins.
Years of small arguments caused a slow attrition of trust between the two brothers.
tc: The team never lost a big match, but steady ______ from injuries over the season left it too weak to win the league.
'Steady' and 'from injuries' point to a gradual wearing down of strength.
se: Constant criticism from the board led to a gradual ______ of the manager's authority.
erosion
Both 'attrition' and 'erosion' describe a slow wearing away, giving the same meaning.

m: not representative of a type, group, or usual pattern
x: It's atypical for my neighbor to leave his car in the street, so I knocked to check he was all right.
This month's surge in sales is atypical, so we shouldn't build next year's budget around it.
The researchers excluded several atypical results that they suspected came from faulty equipment.
Doctors noticed atypical symptoms in a few patients, prompting a wider investigation into the virus.
Such a quiet, sulky mood was atypical of my sister, who usually chats nonstop at dinner.
tc: Most of the region's summers are hot and dry, so last year's cool, rainy season was decidedly ______.
'Most... are hot and dry' sets up a contrast with the cool, rainy season, so the blank must mean unusual.
se: His rude reply was ______ of him; he is usually the most polite person in the office.
uncharacteristic
Both 'atypical of' and 'uncharacteristic of' mean not in keeping with his usual behavior.

m: a sign or omen of what will happen in the future
x: My mother took the rainbow on our wedding morning as a happy augury for the marriage.
Investors read the strong first-quarter results as an augury of a profitable year ahead.
The history seminar examined how Roman priests practised augury by watching the flight of birds.
Many analysts saw the low voter turnout as a grim augury for the country's young democracy.
He took her quick smile across the room as an augury that she might finally forgive him.
tc: Superstitious villagers treated every eclipse as a dark ______, a sign from the heavens of troubles to come.
'A sign from the heavens of troubles to come' defines the blank as an omen.
se: The early arrival of the monsoon was seen as a good ______ for this year's rice harvest.
omen
Both 'augury' and 'omen' mean a sign of what is to come.

m: demanding strict obedience to authority at the expense of personal freedom
x: My uncle's authoritarian style at home meant nobody dared to question his decisions at dinner.
Staff morale collapsed under the new director's authoritarian approach to even the smallest decisions.
The political science course compares authoritarian regimes with democracies across several continents.
Critics warned that the emergency law could push the country toward authoritarian rule.
She left him after realizing how authoritarian he became whenever she made plans of her own.
tc: Far from welcoming debate, the headmaster ran the school in ______ fashion, punishing any student who questioned his rules.
'Far from welcoming debate' and 'punishing any student who questioned' show the blank means demanding strict obedience.
se: The general's ______ government banned opposition parties and jailed journalists.
dictatorial
Both 'authoritarian' and 'dictatorial' describe rule that crushes freedom and demands obedience.

m: new and experimental, especially in art, music, or ideas
x: My cousin's avant-garde haircut drew a lot of stares at the family wedding.
The agency won the account with an avant-garde campaign that broke every rule of traditional advertising.
Our film studies professor screened several avant-garde shorts that had no plot at all.
The city's new museum is devoted entirely to avant-garde art from the last fifty years.
She loved his avant-garde taste in music, even if she couldn't always follow it.
tc: Audiences used to traditional symphonies were baffled by the composer's ______ work, which used typewriters and car horns as instruments.
The contrast with 'traditional symphonies' and the strange instruments show the blank means radically experimental.
se: The gallery is known for showing ______ installations that challenge ideas about what art can be.
experimental
Both 'avant-garde' and 'experimental' describe new, boundary-pushing work.

m: kind, friendly, and helpful toward a younger person, like an uncle
x: Our landlord has an avuncular manner, always asking about our exams and offering us mangoes from his tree.
The senior engineer took an avuncular interest in the new hires and often helped them after hours.
Students loved the old professor's avuncular warmth, which made his difficult lectures feel less intimidating.
The retired newsreader was famous for an avuncular voice that made even bad news sound reassuring.
He gave me an avuncular pat on the shoulder and told me not to worry about the breakup.
tc: Although he was strict in the courtroom, the judge was warm and ______ with the young interns, treating them like his own nephews.
'Warm' and 'treating them like his own nephews' point to uncle-like kindness.
se: With his ______ smile and gentle advice, the old coach was like a second father to the players.
kindly
Both 'avuncular' and 'kindly' describe a warm, caring manner toward younger people.

m: dealing with sex in a humorous but coarse way
x: My aunt blushed when the wedding band started singing a bawdy folk song.
HR reminded everyone that bawdy jokes have no place in the office group chat.
In our literature class, we discussed why Chaucer included so many bawdy tales in his collection.
The comedy club was criticized for advertising its bawdy late-night shows near a primary school.
Their friendship survived years of bawdy teasing about each other's love lives.
tc: The sailors' songs were far too ______ for the children's choir, full of crude jokes about women and drinking.
'Crude jokes about women and drinking' explains why the songs are humorously indecent.
se: The play's ______ humor delighted some audience members but offended others who preferred cleaner comedy.
ribald
Both 'bawdy' and 'ribald' mean coarsely humorous about sex, matching the contrast with 'cleaner comedy'.

m: to resent or envy someone for having something; to give or allow reluctantly
x: I don't begrudge my neighbors their new car; they've worked hard for it.
Few colleagues begrudged her the promotion, since she had carried the team all year.
Some students begrudge every hour spent in the library, but it pays off at exam time.
Taxpayers rarely begrudge money spent on hospitals, but they question costly government receptions.
He never begrudged his younger brother the extra attention their parents gave him after the accident.
tc: She was so generous that she would never ______ a friend success, even when that friend won the prize she had wanted.
'So generous' and 'never' show the blank means to resent another person's good fortune.
se: I don't ______ the time I spend helping my parents; it's the least I can do.
resent
Both 'begrudge' and 'resent' mean to feel unwilling or bitter about giving something.

m: to explain or discuss something for too long or in excessive detail
x: I won't belabor the point, but please remember to lock the gate when you leave.
The presenter belabored minor details while skipping the budget figures everyone wanted to see.
My thesis advisor warned me not to belabor the literature review at the expense of my own findings.
Commentators belabored the minister's spelling mistake while ignoring the policy itself.
She kept belaboring his forgotten birthday until he finally apologized a third time.
tc: The audience grew restless as the speaker continued to ______ a point that everyone had understood ten minutes earlier.
'Everyone had understood ten minutes earlier' shows the blank means to dwell on something excessively.
se: There is no need to ______ the point; we all agree the deadline must move.
labor
Both 'belabor the point' and 'labor the point' mean to keep going over something already clear.

m: to cause constant trouble or difficulty for; to besiege
x: Constant calls from telemarketers beleaguer my elderly parents every evening at dinnertime.
Supply problems continue to beleaguer the factory, delaying orders for months.
Financial worries beleaguered many international students during their first semester abroad.

Doubts beleaguered him the night before he proposed, though he never told her.
tc: Although new problems continued to ______ the project, the team refused to give up and finally delivered on time.
'Although... refused to give up' implies the blank means to beset with troubles.
se: Rising debts and falling sales continue to ______ the struggling airline.
plague
Both 'beleaguer' and 'plague' mean to trouble persistently.

m: in a state of ignorance or intellectual darkness
x: My grandmother thought it benighted that the village still refused to send girls to school.
The consultant dismissed the old filing system as a benighted relic of the pre-computer age.
Early travel writers often described distant peoples as benighted, revealing more about their own prejudices.
The editorial condemned the benighted policy of banning books from public libraries.

tc: Once widely accepted, the ______ belief that illness came from bad smells gave way to an enlightened understanding of germs.
The contrast with 'an enlightened understanding' shows the blank means ignorant.
se: The novel is set in a remote, ______ town where superstition still governs every decision.
unenlightened
Both 'benighted' and 'unenlightened' mean ignorant and backward.

m: to leave property to someone in a will; to pass something on to later generations
x: My grandfather bequeathed his old fountain pen to me, along with a note about using it wisely.

She wanted to bequeath her children something more valuable than money: a love of learning.
tc: Having no children of his own, the wealthy farmer decided to ______ his land to the village school in his will.
'In his will' points to leaving property after death.
se: In her will, she chose to ______ her house to her favorite niece.
leave
Both 'bequeath' and 'leave' mean to give property to someone through a will.

m: out of control with anger or excitement; wild
x: The neighbor's dog goes berserk every time the postman opens the gate.

tc: Normally a gentle animal, the horse went ______ when the fireworks exploded, kicking down its stable door.
'Normally a gentle animal' contrasts with kicking down the door, so the blank means wildly out of control.
se: The crowd went ______ when the band finally walked onto the stage.
wild
Both 'go berserk' and 'go wild' mean to become uncontrollably excited.

He was utterly besotted with her from the moment they met at a friend's wedding.

infatuated
Both 'besotted with' and 'infatuated with' mean foolishly in love with.

irritable

bully
Both 'bludgeon into' and 'bully into' mean to force someone by intimidation.

m: self-assertive in a rude, noisy, or overconfident way

cocky

m: to raise a sensitive or difficult subject for discussion

'Hesitated' and 'delicate topic' show the blank means to bring up a sensitive subject.

raise
Both 'broach' and 'raise' mean to bring a subject up for discussion.

m: irritatingly self-assertive and full of one's own importance

The newspaper mocked a bumptious official who demanded a police escort to open a public toilet.
Her friends found him bumptious at first, but she knew he was just nervous in company.

se: His ______ manner, always boasting about his achievements, made him unpopular at the club.
conceited
Both 'bumptious' and 'conceited' describe someone irritatingly full of himself.

m: large, strong, and heavily built

brawny
Both 'burly' and 'brawny' mean big and muscular.

m: very pale, thin, or bony, like a corpse

emaciated
Both 'cadaverous' and 'emaciated' describe people who are dangerously thin and wasted.

m: shrewd and careful, especially in money or business matters

Canny investors sold their shares just before the market collapsed.
He was canny enough not to mention his ex-girlfriend on their first date.
tc: Unlike his ______ partner, who checked every contract twice, Ahmed signed deals without reading them and lost a fortune.
The contrast with careless Ahmed and 'checked every contract twice' show the blank means shrewd and careful.
se: The ______ shopkeeper stocked up on umbrellas just before the rainy season began.
shrewd
Both 'canny' and 'shrewd' mean clever and careful in business.

m: having a lot of space inside; roomy
x: Her capacious handbag held everything from snacks to a spare umbrella.

Engineers designed the capacious new stadium to hold sixty thousand spectators.

tc: After years in a cramped one-room flat, the family was delighted by the ______ new house with its large rooms and wide hallways.
The contrast with 'cramped' and the 'large rooms' show the blank means roomy.
se: The coat has ______ pockets that can hold a phone, a wallet and a paperback.
roomy
Both 'capacious' and 'roomy' mean having plenty of space inside.

m: to drink alcohol and celebrate in a noisy, lively way
x: Our neighbors carouse every Friday night, and the music rarely stops before two.
After the deal closed, the sales team caroused in a hotel bar until dawn.
Instead of studying, some freshmen carouse their way through the first semester and regret it later.
Police were called after tourists caroused on the beach and damaged several fishing boats.
He used to carouse with his friends every weekend, but fatherhood changed his habits.

'Drinking and singing' until dawn defines the blank as noisy merrymaking.
se: The soldiers loved to ______ in the taverns whenever they were given a weekend's leave.
revel
Both 'carouse' and 'revel' mean to celebrate noisily, usually with drink.

m: a warning or condition that limits or qualifies something
x: You can borrow my car, with one caveat: bring it back with a full tank.

The colon introduces a warning attached to the approval, which defines the blank.
se: The report praised the new policy, with the ______ that its long-term effects remain unknown.
proviso
Both 'caveat' and 'proviso' mean a qualifying condition or warning.

m: loud and clear; strongly urging people to act
x: Her clarion voice carried across the playground, calling the children in for lunch.
The chief executive's memo was a clarion call for every department to cut waste.
The dean's opening speech served as a clarion warning about academic dishonesty.
The climate report issued a clarion call to governments to act before it is too late.
His letter was a clarion declaration of love that left her no room for doubt.
tc: Far from issuing muted suggestions, the activist sent out ______ calls for change that rang out across the country.
'Far from issuing muted suggestions' and 'rang out' show the blank means loud and clear.
se: The trumpet's ______ notes woke the entire camp at dawn.
ringing
Both 'clarion' and 'ringing' describe a loud, clear sound.

m: a split, crack, or narrow opening; a deep division

The merger left a deep cleft between the two management teams that took years to close.
Geology students examined a cleft in the rock where two plates had pulled apart.
Rescuers found the missing climber trapped in a narrow cleft halfway down the cliff.
Their argument over the inheritance opened a cleft between the sisters that never fully healed.
tc: Water seeped into a narrow ______ in the cliff, slowly widening the crack until a huge slab broke away.
'Widening the crack' restates the blank as a split or opening.
se: The lizard disappeared into the narrow ______ in the rock where we could not follow.
crevice
Both 'cleft' and 'crevice' mean a narrow crack or opening.

m: to cooperate secretly with others, especially to cheat or deceive
x: The children colluded to hide the broken vase from their mother.
Two suppliers were caught colluding to fix the prices they charged our company.
The examiners discovered that several students had colluded on the take-home exam.
The investigation found that officials had colluded with smugglers at the border.
She felt betrayed when she learned her friends had colluded with her ex to embarrass her.
tc: The two rival firms appeared to compete fiercely, but in secret they would ______ to keep prices high.
'Appeared to compete' contrasted with 'in secret' shows the blank means to cooperate deceitfully.
se: Investigators believe the two bidders met in secret to ______ against the government on the contract price.
conspire
Both 'collude' and 'conspire' mean to work together secretly for a dishonest purpose.

m: curved inward, like the inside of a bowl
x: She served the soup in shallow concave dishes that kept it warm for longer.
Designers chose a concave screen for the new monitor to reduce glare.
In physics lab, we used a concave mirror to focus sunlight onto a single point.
Engineers gave the stadium roof a concave shape to channel rainwater toward the drains.
She cupped her hands into a concave shape to catch the first raindrops of the monsoon.
tc: Unlike convex lenses, which bulge outward, ______ lenses curve inward and spread light apart.
The contrast with lenses that 'bulge outward' and the phrase 'curve inward' define the blank.
se: The patient's ______ cheeks showed how much weight he had lost.
hollow
Both 'concave' and 'hollow' describe cheeks that curve inward from weight loss.

m: naturally accompanying or associated with something else
x: Moving to a bigger flat brought a concomitant rise in our electricity bills.
The promotion came with concomitant responsibilities that she hadn't expected.
The study found that rising screen time had a concomitant effect on students' sleep.
Rapid urbanization in Dhaka has brought concomitant problems of traffic, pollution and housing shortages.
His growing love for her brought a concomitant fear of one day losing her.
tc: Economic growth often brings ______ costs, such as pollution and congestion, that follow naturally from expansion.
'Follow naturally from expansion' defines the blank as accompanying.
se: War and its ______ hardships forced thousands of families to flee their homes.
attendant
Both 'concomitant' and 'attendant' mean naturally accompanying.

m: to secretly allow or help with wrongdoing; to conspire

Two lab assistants connived to sell copies of the exam papers to students.
The report accused border officials of conniving at the smuggling of fuel.
He suspected his friends had connived with his parents to arrange a meeting with her.
tc: Rather than stopping the fraud, the auditors chose to ______ at it, quietly ignoring the false figures in exchange for bribes.
'Quietly ignoring' wrongdoing for bribes defines the blank.
se: The two clerks began to ______ to steal money from the company's accounts.
conspire
Both 'connive' and 'conspire' mean to plot secretly to do wrong.

m: relationship by blood or common ancestry
x: Family gatherings in our village are huge, since almost everyone shares some degree of consanguinity.

Geneticists study consanguinity to understand why certain inherited diseases cluster in some communities.

tc: Though they had grown up in different countries, DNA tests confirmed their ______, proving they were in fact first cousins.
'Proving they were first cousins' shows the blank means blood relationship.
se: The two families claimed ______ through a shared great-grandfather.
kinship
Both 'consanguinity' and 'kinship' mean a family relationship by blood.

m: the process of coming together or becoming similar

Our seminar explored the convergence of biology and computer science in genetic research.
Scientists noted a convergence of evidence pointing to the same cause of the outbreak.
Their friendship grew from a convergence of interests: cricket, old films and spicy food.
tc: Whereas the two parties' policies had long been far apart, analysts are now struck by the ______ of their positions on taxation.
'Whereas... far apart' signals a contrast, so the blank must mean coming together.
se: The town grew up at the ______ of two rivers, where boats could easily unload goods.
confluence
Both 'convergence' and 'confluence' mean the point where things meet and join.

m: fat; having a large, heavy body
x: The corpulent shopkeeper could barely squeeze between the crowded shelves.
My corpulent boss jokes that the office biscuit tin is his only real weakness.
Our history textbook describes the king as corpulent and too unwell to ride a horse in later life.
Doctors warned that corpulent patients face higher risks of diabetes and heart disease.
He grew corpulent after his wife died, eating alone and rarely leaving the house.
tc: Once lean and athletic, the retired footballer had grown ______ after years of rich food and no exercise.

se: The ______ merchant needed two servants to help him climb into his carriage.
portly
Both 'corpulent' and 'portly' mean heavy and fat.

m: to care for and protect in an overindulgent way; to pamper
x: My grandmother cossets her cat with fresh fish and a velvet cushion by the window.
The company cossets its top clients with free dinners and private airport transfers.

The report claimed that heavy subsidies had cosseted local industries and left them unable to compete.
She was the youngest child, and her parents cosseted her long after she had grown up.
